Exceptions are checked against the fields of each result row, so match on fields the query returns: after stats ... by src, dest, only src, dest and the aggregates exist.

docs.title: Antivirus detections
docs.text:
Eight built-in detections read the Malware data model (see antivirus.md for what each means and what to do). All are on by default and raise findings:

ID Severity Fires when malware-not-removed high A threat was allowed, failed to clean or was restored from quarantine malware-left-clamav high ClamAV found malware and only reported it, so the file is still there malware-detected low A named threat was found (ransomware has its own finding) malware-outbreak high The same threat was found on three or more hosts in a day (not test files, adware or unwanted apps) malware-ransomware critical A threat in the ransomware category was found av-protection-disabled high Protection or tamper protection was turned off av-tamper-blocked medium Tamper protection blocked a change to the antivirus av-exclusion-added medium An antivirus exclusion was added av-definitions-failing low Definitions failed to update twice in a day, or are a week old av-rule-block medium An attack surface reduction or controlled folder access rule blocked something unusual

docs.title: Vulnerability detections
docs.text:
Three built-in detections read the Vulnerabilities data model, which Signalith's own network scans fill (see the Vulnerabilities page). All are on by default, raise findings and add risk to the scanned host. Each raises one finding per host and CVE (or per host, for Telnet) a week: a nightly scan that finds the same vulnerability again raises it again only after seven days.

ID Severity Fires when vuln-known-exploited high A scan found a vulnerability in CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog (known_exploited=true): attackers are using it vuln-critical medium A scan found a critical vulnerability (CVSS 9 or higher) that is not known to be exploited yet vuln-cleartext-remote-login low A scan found Telnet open, which sends passwords in clear text

To see everything a scan found on a host, search datamodel=Vulnerabilities dest=<host>.

docs.title: What a finding contains
docs.text:
The result row, the entities found in it (user, src_user, src, src_host, dest, dest_host, host, process_name, object, member), the detection's severity and ATT&CK techniques, a drilldown search, the asset and identity context of each entity, and an urgency that combines severity with that context. For stats and top detections the drilldown is the detection's filter plus the row's group-by values, so View contributing events shows exactly the events behind that row.

Findings move through new, in_progress, pending, resolved and closed, with an owner, a disposition (true_positive, benign_true_positive, false_positive, undetermined), comments, and a history of every change. They are stored in the OpenSearch index <index_prefix>_findings, which event searches never include.

docs.title: Content packs
docs.text:
Content packs are rule sets from other open source projects, shipped unchanged inside Signalith and converted when it starts. Every pack detection is off until an admin turns it on.

SigmaHQ community rules (internal/detect/packs/sigmahq) holds 2,122 rules from SigmaHQ, pinned to one commit: 1,968 Windows rules for these Sysmon, Security, PowerShell, System and Defender log sources, and 154 Linux rules (see Linux endpoints and the Linux audit log):

Sigma log source Windows events Data model process_creation Sysmon 1, Security 4688 Endpoint network_connection Sysmon 3 Network_Traffic process_access, create_remote_thread Sysmon 10, 8 Endpoint image_load, driver_load Sysmon 7, 6 Image_Load file_event, file_delete Sysmon 11; 23 and 26 Filesystem registry_add, registry_delete, registry_set, registry_event Sysmon 12; 12; 13; 12, 13 and 14 Registry dns_query Sysmon 22 Network_Resolution pipe_created Sysmon 17 and 18 (named pipe created or connected to) Endpoint create_stream_hash Sysmon 15 (alternate data stream written, such as a download's Zone.Identifier) Filesystem raw_access_thread Sysmon 9 (a drive read directly; Device is device) Endpoint ps_script PowerShell 4104 Script service: system System 7045 (service installed) Change service: windefend Microsoft Defender Antivirus events (threats, attack surface reduction blocks, protection turned off, settings changed; Path is file_path, ProcessName process_path, NewValue new_value, SourceName detection_source, a 5013's Value setting) Malware service: security The Security log events in the next table See the next table

A Security log rule names its event's own fields (TargetUserName, LogonType, ServiceFileName, ObjectName), so each one converts for the one Security event it is about, or for events that carry the same data: a handle request and the access made with it (4656 and 4663), or a scheduled task deleted or disabled (4699 and 4701). Rules about other Security events, or other sets of events, are left out. Event IDs of Windows 2000 and XP (below 1000, such as 517 for the log cleared) that a rule names beside current ones are ignored, since those systems' events never reach Signalith. Windows logs each event only with its audit policy setting on:

Security events Data model Audit policy setting 4624, 4625 (logon, failed logon), 4648 (logon with explicit credentials) Authentication Audit Logon 4768, 4769 (Kerberos tickets, on domain controllers) Authentication Audit Kerberos Authentication Service, Audit Kerberos Service Ticket Operations 4697 (service installed) Change Audit Security System Extension 4698, 4699, 4701, 4702 (scheduled task created, deleted, disabled, updated) Change Audit Other Object Access Events 4720, 4738 (user account created or changed), 4732 (member added to a local group), 4728, 4729 (member added to or removed from a global group), 4730 (global group deleted) Change Audit User Account Management, Audit Security Group Management 1102 (Security log cleared) Change Always logged 4719 (audit policy changed) Change Audit Audit Policy Change 4706 (domain trust created), 4794 (DSRM password set) Change Audit Authentication Policy Change, Audit User Account Management 4656 (handle requested), 4663 (object access) Filesystem for a file, Registry for a key Audit Handle Manipulation, Audit File System or Audit Registry 4661 (handle to a SAM or directory object) none (searched in every model) Audit SAM 4657 (registry value modified) Registry Audit Registry 5145 (network share access) Filesystem Audit Detailed File Share 5140 (network share accessed, once per session) Filesystem Audit File Share 5136 (directory object changed), 4662 (operation on a directory object) Change Audit Directory Service Changes, Audit Directory Service Access (domain controllers) 5156, 5157 (connection allowed or blocked) Network_Traffic Audit Filtering Platform Connection

Handle requests, object accesses and registry value changes are logged only for objects whose auditing (SACL) asks for them. Directory object types and properties are kept as Windows records them (%{19195a5b-...}), so a rule that compares one to a bare GUID matches only events that already carry the name. An access list (AccessList) is searched by its codes (%%4417) and by their names (WriteData), since rules use both.

Each pack rule only searches its own log source's event IDs, since several kinds of event share a data model (a process creation and a process access are both Endpoint). Sysmon only records the events its configuration asks for, so a rule fires only when your Sysmon configuration logs that kind of event.

docs.title: Linux endpoints (Sysmon for Linux)
docs.text:
Sysmon for Linux (open source, MIT) records process creations, network connections and file creation and deletion with the same event IDs and fields as Sysmon on Windows, and writes them to syslog. Signalith reads them into the same data models, with sourcetype sysmon:linux:

Sigma log source (Linux) Sysmon for Linux events Data model process_creation 1 Endpoint network_connection 3 Network_Traffic file_event 11 Filesystem

The SigmaHQ pack's Linux rules and the Splunk pack's Linux rules read these events. Sigma Linux rules search every Linux event of their data model; Splunk's search only Sysmon for Linux events. To collect them, install Sysmon for Linux with a configuration, then on Add data choose Linux, turn on Include Sysmon for Linux and use the new agent configuration: the agent reads Sysmon's events from the systemd journal.

docs.title: Linux audit log (auditd)
docs.text:
The Linux audit system (auditd, open source) records what its audit rules ask for: programs run, files opened, services stopped, accounts added. The Linux agent reads its log, /var/log/audit/audit.log, and the syslog receiver reads audit records forwarded by auditd's syslog plugin. Each record is one event in the Other data model, with sourcetype linux:audit. Every field is kept by auditd's own name with auditd_ in front (exe is auditd_exe, a0 is auditd_a0, the record type is auditd_type). The names an ENRICHED record gives numbers, which rules write in capitals (UID, SYSCALL), get _name at the end (auditd_uid_name, auditd_syscall_name). Text auditd writes in hex, such as a command line, is decoded. A program's arguments are also joined as auditd_execve_command, and the program, its process ID and the logged-in user are in the usual process, process_path, process_name, process_id and user fields. Records that ausearch -i printed are read too.

40 SigmaHQ rules (service: auditd) and 46 Splunk rules (the linux_auditd macro) read these records, for example capabilities discovery, clipboard and screen capture, hidden files run, kernel modules loaded, firewalls turned off, LD_PRELOAD and /etc/ld.so.preload changes, SUID binaries made, and audit or Sysmon stopped. Each Splunk rule also fires on Splunk's own recording of its attack.

Most of these rules need auditd to record each program run, which it does not do by default. Install auditd and add a rule such as:

sudo auditctl -a always,exit -F arch=b64 -S execve -k exec
echo '-a always,exit -F arch=b64 -S execve -k exec' | sudo tee /etc/audit/rules.d/signalith.rules

The OpenTelemetry Collector runs as its own user and cannot read the audit log, so collect it with the Fluent Bit agent, or forward it with auditd's syslog plugin.

docs.title: PowerShell script blocks
docs.text:
The ps_script rules read event 4104, which Windows PowerShell writes for each script it runs once script block logging is on (it is off by default). Turn it on with Group Policy (Administrative Templates > Windows Components > Windows PowerShell > Turn on PowerShell Script Block Logging) or, in an elevated PowerShell:

$k = 'HKLM:\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\PowerShell\ScriptBlockLogging'
New-Item -Path $k -Force | Out-Null
Set-ItemProperty -Path $k -Name EnableScriptBlockLogging -Value 1

Then collect the Microsoft-Windows-PowerShell/Operational channel: Include PowerShell on the Add data page adds it to the Windows agent and the OpenTelemetry Collector. PowerShell 7 logs to its own PowerShellCore/Operational channel, which Signalith does not read yet.

Script blocks are long (up to about 20,000 characters, and a longer script arrives in parts with script_part and script_parts), so script_block_text is a wildcard field, which finds text anywhere in a value of any length. That field type needs OpenSearch 2.15 or later. On older versions Signalith maps it as a keyword instead, and then the text of a script block longer than 8,191 characters cannot be searched. The type applies to indices created after an upgrade, so from the next day's index on. Rules that would list more script snippets than OpenSearch allows in one search (1,024 clauses by default) are left out of the pack.

A rule is only shipped when:

  • its status is stable or test (not experimental or deprecated), and its level is not informational;
  • it converts exactly: every field maps to a Signalith field and every modifier is supported (strict mode, below);
  • it fires on its test events and stays quiet on its near misses. Test events are made from the rule itself (every way the rule can match, plus events with each field removed or changed and events hitting each exclusion), and SigmaHQ's own recorded events are added where they exist. Each event goes through the real Windows parser, and two independent readings must agree: a Sigma evaluator on the raw event, and the converted query on the stored event.

internal/detect/packs/sigmahq/REPORT.md lists every rule left out and why. CI runs the same checks on every change (TestPackRulesFireOnTheirTests) and repeats them against a real OpenSearch (TestPackRulesAgainstOpenSearch), so a change to the parser, the field mappings or the query compiler that breaks a shipped rule fails the build.

Pack detections get these defaults: the title names the host, at most one finding per host, user and command line a day (per host, program, destination and port for network rules), and risk on the user and the host by Sigma level (low 10, medium 25, high 50, critical 80). Low level rules only add risk and raise no finding, so they feed risk-based alerting without flooding the queue. Each is tagged sigma, the pack name, the product and the log source.

On the Detections page, the pack card shows how many rules are on. Turn on N high and critical rules is the suggested start; Browse rules lists the pack so you can filter, read a rule's source and turn rules on or off one at a time or all shown at once (with Undo). Pack rules cannot be deleted, only turned off; editing one saves an override that keeps the credit.

Licence: the SigmaHQ rules are under the Detection Rule License 1.1 (full text in the pack folder). As it requires, every finding from a pack rule carries a credit line naming the rule's author, the pack and the licence, shown on the finding and stored as its credit field.

To refresh the pack from a newer SigmaHQ commit:

git clone https://github.com/SigmaHQ/sigma /tmp/sigma
go run ./internal/detect/packgen -sigma /tmp/sigma
go test ./internal/detect/

The generator keeps each rule's Signalith ID across runs, rewrites rules/, tests/, pack.yaml and REPORT.md, and only lists rules whose checks pass.

docs.title: Splunk Security Content
docs.text:
Splunk Security Content (internal/detect/packs/splunk) holds 988 Windows and Linux detections from Splunk's Threat Research Team (security_content), pinned to one commit. They are the production TTP and anomaly rules that search the CIM Endpoint.Processes, Endpoint.Filesystem and Endpoint.Registry nodes with tstats, plus the PowerShell script block rules. Signalith uses the same CIM field names, so each rule's where clause becomes a Signalith filter field for field:

Splunk node Windows events Data model Endpoint.Processes Sysmon 1, Security 4688 Endpoint Endpoint.Filesystem Sysmon 11, 23 and 26 Filesystem Endpoint.Registry Sysmon 12, 13 and 14 Registry Network_Traffic.All_Traffic Sysmon 3 (app is the program's path, dest_ip and src_ip are dest and src) Network_Traffic `powershell` EventCode=4104 (raw search) PowerShell 4104 Script `sysmon` EventCode=1 (raw search) Sysmon 1 Endpoint `sysmon` EventCode=3 (raw search) Sysmon 3 Network_Traffic `sysmon` EventCode=7 (raw search) Sysmon 7 Image_Load `sysmon` EventCode=22 (raw search) Sysmon 22 Network_Resolution `sysmon` EventCode=11, 23 or 26 (raw search) Sysmon 11, 23 and 26 Filesystem `sysmon` EventCode=12, 13 or 14 (raw search) Sysmon 12, 13 and 14 Registry `sysmon` EventCode=8 or 10 (raw search) Sysmon 8 and 10 Endpoint `sysmon` EventCode=17 or 18 (raw search) Sysmon 17 and 18 (named pipe created or connected to; PipeName is pipe_name) Endpoint `sysmon` EventCode=15 (raw search) Sysmon 15 (alternate data stream written; Contents is file_contents) Filesystem `sysmon` EventCode=5 or 9 (raw search) Sysmon 5 (process terminated) and 9 (a drive read directly; Device is device) Endpoint `wineventlog_security` EventCode=4624 or 4625 (raw search) Security 4624 (successful logon) and 4625 (failed logon) Authentication `wineventlog_security` EventCode=4698 (raw search) Security 4698 (scheduled task created) Change `wineventlog_security` EventCode=4663 (raw search) Security 4663 (object access) Filesystem for a file, Registry for a key `wineventlog_system` EventCode=7045 (raw search) System 7045 (service installed) Change `wineventlog_security` EventCode=5136 (raw search) Security 5136 (directory object changed) Change `wineventlog_security` EventCode=5145 (raw search) Security 5145 (network share access) Filesystem `wineventlog_security` EventCode=4768 or 4769 (raw search) Security 4768 and 4769 (Kerberos tickets) Authentication `wineventlog_security` EventCode=4738 or 4732 (raw search) Security 4738 (user account changed) and 4732 (member added to a local group) Change `wineventlog_security` EventCode=4648, 4776 or 4771 (raw search) Security 4648 (logon with explicit credentials), 4776 (NTLM credential check) and 4771 (Kerberos pre-authentication failed) Authentication `wineventlog_security` EventCode=4741, 4742, 4781, 4727, 4730 or 4737 (raw search) Security 4741 and 4742 (computer account created or changed), 4781 (account renamed), 4727, 4730 and 4737 (global group created, deleted or changed) Change `wineventlog_security` EventCode=4798, 4799, 4886 or 4887 (raw search) Security 4798 and 4799 (local group membership listed), 4886 and 4887 (certificate requested and issued) Change Endpoint.Processes (Sysmon for Linux rules) Sysmon for Linux 1 Endpoint Endpoint.Filesystem (Sysmon for Linux rules) Sysmon for Linux 11 and 23 Filesystem `linux_auditd` (raw search) Linux audit records, each field by auditd's name (see the Linux audit log) Other

The rule files and the macros they use ship unchanged; Signalith converts them when it starts, reading the search the way Splunk does: * is the only wildcard (? is literal, so rules with one are left out), case is ignored, != only matches when the field is present, OR binds tighter than AND (a b OR c is a AND (b OR c)), and \\ is one backslash, quoted or not, as in Splunk's search syntax. Sysmon's user (NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM) compares as the name alone (SYSTEM), the way Splunk's Sysmon add-on reads it. TTP rules raise findings and add risk; anomaly rules only add risk, as in Splunk ES risk-based alerting. Severity follows the rule's risk score (TTP: 80 and up critical, 64 high, 30 medium; anomalies low). Each is tagged splunk, the pack name, ttp or anomaly, and the node, and keeps the rule's known false positives as triage guidance.

PowerShell rules, and Sysmon image load, remote thread and process access rules, search the events themselves rather than a data model: their event fields become Signalith's (ScriptBlockText is script_block_text, ImageLoaded is loaded_file_path, TargetImage is target_process_path, and so on), and their fillnull and stats stages only count the events. (Without fillnull, Splunk's stats also drops events that miss one of its by fields; Signalith keeps them.) PowerShell rules need script block logging turned on (Include PowerShell on Add data).

Scheduled task rules search the task's name (TaskName is task_name) and its XML definition (TaskContent is task_content); after xmlkv, the command and arguments of its first action are task_command and task_arguments. Splunk keeps that XML escaped (<Hidden>); Signalith stores it as it is, so the rule's values are unescaped to match. Security 4698 is logged when Audit Other Object Access Events is on.

Object access rules (Security 4663) search the object's path whatever its type (ObjectName and object_file_path are object_path, object_file_name is object_name), the program (ProcessName is process_path), ObjectType, AccessList and AccessMask. Files are stored in Filesystem and registry keys in Registry (action read, modified or deleted), and a rule searches both, as in Splunk. Windows logs 4663 only for objects whose auditing (SACL) asks for it, with Audit File System or Audit Registry on.

Directory change rules (Security 5136) search the object's DN (ObjectDN is object), ObjectClass (ad_object_class), the attribute (AttributeLDAPDisplayName is ad_attribute), its value (AttributeValue is ad_value) and OperationType (ad_operation, %%14674 for a value added). Share access rules (Security 5145) search ShareName (share_name), the path inside the share (RelativeTargetName is share_target), the client (IpAddress is src), AccessMask and AccessList.

Kerberos rules (Security 4768 for a ticket-granting ticket, 4769 for a service ticket) search the account (TargetUserName is user), the service (ServiceName is kerberos_service), TicketOptions (ticket_options), TicketEncryptionType (ticket_encryption_type, 0x17 for RC4), Status (kerberos_status, 0x0 when granted) and the client (src_ip is src, stored without the ::ffff: Windows puts before an IPv4 address). They are stored in Authentication with app win:kerberos, action success or failure.

Account rules (Security 4738 for a user account changed, 4732 for a member added to a local group) search the account or group (TargetUserName is object), who made the change (SubjectUserName is user), the account's UserAccountControl flags (user_account_control, such as %%2096 for Kerberos pre-authentication turned off), and the member added (MemberSid is member_sid). They are stored in Change with object_category user or group.

Sign-in rules search the account (TargetUserName is user): a logon with explicit credentials (4648) by who used them (SubjectUserName, or the add-on's Caller_User_Name, is src_user), an NTLM credential check (4776) by the computer it came from (Workstation is src_host) and its result (Status is ntlm_status, 0xc0000064 for an account that does not exist), and a failed Kerberos pre-authentication (4771) by the client (IpAddress is src) and Status (kerberos_status, 0x18 for a wrong password).

Computer account rules (4741, 4742) search the account (TargetUserName is object), its UserAccountControl, NewUacValue and service principal names (ServicePrincipalNames is service_principal_names, one space between names). A renamed account (4781) has its new name as object and its old one as old_object. Local group listing rules (4798, 4799) search the program that asked (CallerProcessName is process_path), and certificate rules (4886, 4887) the requester (Requester is cert_requester) and the request's Attributes (cert_attributes, such as its template and any subject alternative name).

Service install rules (System 7045, from the Sigma service: system log source or Splunk's wineventlog_system) search the service's name (ServiceName is service_name), what it runs (ImagePath is service_path, a path or a whole command line), ServiceType (service_type), StartType (service_start_type) and AccountName (service_account). They are stored in Change with object_category service and action created. The Service Control Manager logs 7045 on every Windows version without any audit setting, and the Windows agent collects the System log. Of the System log's events, Signalith reads only service installs; other System rules (services stopping, for example) are left out of the packs, and importing one says so.

Registry values that Sysmon writes as DWORD (0x00000001) compare as 0x00000001, the way Splunk's Sysmon add-on reads them.

A rule is shipped only when its whole search converts exactly (a tstats search whose later stages only rename fields, format times, keep rows that have a field (where isnotnull(...)), keep rows a regular expression matches (regex field="...", or where match(field, "...") joined by AND or OR) or apply the rule's empty _filter macro) and, on test events made from its where clause and passed through the real Windows parser, the converted detection agrees with Splunk's reading of the clause on every event. A regular expression converts when it is also valid in Go's syntax (no lookarounds) and OpenSearch can search it exactly (no word boundaries). A value with a ?, which Splunk reads literally, is searched as a regular expression too. An address range (dest_ip IN ("10.0.0.0/8", ...)) matches the addresses in it, as in Splunk. Raw searches that test an access mask bit by bit (eval m = tonumber(GrantedAccess, 16), bit_and(m, 16) and a where on the result being the mask, 0 or not 0) convert to a regular expression over the mask's hex digits.

Rules that count events convert too: a tstats count by some fields and _time span=1m (or a raw search's bucket span=5m _time and stats ... by), then a where limit on the count (where count >= 10, where unique_accounts > 30, several joined by AND). The detection runs | stats count, dc(field) as name by fields and the same limit. Each run counts the rule's span plus the time since the last run (every minute for spans under 5 minutes, every 5 minutes otherwise; a count without a span covers an hour, as Splunk's default schedule does), so a burst Splunk finds in one of its fixed buckets is counted even when its events arrive a little late, and each group is found once a day. Fields of Splunk's add-ons that only restate which event it is (signature, vendor_product, dvc, app, user_id, authentication_method) are left out of the grouping; an event's Computer is host. A rule ships only when its test events carry every field it groups by and counts. Counts compared with an average (eventstats) are left out.

A test that only leaves out the other platform's events (NOT Processes.os="Linux" in a Windows rule) is always true for the rule's own events, whether Splunk's add-on sets os or not, so it is dropped; other tests of os or vendor_product are left out. A \/ in a value is left out too, since Splunk's documented escapes do not say how it reads it.

Searches with other evals, rex, lookup, and other raw searches are left out for now; internal/detect/packs/splunk/REPORT.md lists every rule left out and why. The same CI checks as the SigmaHQ pack run on it.

Each rule is also checked on the real attack it was written for: Splunk records one for most rules (tests.attack_data, from attack_data). Every recorded Windows event goes through Signalith's parser, and the detection must read it as the rule does and find the attack. 715 of the 717 shipped rules with a Windows recording do, and up to two recorded events each rule finds are kept with its test events, so CI checks real events too:

go run ./internal/detect/attackgen -write   # downloads the recordings, about 2 GB

On the pack card, Turn on N TTP rules is the suggested start.

Licence: the rules are © Splunk Inc. under the Apache License 2.0 (the licence text is in the pack folder and the attribution in NOTICE). Findings credit the rule's authors and link to the rule at the pinned commit. Signalith is not affiliated with or endorsed by Splunk.

To refresh the pack from a newer commit:

git clone https://github.com/splunk/security_content /tmp/security_content
go run ./internal/detect/splunkgen -splunk /tmp/security_content
go test ./internal/detect/ ./internal/splcheck/

docs.title: Content updates
docs.text:
Pack rules can be updated without a new Signalith release. Every week the Signalith project rebuilds both packs from the newest SigmaHQ and Splunk rules, runs every check above on them (in memory and against a real OpenSearch), and publishes the ones that pass as one signed bundle. A server only installs a bundle that:

  • is signed by a key built into Signalith (Ed25519; the keys are in internal/content/trusted.keys), so a copy from anywhere else is as good as the original, and a changed byte is refused;
  • is newer than the rules it uses, so an old bundle cannot roll rules back;
  • this version of Signalith can read. A rule for something it does not know yet, such as a new log source, is left out and counted on the Detections page.

Under the pack cards on the Detections page, the line says how new the rules are. Admins can:

  • Check for updates: download and install the newest bundle.
  • Upload update…: for a server without internet access. Download signalith-content.tar.gz and signalith-content.tar.gz.sig from the content release on another computer, then choose both files together.
  • Use built-in rules: go back to the rules that came with this version of Signalith.

Rules you turned on stay on, exceptions stay, and new rules start off. A rule that an update drops stops running; your choices for it come back if it returns.

The Content pack updates setting (detections.content_updates) can be Daily: the server then checks once a day and installs what it finds. Content update address (detections.content_url) points servers at a copy on your own web server; the bundle's signature is read from the same address plus .sig. Each server keeps its update in content/ in its detections folder. Upgrading Signalith to a version with newer rules built in uses those instead of an older update.

From the command line (as the service, with -c for the config file):

signalith content status
signalith content install signalith-content.tar.gz   # reads signalith-content.tar.gz.sig too
signalith content remove

Restart Signalith after install or remove so a running server uses the change, or upload on the Detections page instead.

docs.title: Sigma rules
docs.text:
Import Sigma rule on the Detections page (or POST /api/detections/sigma) converts a rule and shows the result for review. Supported:

  • Log sources process_creation (Endpoint), network_connection and firewall (Network_Traffic), authentication and Linux auth (Authentication), and antivirus (Malware, where Signature maps to signature and Filename to file_path), plus the Sysmon and PowerShell log sources in the table above. Other log sources search all data and say so. product: windows limits the search to Windows event logs (and, for the log sources in the table, to their event IDs), and linux or macos leave them out.
  • For ps_script, ScriptBlockText maps to script_block_text, ScriptBlockId to script_block_id and Path to script_path.
  • For the Sysmon log sources other than process creation, fields map by log source: TargetFilename to file_path; TargetObject to registry_path, Details to registry_value_data and EventType (SetValue, CreateKey...) to registry_event_type; QueryName to query and QueryResults to answer; ImageLoaded to loaded_file_path with Signed, Signature and SignatureStatus, and the loaded file's Hashes to loaded_file_hash (for DLLs, also OriginalFileName, Description, Product and Company to loaded_original_file_name, loaded_file_description, loaded_file_product and loaded_file_company); SourceImage, TargetImage, GrantedAccess, CallTrace, StartAddress, StartModule and StartFunction for process access and remote threads. A field not listed for its log source (such as CommandLine in image_load, which Sysmon does not record there) has no mapping.
  • Sysmon and Windows Security field names, mapped to Signalith fields (Image to process_path, or process_name for endswith a file name; CommandLine to process; OriginalFileName to original_file_name; ParentUser, IntegrityLevel, CurrentDirectory, Description, Product, Company, FileVersion, LogonId, ProcessGuid, SourceHostname, Initiated and more; TargetUserName to user; IpAddress to src; SourceIsIpv6 to src_is_ipv6; Provider_Name to provider; and so on). In a successful logon (4624) the requesting account's SubjectUserSid and SubjectUserName map to src_user_sid and src_user, and KeyLength, ImpersonationLevel, ElevatedToken and TargetOutboundUserName to key_length, impersonation_level, elevated_token and target_outbound_user; a Security service install's (4697) ClientProcessId and ParentProcessId to client_process_id and parent_process_id. Unmapped fields are searched as-is and listed as warnings.
  • Modifiers contains, startswith, endswith, all, windash, exists, base64, base64offset, utf16le, utf16be, utf16, wide, cidr (IPv4 and IPv6) and re (with i, m and s), searched as a regular expression (field=~"..."); escaped wildcards (\*, a literal asterisk) also become a regular expression; lists, null and empty values, keyword lists; conditions with and, or, not, parentheses, 1 of, all of, them and selection_* patterns.

Not supported, and reported as an error: other modifiers, regular expressions with word boundaries (\b) or line anchors, and aggregation conditions (| count() > 10).

Strict mode, used for content packs, also refuses anything that would only be approximated: unmapped fields, keyword (free text) searches, rules with no data model, and cased.

Imported rules start disabled with a 5 minute schedule and 10 minute lookback.

docs.title: API
docs.text:
Method and path Purpose GET /api/detections All detections with their run state: last run, next run, errors, skipped runs and the last Run now. Every server returns the same state POST /api/detections Create (400 lists every problem) GET, PUT, DELETE /api/detections/{id} Read, save, delete or revert GET /api/detections/{id}/yaml Export as YAML POST /api/detections/test Run an unsaved detection; returns rows and titles, raises nothing POST /api/detections/{id}/run Run now on this server and raise findings (admin). Searches the lookback up to now, does not change the schedule, and is recorded as the detection's last Run now with who ran it POST /api/detections/sigma Convert a Sigma rule (YAML body, or JSON {"rule": "..."}) GET /api/detections/packs Content packs with their rule IDs, how many are on, and counts by severity GET /api/detections/content Content update status: the version in use, whether it is an update, the last check and the content_updates mode POST /api/detections/content/check Download and install a newer content update (admin; 502 with the reason when it fails) POST /api/detections/content/upload Install an update from a form with the files bundle and signature (admin; 409 when it is not newer) DELETE /api/detections/content Remove the update and use the rules built into Signalith (admin) POST /api/detections/{id}/exceptions Add an exception: {"match": {"host": "web*"}, "for": "7d", "from", "until", "comment"} (admin) DELETE /api/detections/{id}/exceptions/{exception} Remove an exception (admin) POST /api/findings/{id}/suppress Don't alert on this again: {"fields": ["host", "user"], "for": "30d", "comment", "update": {"status": "closed", "disposition": "false_positive"}} adds an exception for the finding's values of those fields and can update the finding (admin) POST /api/detections/enable {"ids": [...], "enabled": true}: turn up to 5,000 detections on or off at once (404 and no change if any ID is unknown) GET /api/coverage ATT&CK matrix with coverage GET /api/findings?status=&severity=&urgency=&owner=&detection=&q=&since=7d&limit= Queue GET, PATCH /api/findings/{id} Read; update status, owner, severity, disposition, comment POST /api/findings/bulk {"ids": [...], "update": {...}} POST /api/findings Raise a finding by hand GET /api/findings/summary Open counts by status, severity and urgency GET /api/cases?status=&owner=&q=&finding=&limit= Cases, most recently updated first, without timelines POST /api/cases {"title", "description", "severity", "owner", "findings": [...]}; the title defaults to the first finding's GET, PATCH /api/cases/{id} Read with linked findings; update title, description, status, severity, owner, resolution, comment, and close_findings with disposition POST /api/cases/{id}/findings {"ids": [...]}: add findings, moving them from another case DELETE /api/cases/{id}/findings/{finding} Remove a finding POST /api/cases/{id}/entries Add {"kind": "note", "text"}, {"kind": "search", "query", "earliest", "latest"} (runs it and keeps 50 rows) or {"kind": "event", "event": {...}} DELETE /api/cases/{id}/entries/{entry} Remove a timeline entry POST /api/cases/{id}/entities {"field", "value"} GET /api/cases/summary Open cases, and open cases you own GET /api/risk?since=24h&type= Risk objects by total score, with context GET /api/risk/object?object=&type=&since=7d Risk events for one object GET, PUT /api/lookups/assets, /api/lookups/identities List or replace a list (CSV body of up to 16 MB and 1,000,000 rows; 400 lists every bad line) GET /api/lookups/assets.csv, /api/lookups/identities.csv Download the current CSV GET /api/lookups/context?field=&value= Context for one value

Changes to findings and cases are saved only over the version they were made on, and made again on a newer one when someone changed the item meanwhile (on any server), so nothing is lost. When other changes keep getting in first, PATCH /api/findings/{id} and the case changes answer 409 with "Someone else changed this ... at the same moment. Try again."; nothing was changed. In POST /api/findings/bulk such a finding is listed under failed and the others are still updated.

docs.title: Encryption
docs.text:
Signalith keeps passwords and API keys: the OpenSearch password, shared agent tokens, the AI model's API key, the directory (Active Directory or LDAP) service account password, and the keys and passwords of threat intel feeds. This page covers how they and your events are protected:

What protects it What you do In transit (on the network) HTTPS and TLS Nothing: HTTPS is on by default; see docs/https.md At rest (on disk) Signalith encrypts the passwords and keys it stores; disk encryption protects everything else Back up the master key; turn on disk encryption In use (in memory) The service is locked down so other programs cannot read its memory Nothing, or a confidential VM for more

docs.title: In transit
docs.text: Signalith serves the web UI and the API (agents send events over it, each with its own agent token) over HTTPS by default, with a certificate from a small certificate authority of its own; docs/https.md covers trusting it, using your own certificate, and syslog over TLS. Use TLS for syslog where devices support it, https:// for OpenSearch, and ldaps:// or StartTLS for directory sign-in. Signalith refuses to send the OpenSearch password over plain http to another machine unless you allow it, and warns while certificate checks are off.

docs.title: What Signalith encrypts
docs.text:
Every password and API key Signalith keeps in its settings files is encrypted (files that hold a key on their own are not; see below). Per-agent tokens made on Add data are not kept anywhere: OpenSearch holds only a SHA-256 hash of each (see agent-tokens.md).

File Encrypted values Written by signalith.yaml opensearch.password, assistant.api_key, auth.ldap.bind_password, each of ingest.tokens (shared agent tokens from older setups), and intel.feeds[].password and header values You, signalith init and signalith secrets. The server never changes this file settings.yaml (lookups folder, or SIGNALITH_SETTINGS_FILE) The OpenSearch password and the AI model's API key saved on the Settings page The server, and signalith settings reset directory.json (lookups folder) The service account password of directory sign-in set up on the Users page The server intel_feeds.yaml (lookups folder) Passwords and header values (API keys) of feeds added on the Threat intel page The server

An encrypted value looks like this:

opensearch:
  password: enc:v1:9096cd23:zNhdzHvpeSnrdiqQHGOGMRlih2VUzUrwcOjWVF3w4lW1dAVcs-fPcn_nBiPB6wM

9096cd23 is the id of the master key that encrypted it. A plain value still works: paste a password into signalith.yaml and the server uses it, but signalith validate, the server log and the Health page say so:

Warning: 1 password or key in signalith.yaml is stored as plain text (assistant.api_key). Run: signalith secrets encrypt

signalith secrets encrypt then encrypts it where it stands, keeping your comments and layout:

-    api_key: sk-ant-PASTED-BY-HAND   # pasted in by hand
+    api_key: enc:v1:dea48fde:Nqfes8VQxocc4uRLZGjXal83RwCznSCgI0samMWNTPIlepfiZhj50zH8iGnwjRE1Ag   # pasted in by hand

The server encrypts the plain values in the files it writes itself (left by an older version, which kept the passwords saved on the Settings page as plain text in settings.yaml, or written there by hand) when it starts, and again when the Settings page restarts it, and logs it only when it changed something:

level=INFO msg="encrypted the passwords and keys stored in a file" file=/var/lib/signalith/lookups/intel_feeds.yaml values=1

Passwords in addresses. A password written into an address cannot be encrypted there, so Signalith counts it as plain text:

  • In opensearch.url (https://admin:secret@opensearch:9200), signalith secrets encrypt takes it out of the address and writes it as opensearch.username and an encrypted opensearch.password.
  • In opensearch.proxy, it is only reported: set the proxy with the SIGNALITH_OPENSEARCH_PROXY environment variable instead.
  • A key in a feed's address (https://feed.example/list?apikey=...) is only reported: if the feed accepts it as a header, send it that way, since headers are encrypted.

Not encrypted, because they need not be:

  • User passwords (the built-in admin's and those on the Users page) are stored as bcrypt hashes, which cannot be turned back into the password.
  • Environment variables (SIGNALITH_OPENSEARCH_PASSWORD and the others) are used as they are and never written to a file, even when Signalith saves a file.
  • A value written as ${ENV_VAR} (in a feed in signalith.yaml) holds no secret.
  • Events, in OpenSearch and in archives, are protected by disk encryption (below).

How: each value is encrypted with AES-256-GCM, under a key derived from the master key for that setting alone. A value copied to another setting, or changed, does not decrypt. A feed's password and header values in signalith.yaml are tied to the header's name, not to the feed's: rename a feed as you like, but after renaming a header (X-API-Key to X-Auth-Key) enter its value again. Header names ignore case, so x-api-key is the same header.

docs.title: Not encrypted by the master key
docs.text:
Some keys and secrets are files of their own, kept as plain text and protected only by their permissions (readable by Signalith's account and administrators). Keep them out of backups that many people can read, as you keep the master key:

  • Signalith's HTTPS keys, ca.key and server.key in the tls folder of the state folder, next to keys (/var/lib/signalith/tls, C:\ProgramData\Signalith\tls, and in Docker the signalith-data volume). Whoever has ca.key can make certificates that browsers and agents trusting Signalith's CA accept; see docs/https.md.
  • The sign-in key, signin.key in the state folder. It signs the cookie that lets a browser that signed in to an account before keep signing in while someone else is guessing that account's password (see failed sign-in limits). Whoever has it can make such cookies, but still needs the password to sign in.
  • The Docker quick start's signalith-secrets volume, made by its setup step: the first admin password (initial-admin-password), the shared agent token agents set up before per-agent tokens use (ingest-token; see Replace a shared token) and Signalith's OpenSearch client key (opensearch-client-key.pem). OpenSearch's own keys are in the opensearch-certs volume.
  • Files named by SIGNALITH_*_FILE variables (SIGNALITH_OPENSEARCH_PASSWORD_FILE and the others), such as Docker or Kubernetes secrets and systemd credentials. Signalith only reads them.
  • Key files you name in signalith.yaml or on the Settings page, such as server.tls_key and opensearch.key_file.

docs.title: The master key
docs.text:
The master key is 32 random bytes. Signalith makes it the first time it stores a password or key (signalith init does), and looks for it in this order:

  1. $CREDENTIALS_DIRECTORY/master.key: a systemd credential (see below).
  2. The file SIGNALITH_MASTER_KEY_FILE names, such as a Docker or Kubernetes secret.
  3. SIGNALITH_MASTER_KEY: the key itself, in base64. It works, but other programs can sometimes read a program's environment (docker inspect, /proc), so Signalith warns while it is used.
  4. The key file Signalith makes, keys/master.key (on Windows keys\master.key.dpapi), in the state folder (SIGNALITH_STATE_DIR, or the folder that holds the lookups folder; docs/servers.md says when another folder is used), then next to signalith.yaml, then on Linux in /var/lib/signalith. For a config in /etc on Linux, /var/lib/signalith comes first, so the key is never made next to signalith.yaml, where a copy of /etc would carry both.

Where it ends up:

Install Master key Linux (systemd) /var/lib/signalith/keys/master.key, made by signalith init Docker quick start /var/lib/signalith/keys/master.key, in the signalith-data volume Windows C:\ProgramData\Signalith\keys\master.key.dpapi Elsewhere keys/master.key next to the lookups folder

The key file can be read only by Signalith's own account: mode 0600 in a 0700 folder on Linux, and on Windows an access list of its own (SYSTEM, Administrators and the service account, NT SERVICE\Signalith). On Windows the key is also encrypted with DPAPI for the computer, so a copy of the file is useless on another computer.

On Linux, Signalith warns (in signalith secrets status, signalith validate, the log and the Health page) when other accounts can read or change the key file, such as a key restored from a backup with cp, and says how to fix it (chmod 600). A key file it is not allowed to read is an error that names the file and the fix (sudo chown -R signalith /var/lib/signalith/keys); Signalith never makes a second key while there is one it cannot read.

A key file you make yourself holds one line of base64 (or hex), or the 32 bytes as they are. Make one with openssl rand -base64 32 > master.key. A 32-character passphrase is refused: typed text is far easier to guess than random bytes.

signalith secrets status shows where the key is and how every value is stored:

$ sudo signalith secrets status
Using the settings the signalith service is given (systemctl show signalith):
  SIGNALITH_ARCHIVE_DIR=/var/lib/signalith/archive
  SIGNALITH_DASHBOARDS_DIR=/var/lib/signalith/dashboards
  SIGNALITH_DETECTIONS_DIR=/var/lib/signalith/detections
  SIGNALITH_LOOKUPS_DIR=/var/lib/signalith/lookups
  SIGNALITH_STATE_DIR=/var/lib/signalith

Master key:    /var/lib/signalith/keys/master.key, key id 9096cd23

/etc/signalith/signalith.yaml
  opensearch.password  encrypted
  ingest.tokens[0]     encrypted

/var/lib/signalith/lookups/directory.json
  bind_password (service account password)  encrypted

/var/lib/signalith/lookups/intel_feeds.yaml
  feeds[legacy-cti] header X-API-Key  encrypted
  feeds[otx] password                 encrypted
  feeds[otx] header X-OTX-API-KEY     encrypted

/var/lib/signalith/lookups/settings.yaml
  opensearch.password  encrypted

7 encrypted, 0 plain text.

A command run by hand does not see the settings the service is given, so signalith secrets, signalith settings, signalith validate and signalith init read them: on Linux the systemd unit's Environment=, EnvironmentFile= and LoadCredential= lines, and on Windows the Signalith service's Environment value in the registry. They find the server's files and key that way (only its folders, the files it keeps and the master key are taken, never other settings or secrets: a secret given in a file, such as SIGNALITH_OPENSEARCH_PASSWORD_FILE naming a systemd credential, is read by the server alone). signalith passwd reads them too, so a new admin password goes where the service uses it.

docs.title: Keeping the key elsewhere
docs.text:
• systemd credential: systemd hands the key to the service when it starts, from a file only root can read, away from the service's own folder and from /etc/signalith. To move the key there:
sudo signalith secrets status      # "Master key:" names the key file; with a "Previous key:" line, prune it first
sudo systemctl stop signalith
sudo install -d -m 0700 /etc/credstore
sudo mv /var/lib/signalith/keys/master.key /etc/credstore/signalith-master.key
sudo chown root:root /etc/credstore/signalith-master.key
sudo sed -i 's|^# LoadCredential=|LoadCredential=|' /etc/systemd/system/signalith.service
sudo systemctl daemon-reload
sudo systemctl start signalith
sudo signalith secrets status      # "Master key: /etc/credstore/signalith-master.key"

signalith secrets commands use the same file. The service reads the key only when it starts, so after rotate-master, restart it and run signalith secrets encrypt once (for anything it saved in between) before rotate-master -prune; -prune waits for that restart. If the file is missing, the service does not start. - Docker or Kubernetes secret: mount the key file into the container and set SIGNALITH_MASTER_KEY_FILE to its path; Docker below shows it with Docker Compose. - Windows, a key you can move: the DPAPI-protected key works only on the computer that made it. To use a key file you can restore on another server, in a PowerShell opened as Administrator:

$exe = "$env:ProgramFiles\Signalith\signalith.exe"
Stop-Service Signalith
& $exe secrets decrypt          # values back to plain text, while the old key still works
$key = New-Object byte[] 32
[Security.Cryptography.RandomNumberGenerator]::Create().GetBytes($key)
[IO.File]::WriteAllText("$env:ProgramData\Signalith\keys\master.key", [Convert]::ToBase64String($key))
Set-ItemProperty HKLM:\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\Signalith -Name Environment -Type MultiString `
  -Value 'SIGNALITH_MASTER_KEY_FILE=C:\ProgramData\Signalith\keys\master.key'
& $exe secrets encrypt          # encrypted again, with the new key
Remove-Item "$env:ProgramData\Signalith\keys\master.key.dpapi"
Start-Service Signalith

The new file takes the keys folder's access list (SYSTEM, Administrators and the service). Every signalith command, and install.ps1 when you upgrade, reads the service's Environment value, so they all use this key.

docs.title: Docker
docs.text:
In the Docker quick start the key is /var/lib/signalith/keys/master.key in the signalith-data volume, together with directory.json, intel_feeds.yaml and settings.yaml. A backup of the volume therefore holds both the key and the values it decrypts. The same volume holds Signalith's HTTPS keys (tls/ca.key and tls/server.key), and the signalith-secrets volume the first admin password, the shared agent token and Signalith's OpenSearch client key, none of them encrypted (see above): keep backups of both volumes as private as the key. Copy the key out and keep it apart (in a password manager or a vault). From the repository folder, in a shell or PowerShell:

docker compose -f deploy/docker/docker-compose.yml cp signalith:/var/lib/signalith/keys/master.key "$HOME/signalith-master.key"

If you back up the volume, keep the key out of it instead, as a Docker secret. In deploy/docker/docker-compose.override.yml:

services:
  signalith:
    environment:
      - SIGNALITH_MASTER_KEY_FILE=/run/secrets/signalith_master_key
    secrets: [signalith_master_key]
secrets:
  signalith_master_key:
    file: ./master.key

Put the key copied out above in deploy/docker/master.key (or make a new one with openssl rand -base64 32 > deploy/docker/master.key before the first start). The container's account (uid 65532) must be able to read it: sudo chown 65532 deploy/docker/master.key && sudo chmod 0400 deploy/docker/master.key. Git ignores that file. Compose reads the override file by itself only when run from its folder without -f, so from then on start Signalith with cd deploy/docker and docker compose up -d. The copy left in the volume is then not used; signalith secrets status notes it, and docker run --rm -v docker_signalith-data:/data busybox rm /data/keys/master.key removes it (docker volume ls shows the volume's name).

signalith.yaml is mounted read-only in the container, so to encrypt a password you pasted into it (as the warning on the Health page asks), run the command in a container of its own that may write the file's folder and uses the same volumes, and so the same key. From deploy/docker, in a shell or PowerShell:

docker compose run --rm --no-deps --user 0 --cap-add CHOWN --cap-add DAC_OVERRIDE --cap-add FOWNER -v "${PWD}:/work" signalith secrets encrypt -c /work/signalith.yaml
docker compose restart signalith

That container has the service's hardening (no privileges, a read-only file system), so the command gives back only what it needs. --user 0 with DAC_OVERRIDE reads the setup step's secrets and the key, which belong to the container's account, and writes your file; CHOWN and FOWNER keep your file's owner and permissions and give a key it makes to the container's account, so the server can read it. The folder is mounted, not just the file, because the file is replaced through a temporary file next to it. Any other signalith secrets command runs the same way (set asks for the value in the terminal).

A password not pasted yet needs none of this: enter the OpenSearch password and the AI model's API key on the Settings page, which keeps them encrypted in the volume, or give a secret to the container in a file with a SIGNALITH_*_FILE variable (see Configuration).

docs.title: Backing up the key
docs.text:
Back up the key file, and keep the copy apart from backups of signalith.yaml and the lookups folder: whoever has both can decrypt the passwords. A password manager or a vault is a good place; the file is short text on Linux and Docker. After rotate-master, back up the new key.

On Windows the .dpapi file can only be read on the same Windows installation, so a copy helps when you restore that server (a VM snapshot or system backup), not on a new one. Keep the passwords themselves in your vault too, or use a key file you can move (above).

A backup of the state folder (or of the Docker volumes) also holds the files the master key does not encrypt, such as Signalith's HTTPS CA key (tls/ca.key; see Not encrypted by the master key). Give such a backup the same care as the key, or leave the tls folder out: a server restored without it makes a new CA, which browsers and agents then have to trust again.

docs.title: Losing the key
docs.text:
Losing the key loses only the stored passwords and keys, never events, and the server keeps running. Enter them again:

  • In signalith.yaml, each value that cannot be decrypted is left out, as if it were not set, and the server log, signalith validate and the Health page name it with the command that replaces it:
Warning: In signalith.yaml, ingest.tokens[0] is encrypted with master key c656730c, but no master key was found. Restore the master key it was encrypted with, or enter the value again; without that key only stored passwords and keys are lost, never events. Remove it from ingest.tokens and add a token with: signalith secrets set ingest.tokens. Signalith runs without it until then.

Agents that send with that token are refused until it is replaced, and without opensearch.password OpenSearch refuses Signalith (the Health page shows it); the web pages, syslog and other tokens keep working.

signalith secrets set opensearch.password (or assistant.api_key, auth.ldap.bind_password) replaces a value; for a shared agent token, remove the line and add one with signalith secrets set ingest.tokens (or, better, give the agents their own tokens; see agent-tokens.md). While the file holds values encrypted with a key that is not found, set and encrypt stop rather than make a new key, since the key may only be elsewhere (such as in a variable the service has and your shell does not). When it really is lost, add -new-key to the first command: sudo signalith secrets set opensearch.password -new-key. - A password or API key saved on the Settings page that cannot be decrypted is left out too, as if it were not set; the other settings saved there are still used. Its field on the Settings page, the server log, signalith validate and the Health page say so. Enter it again on the Settings page, or take it off the page there (or with signalith settings reset opensearch.password) to use the one in signalith.yaml again: signalith secrets set writes only signalith.yaml, and says when the page has its own, which is used instead. When OpenSearch refuses Signalith without it, a restart says why and sets none of the page's settings aside. - Directory sign-in keeps running but cannot search for users until you enter the service account password again on the Users page, under Directory sign-in. The Health page and the log say so. Signalith does not try a wrong password, so the account is not locked out. - A threat intel feed whose key cannot be decrypted stops downloading and shows why on the Threat intel page. For a feed added on the page, edit it and enter the key again; for one in signalith.yaml, replace the value with the plain one and run signalith secrets encrypt. Other feeds keep running.

signalith secrets status lists everything that cannot be decrypted.

docs.title: Changing the key
docs.text:
Change the master key when someone who could read it leaves, or when a copy may have leaked:

$ sudo signalith secrets rotate-master
New master key dea48fde in /var/lib/signalith/keys/master.key.
Encrypted 2 values again in /etc/signalith/signalith.yaml
Encrypted 1 value again in /var/lib/signalith/lookups/directory.json
Encrypted 3 values again in /var/lib/signalith/lookups/intel_feeds.yaml
Encrypted 1 value again in /var/lib/signalith/lookups/settings.yaml
The previous key (9096cd23) is kept as /var/lib/signalith/keys/master.key.old, so files saved before now can still be read.
A running server picks up the new key by itself.
Next: back up the new key, then remove the previous one with: signalith secrets rotate-master -prune

Every file is written next to its place first and checked; if any cannot be put in place, everything (the key included) is put back as it was and the command says "Nothing was changed". The previous key is kept so that a file restored from an older backup can still be read. When nothing needs it any more:

$ sudo signalith secrets rotate-master -prune
Removed the previous master key /var/lib/signalith/keys/master.key.old (key id 9096cd23).
Backups of files from before the rotation now need a backup of that key to be read.

-prune keeps the previous key, and says why, while a value still needs it (such as a file restored from a backup; signalith secrets encrypt encrypts it with the new key), while a value cannot be decrypted at all (it might need that key), or while the previous key cannot be read. A key in SIGNALITH_MASTER_KEY cannot be rotated by Signalith: change the variable yourself, or move the key to a file.

docs.title: Commands
docs.text:
Command What it does signalith secrets status [-c file] Where the master key is, and how each stored password or key is kept signalith secrets encrypt [-c file] Encrypts plain values (and values still under the previous key), changing nothing else in the files signalith secrets set <setting> [-c file] Stores opensearch.password, assistant.api_key, auth.ldap.bind_password, or another of ingest.tokens (a shared agent token; per-agent tokens come from signalith tokens create), encrypted. It asks twice without showing what you type, or reads one line from a pipe; for an agent token, press Enter to have one made signalith secrets encrypt -new-key, set <setting> -new-key The same, making a new master key although the files hold values encrypted with one that is not found (when that key is lost) signalith secrets rotate-master [-c file] Makes a new master key and encrypts every stored value again with it signalith secrets rotate-master -prune [-c file] Removes the previous master key once nothing needs it signalith secrets decrypt [-c file] Writes every stored password and key as plain text again, before going back to an older version (below)

All of them write each file whole through a temporary file (a crash never leaves half a file) and keep its permissions and owner. When a file is a link, the file it points to is written and the link stays.

docs.title: Going back to an older version
docs.text:
Versions of Signalith from before encryption cannot read encrypted values: they would use the enc:v1:... text itself as the password, and for directory sign-in repeated wrong passwords can lock the service account out. So before putting an older version back, stop the server and write the values as plain text again:

sudo systemctl stop signalith
sudo signalith secrets decrypt
sudo install -m 0755 signalith-old-version /usr/local/bin/signalith
sudo systemctl start signalith

On Windows, in a PowerShell opened as Administrator, run Stop-Service Signalith and & "$env:ProgramFiles\Signalith\signalith.exe" secrets decrypt, then the older version's install.ps1. In Docker, from deploy/docker (the second command is the one Docker explains):

docker compose stop signalith
docker compose run --rm --no-deps --user 0 --cap-add CHOWN --cap-add DAC_OVERRIDE --cap-add FOWNER -v "${PWD}:/work" signalith secrets decrypt -c /work/signalith.yaml

then check out the older version and start it. If you skip this, enter the directory password and feed keys again in the older version, and the OpenSearch password and AI API key saved on the Settings page (an older version with that page would send their encrypted text as they are), or restore the files from a backup made before the upgrade. Going forward again needs nothing: the new version encrypts them again.

docs.title: Disk encryption
docs.text:
The master key protects passwords and keys in copies of files: a backup, a support ticket, a Git commit. Events, archives and the key itself are protected on the server by encrypting its disks:

  • Windows: BitLocker on the system drive and the drives holding OpenSearch data and archives (manage-bde -on C:, or Settings > Privacy & security > Device encryption).
  • Linux: LUKS. Choose "encrypt" when installing the system, or use cryptsetup luksFormat for a data disk and put OpenSearch's data folder and the archive folder on it.
  • Docker Desktop: its virtual disk lives on your computer's drive; encrypt that drive (BitLocker on Windows, FileVault on macOS).
  • Cloud servers: Azure (managed disks) and Google Cloud encrypt disks by default; on AWS turn on "EBS encryption by default" for the region, or encrypt each volume. Make sure snapshots and backups are encrypted too.
  • OpenSearch snapshots and archives you copy elsewhere need the same protection at their destination.

The Security page (Settings > Security) and signalith security show whether the disk under Signalith's files, its archives and OpenSearch's data is encrypted, as far as the server can tell, and how to check by hand where it can't (see Disk encryption in docs/security.md).

docs.title: In use
docs.text:
While it runs, the server holds decrypted passwords and keys in memory. Signalith keeps them there:

  • Not printed: logs, API replies and errors show [redacted] or *** instead of passwords and keys.
  • No dumps: on Linux the server turns off core dumps and marks itself not-dumpable when it starts, which also stops other programs running as the same account from reading its memory. A crash prints only the failing goroutine (unless GOTRACEBACK asks for more) and never writes a core file.
  • systemd unit (deploy/systemd/signalith.service): no swap (MemorySwapMax=0), no core dumps (LimitCORE=0), private /tmp, other processes hidden, the system read-only, and only the system calls an ordinary service needs. systemd-analyze security signalith rates it 1.7 (OK).
  • Windows service: runs as its own account, NT SERVICE\Signalith, not LocalSystem. Only Administrators and SYSTEM can read another account's memory.

What remains: an administrator or root on the server can read any process's memory. Go cannot reliably wipe a value from memory once it is a string, so decrypted passwords may stay in memory until it is reused (Signalith clears the master key and decrypted bytes where it can).

To protect memory from the people who run the hardware too (a cloud provider, a hosting company), run Signalith and OpenSearch on a confidential VM, where the processor encrypts the VM's memory: Azure confidential VMs (DCasv5, ECasv5 and DCesv5 series), Google Cloud Confidential VMs (N2D with AMD SEV, C3 with Intel TDX), or AWS EC2 instances with AMD SEV-SNP (M6a, C6a, R6a). Nothing in Signalith needs to change.

The Security page and signalith security check that crash dumps are off, whether swap could hold Signalith's memory, and whether the service runs with its protections. They also say when they find a confidential VM. See Memory and Service protections in docs/security.md.

docs.title: Environment variables
docs.text: Variable Meaning SIGNALITH_STATE_DIR Folder for files Signalith makes for itself: its master key (in keys/), its HTTPS certificate (in tls/) and this server's identity (node.id). Default: the folder that holds the lookups folder (see docs/servers.md for when another one is used). The systemd unit and the Docker image set /var/lib/signalith SIGNALITH_MASTER_KEY_FILE A file holding the master key (32 bytes, or one line of base64 or hex) SIGNALITH_MASTER_KEY The master key itself, in base64. Weaker than a file; Signalith warns while it is used CREDENTIALS_DIRECTORY Set by systemd for LoadCredential=; Signalith reads master.key there

docs.title: Endpoints (osquery)
docs.text:
Signalith can manage hosts that run osquery, the open-source endpoint agent. Signalith is osquery's management server: hosts enroll with an ingest token, fetch what to collect from Signalith, and send their results back. Nothing else is set up on the host, and changes on the Endpoints page reach every host within five minutes.

Each host reports:

What Data model When Files created, changed, renamed or deleted in the watched folders, with their SHA-256 on Linux and macOS Filesystem within a minute Listening ports and the program behind each Inventory (inventory_type=port) every 10 minutes Operating system, installed software, accounts, services and startup items, as they are added or removed Inventory (inventory_type=os, software, user, service, startup) every hour (adjustable) Configuration checks, when a result changes Configuration_Check every hour (adjustable)

Inventory and checks are sent the first time in full, then only what changed, so an unchanged host sends nothing. osquery runs them on the hour, so a newly enrolled host's inventory and check results appear within the hour; a live query shows anything sooner.

Hosts found this way are also added to the asset list (Risk and context), as category=endpoint with their platform, unless your own list already has them.

docs.title: Adding hosts
docs.text:
1. Open Add data, pick osquery, and choose the platform the hosts run.
  2. Install osquery 5 on each host from https://osquery.io/downloads.
  3. Download the setup script and run it on each host:
  4. Linux and macOS: sudo sh signalith-osquery-setup.sh
  5. Windows, in an elevated PowerShell: powershell -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File "$env:USERPROFILE\Downloads\signalith-osquery-setup.ps1"
  6. On macOS, give osqueryd Full Disk Access (System Settings, Privacy & Security, Full Disk Access, add /opt/osquery/lib/osquery.app).

The script saves three files next to osquery (/etc/osquery on Linux, /var/osquery on macOS, C:\Program Files\osquery on Windows): Signalith's CA certificate, the enroll secret (readable only by root, or SYSTEM and Administrators), and osquery.flags, which points osquery at Signalith. It then restarts osquery. The host appears on the Endpoints page within a minute.

The script holds an agent token of its own, made when you copy or download it on Add data, so keep it private. osquery always checks Signalith's certificate. It checks it against the address it connects to, so use a host name the certificate covers; an IP address works only with the certificate Signalith makes itself.

Each host is one row, keyed by its hardware UUID, even when osquery is reinstalled.

docs.title: The Endpoints page
docs.text:
Analysts and admins can open Endpoints:

  • Hosts lists every host with its status (online when seen in the last three minutes), failing checks, address and osquery version, plus the log agents sending from each computer (a Log agent column, and rows of their own for computers without osquery; see Log agents). Open one for its hardware, addresses, configuration fetch, osquery's own errors, and every check result with how to fix it. Links there open the host's file changes and inventory changes in Search.
  • Configuration checks lists every check with how many hosts pass and fail, and which hosts fail.
  • Live query (admins) runs osquery SQL on hosts now: all hosts, one platform, or one host, optionally only those online. Online hosts answer within about ten seconds. Results can be saved as CSV. A query stays open for ten minutes, returns at most 1,000 rows and 4 KB per value per host, and is recorded in the audit log. The table reference is at https://osquery.io/schema/.

Admins also have:

  • What hosts collect: turn file monitoring and checks on or off, edit the watched paths and the paths left out per platform, and set how often inventory and checks run (5 minutes to 24 hours). Paths use osquery's patterns: % matches within one folder level and %% matches everything below. Saving warns when someone else saved since you opened it.
  • Remove: deletes the host's record so its key stops working. A host still running osquery enrolls again at its next contact, unless you also choose Block: then it is refused until you unblock it. Events it already sent stay in Search.

docs.title: Watched paths by default
docs.text:
Platform Paths Linux /etc, /bin, /sbin, /usr/bin, /usr/sbin, /usr/local/bin, /usr/local/sbin, /boot, /root/.ssh, /home/*/.ssh, /var/spool/cron (leaving out /etc/mtab and /etc/ld.so.cache) Windows drivers\etc, System32\Tasks, System32\GroupPolicy, and the all-users and per-user Startup folders macOS /etc, /Library/LaunchDaemons, /Library/LaunchAgents, ~/Library/LaunchAgents, /usr/local/bin, ~/.ssh, /var/root/.ssh

These are the places attackers change to stay on a host or gain rights. Watching large, busy folders makes osquery work harder; add only what you need.

docs.title: Log agents
docs.text:
The Hosts list also shows the log agents (Fluent Bit and OpenTelemetry Collectors) that send events to Signalith, from every server that shares this OpenSearch. There is no separate list: an agent on a computer that also runs osquery is shown on that host's row, matched by computer name (the part before the first dot, ignoring capitals), and an agent on a computer without osquery gets a row of its own marked Log agent only.

The Log agent column says one of:

  • Sending, 2m ago: events arrived recently.
  • Silent since 10:42: nothing for more than an hour. Check that the agent runs and can reach Signalith.
  • Needs a new configuration: open the row to see why, in plain words:
  • it trusts a different certificate authority than this server uses, so its connections fail (this also shows for a computer that keeps refusing this server's certificate, even though none of its events got through);
  • it sends without encryption (plain HTTP) from another computer (plain HTTP from the Signalith computer itself never crosses the network, so it is fine);
  • its agent token was revoked.

Use the All / Silent / Needs a new configuration buttons to narrow the list. Opening an agent shows its addresses, the servers it sends to, HTTPS or plain HTTP, its agent token, its events in the last hour, and when it was first and last seen. Admins get Get a new configuration, which opens Add data on the agent's system: make the new configuration there (it comes with a new agent token) and put it on the computer.

Fluent Bit configurations made on Add data from this version on tell Signalith the computer's name. An agent set up before that is listed by its address and agent token, with a note that a new configuration would show its computer name; it keeps working as it is. An OpenTelemetry Collector is named by the computer name on its events; one that passes on events from several computers is listed by its address and agent token. A configuration made while a new certificate authority is being prepared trusts both, so the agent is still fine after the switch. Two computers with the same name are shown as one row with both addresses. An agent not heard from for 30 days is removed from the list. The computer name an agent sends is only a label: it never lets anyone in.

docs.title: Configuration checks
docs.text:
91 checks ship with Signalith: 45 for Linux, 26 for Windows and 20 for macOS. Each says what a passing host does, why it matters, and how to fix it.

  • The Linux checks are based on rules in the SCAP Security Guide (BSD-3-Clause), and name the rule and its NIST SP 800-53 controls. Search finds them with datamodel=Configuration_Check benchmark="SCAP Security Guide".
  • The Windows and macOS checks follow the vendors' own hardening guidance.

A result is pass, fail, n/a (the check does not apply, such as SSH settings on a host without an SSH server) or error. Each change of result is an event, so datamodel=Configuration_Check result=fail | stats count by check, dest shows what fails where.

docs.title: Searching
docs.text:
datamodel=Filesystem dest=web1 action=modified
datamodel=Filesystem file_path="/etc/sudoers*"
datamodel=Inventory inventory_type=software action=added | stats count by name, version
datamodel=Inventory inventory_type=port dest_port=3389
datamodel=Configuration_Check result=fail severity=high

Every osquery event has vendor_product=osquery, sourcetype=osquery:<query> and endpoint_id, the host's ID on the Endpoints page.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
osquery uses its TLS remote API with these routes on Signalith's HTTPS port:

Route Use POST /api/osquery/enroll The host sends the enroll secret (an agent token) and gets its own node key POST /api/osquery/config The host fetches what to collect, every five minutes POST /api/osquery/log Results and osquery's own status messages POST /api/osquery/distributed/read The host asks for live queries, every ten seconds POST /api/osquery/distributed/write Live query answers

They take a token or node key instead of a signed-in user. Node keys are random; Signalith stores only their hash. Hosts and settings are kept in OpenSearch (the <prefix>_endpoints index), so every Signalith server knows every host, and a host sending to another server runs each live query once.

Revoking the agent token a host enrolled with, or choosing Stop accepting on a shared token, removes every host enrolled with it, on every server, and their next request is refused at once. A host whose shared token was deleted from signalith.yaml or the environment is refused too. They enroll again with an active token. See agent-tokens.md.

docs.title: Getting started
docs.text:
Signalith needs two things: OpenSearch 2.x, where events are stored, and the signalith server, a single program with the web UI built in. The Docker quick start runs both for you; on Linux and Windows you install OpenSearch first and then Signalith next to it.

Way to run it Good for Takes Docker quick start Trying Signalith, labs, small sites Two commands Linux A systemd service on a server OpenSearch, then a few commands Windows A Windows service OpenSearch, then one script

docs.title: Docker quick start
docs.text:
Clone the repository and start it (later, run the commands from that folder):

git clone https://github.com/jrsamsanchez/Signalith.git signalith
cd signalith
docker compose -f deploy/docker/docker-compose.yml up -d
docker compose -f deploy/docker/docker-compose.yml exec signalith signalith initial-password

The up command starts OpenSearch and Signalith. On the first start a setup step makes the admin password, the agents' ingest token and the certificates OpenSearch and Signalith use with each other, and keeps them in Docker volumes; no password is written in the compose files. The last command shows the admin password.

Open https://localhost:8080 and sign in as admin with that password.

The browser warns about the certificate

Signalith serves HTTPS with a certificate it makes for itself, so the browser warns until you trust it. The sign-in page has a Download the server certificate link; HTTPS shows how to trust it on Windows, macOS and Linux.

OpenSearch runs with its security plugin on: it answers only over HTTPS, publishes no port, and lets in only Signalith's certificate, which may use only Signalith's own indices. See Securing OpenSearch.

To change the admin password (the first one then stops working):

docker compose -f deploy/docker/docker-compose.yml exec signalith signalith passwd
docker compose -f deploy/docker/docker-compose.yml restart signalith

Settings changed on the Settings page are kept in the signalith-data volume, so they survive updates. To update, run git pull and then the up command again; it downloads the Signalith image built from the newest code. To run a release instead, or to build the image from your own checkout, see Running a release, or building the image yourself. After a reboot everything starts again by itself once Docker is running (in Docker Desktop, turn on Start Docker Desktop when you sign in).

Coming from an older quick start?

Earlier versions served plain HTTP and took the admin password from docker-compose.yml. The README has step-by-step upgrade instructions that keep your events, findings, users and detections.

docs.title: Try it with sample data
docs.text:
No logs to hand? On the Add data page (under Data, admins only), Load sample data fills Signalith with a week of made-up activity for a fictional company, with a handful of attacks hidden in it, so detections fire, the triage queue fills, risk builds up, threat intel matches and the dashboards light up. Everything is fictional and kept apart from your own data, and one click removes all of it. From the shell:

docker compose -f deploy/docker/docker-compose.yml exec signalith signalith sample-data load

Sample data has a guided tour of the attacks it contains.

docs.title: Linux
docs.text:
1. Install OpenSearch 2.x (instructions).

  2. Install Signalith:

    sudo install -m 0755 signalith-linux-amd64 /usr/local/bin/signalith
sudo useradd --system --no-create-home signalith
sudo signalith init -c /etc/signalith/signalith.yaml -opensearch http://127.0.0.1:9200
sudo chown -R signalith /etc/signalith /var/lib/signalith
sudo cp deploy/systemd/signalith.service /etc/systemd/system/
sudo systemctl enable --now signalith

    init prints the admin password once, and where it put the master key that encrypts the passwords and keys Signalith stores (/var/lib/signalith/keys/master.key). Back that file up, apart from the config; see Encryption.

  3. Open https://<server>:8080 and sign in as admin.

  4. Replace OpenSearch's demo security setup, whose passwords and certificates are public, and have Signalith sign in with a certificate of its own: Securing OpenSearch.

To upgrade, stop the service, replace the program and the unit, encrypt passwords an older version kept as plain text, and start it again:

sudo systemctl stop signalith
sudo install -m 0755 signalith-linux-amd64 /usr/local/bin/signalith
sudo cp deploy/systemd/signalith.service /etc/systemd/system/
sudo systemctl daemon-reload
sudo signalith secrets encrypt
sudo systemctl start signalith
sudo signalith secrets status

Older versions cannot read encrypted values: before going back to one, run sudo signalith secrets decrypt (see Going back to an older version).

docs.title: Windows
docs.text:
1. Install OpenSearch 2.x for Windows (instructions).

  2. In an elevated PowerShell, from the folder holding signalith.exe and deploy\windows\install.ps1:
