Open Add data, pick OpenTelemetry, and choose where the Collector runs:

  • Linux: reads /var/log/auth.log or /var/log/secure, or the systemd journal, like the Fluent Bit agent.
  • Windows: reads the Security event log, Sysmon when Include Sysmon is on, and PowerShell script blocks when Include PowerShell is on.

Either way the Collector also listens on 127.0.0.1:4317 (gRPC) and 127.0.0.1:4318 (HTTP) for apps on that host that export OTLP logs, and passes those on too.

The page gives the steps and a complete config.yaml for the Collector Contrib distribution (otelcol-contrib, 0.100 or later): it already holds this server's address, an agent token of its own (made when you copy or download the configuration) and, over HTTPS, Signalith's CA certificate to check the server with. It keeps unsent logs and its place in each log on disk, so a restart or an outage of Signalith neither loses nor repeats events.

If the Collector already sends elsewhere, keep your config and add Signalith's parts to it: the otlphttp/signalith exporter (and file_storage/signalith, which it uses), plus a pipeline, or add the exporter to an existing logs pipeline.

docs.title: Send from your own Collector or SDK
docs.text:
Any OTLP/HTTP sender works. Point it at:

Setting Value Logs endpoint https://<server>:8080/api/otlp/v1/logs (or endpoint https://<server>:8080/api/otlp, to which the exporter adds /v1/logs) Header Authorization: Bearer <agent token>; make one on Add data under Agent tokens, or with signalith tokens create (see agent-tokens.md) Encoding protobuf (application/x-protobuf, the Collector's default) or JSON (application/json) Compression gzip (the Collector's default) or none CA Signalith's CA certificate (/api/tls/ca.pem), unless the server has a certificate your systems trust

For example, with curl:

curl --cacert signalith-ca.pem https://siem.example.com:8080/api/otlp/v1/logs \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"resourceLogs":[{"resource":{"attributes":[{"key":"service.name","value":{"stringValue":"shop"}}]},
       "scopeLogs":[{"logRecords":[{"severityText":"ERROR","body":{"stringValue":"payment failed"}}]}]}]}'

Only logs are taken: gRPC, metrics and traces are not. Over plain HTTP to the HTTPS port, OTLP follows server.tls.plaintext_ingest, as the agents do.

docs.title: How records are mapped
docs.text:
Records from the Collector's own receivers for sources Signalith already parses are mapped as the Fluent Bit agent's records are, so the built-in detections fire whichever agent collects them:

Receiver Becomes windowseventlog (Security log 4624, 4625, 4648, 4656, 4657, 4661, 4662, 4663, 4688, 4697, 4698, 4706, 4719, 4720, 4726, 4728, 4732, 4738, 4756, 4768, 4769, 4794, 5136, 5145, 5156, 5157; System 7045; Sysmon 1, 3, 6, 7, 8, 10, 11, 12, 13, 14, 15, 17, 18, 22, 23, 26; PowerShell 4104) Authentication, Endpoint, Change, Network_Traffic, Image_Load, Filesystem, Registry, Network_Resolution, Script filelog on auth.log or secure (or any syslog-format file) Authentication and Change for sshd, sudo, su and account changes journald as the agent's journal input syslog as Signalith's own syslog receiver

Both of the windowseventlog receiver's event_data_format settings work (map, the default in recent versions, and array).

Any other record is an Other event with sourcetype=otel:

  • message is the body (a structured body as JSON, with its top-level keys also as fields).
  • Attributes, then resource attributes, become fields, with dots turned into underscores (http.route becomes http_route). Common semantic-convention names map onto Signalith's own: user.name and enduser.id to user, client.address and source.address to src, server.address and destination.address to dest (and their ports to src_port and dest_port), http.request.method to http_method, http.response.status_code to status, url.full to url, user_agent.original to http_user_agent, process.pid, process.executable.path and process.command_line to process_id, process_path and process, and file.path and file.name to file_path and file_name.
  • The resource's host.name is host, and service.name is service.
  • severity is the severity text (or the name of the severity number), and severity_id the number; trace_id, span_id and otel_scope (the instrumentation scope) are kept, so a search can follow one request.

Every record also gets host, service, trace_id and span_id when it has them.

The event's time is the record's own time, else the time in its log line, else when the Collector saw it. As for every source, a time older than ingest.max_event_age or more than an hour ahead is filed under the time it arrived (see Ingest limits).

docs.title: Limits and errors
docs.text: The same limits as agent batches apply: up to 16 MB per request (also after gzip is undone), 200,000 records of at most 1 MB each, values nested at most 32 levels. A request over a limit or that does not decode is refused with 4xx and a message saying why, and nothing from it is stored; the Collector logs the message and drops the batch, so keep batches small (the generated config's batch processor sends at most 5,000 records). When Signalith is busy or OpenSearch is down the answer is 503 with Retry-After, and the Collector keeps the batch and sends it again. Records OpenSearch turns away are counted in the answer's partial success.

docs.title: Playbooks
docs.text:
A playbook does the first steps for you when a detection raises a finding: tell the team, block the address once an analyst approves it, open a case, set the finding to In progress. Set playbooks up on the Playbooks page, under Detect & respond. Only admins see that page. Analysts approve or reject the steps that wait for them on the Approvals page, under Monitor.

A playbook has three parts:

  • When: the detections it starts for (any detection, or only some) and the least urgency, such as "high or above".
  • Then: the steps, in order.
  • Ask for approval in: an optional notification channel that is told when a step waits for approval.

The page sums each playbook up in one sentence, for example:

When brute-force fires at high or above: notify Slack #soc, then block IP on the edge firewall for the source IP after approval, then open a case (or add to the one it opened), then set the finding to In progress.

A playbook runs once per finding. It starts for findings raised after it was added or turned on, never for older ones, so turning a playbook on does not replay last week's findings. Findings from the one-click sample data are skipped unless Include sample data (under More options) is on. With it on, the steps still really run, so a sample finding can block a real address or send a real message.

docs.title: Steps
docs.text:
Step What it does Notify a channel Sends the finding to one notification channel, as a rule would. It does not wait for the notification rules: it sends even when no rule matches. A finding goes to a channel once, so when a rule already sent it there, the step says so and sends nothing more, and a rule that matches later sends nothing either. A message that fails is tried again, as a rule's is, and shows under Recent deliveries. Run a response action Runs one response action on a target taken from the finding. See below. Open a case Opens an investigation with the finding in it. The title may use {title} {detection} {urgency} {src} {dest} {user} {host} {finding_id} (it is the finding's title when left empty), and an owner may be set. With Add later findings to the case this playbook opened on, a later finding goes into the last case this playbook opened while that case is still open, instead of opening another one. Set the finding Sets the finding's status, its owner, or both.

A playbook has at most 20 steps, and a server at most 100 playbooks.

docs.title: Response actions in a playbook
docs.text:
Pick the action and its target:

  • Source, Destination, User or Host: the finding's src, dest, user or host entity.
  • First entity that fits: the first of the finding's entities the action can act on (an IP for an IP action, a user for a user action, and so on).
  • A fixed value: always the same target, such as a webhook that takes no target, or a quarantine group.

The target is checked exactly as when an analyst runs the action by hand. If the finding has no such value, or it is not the right kind (a user name for an IP action), the step fails and the playbook stops.

Disruptive actions always wait for approval. An action marked disruptive on the Response actions page (block an IP, disable an account, isolate a host) cannot run without an analyst saying yes, whatever the playbook says. Other actions wait too when Wait for an analyst to approve is on. A webhook that only opens a ticket or starts a workflow can run without approval.

Every run of an action is recorded in the response actions log, like a run by hand, with the reason "Playbook name, for finding title (id)." It is run by the playbook (automatic), and an approved one names the analyst who approved it (approved_by).

docs.title: Approvals
docs.text:
When a playbook reaches an action that waits for approval, it stops there and the step shows on the Approvals page with the same sentence the Respond dialog shows, such as what will be sent, to which server, with the target in bold. The navigation counts the steps that wait, the finding says so at the top of its Overview, and the playbook's approval channel, if it has one, gets a message with a link to the page.

  • Approve runs the action, then the rest of the playbook, within a few seconds. The analyst who approved is recorded on the action run, in the audit log, on the finding and on the case.
  • Reject stops the playbook for this finding. The steps after it do not run.
  • Either can take a note, such as a ticket number. It is kept with the decision and shown on the finding.
  • A step nobody approves within 24 hours expires. It is not done, and the playbook stops for that finding.

Only one decision counts. If two analysts press Approve at the same moment, one wins and the other is told "It was already approved by ann." The action runs once. Viewers see neither the page nor the buttons.

Everything a playbook does is written down twice: as a comment on the finding, by "playbook name", and on the case's timeline once the playbook has opened or used a case.

docs.title: A run, step by step
docs.text:
1. A detection raises a finding. Within 15 seconds the server that runs the background jobs sees it, and every playbook that is on and matches it starts.
  2. The steps run in order. Each result is saved as it happens and listed under Recent runs on the Playbooks page.
  3. A step that waits for approval pauses the run (Waiting for approval).
  4. A step that fails stops the run (Failed). The steps after it do not run, and the finding says why. Nothing is retried, since an action that half-ran could do harm the second time; run it from the finding with Respond if it should still happen.
  5. When every step is done, the run is Done.

Runs are kept for 90 days in the <prefix>_playbook_runs index.

Changing a playbook does not change the runs it already started. A run waiting for approval keeps the steps it started with, so what an analyst approves is what was planned. Deleting or turning off a playbook stops new runs; runs that already wait can still be approved or rejected.

docs.title: Which server runs playbooks
docs.text:
Only one server runs playbooks: the server that holds the background jobs (see servers.md), in the job playbooks. It checks it still holds them before each step. Approving and rejecting work on every server; the server running the jobs picks the decision up within 15 seconds.

  • Each run is claimed by creating a record whose ID is made from the finding and the playbook, so it is the same on every server. Only one server can create it, so a playbook runs at most once for a finding, even right after the jobs move to another server.
  • If the jobs move between two steps, the next server goes on with the next step.
  • If a server stops in the middle of a step, that step may or may not have happened, so the run is not started again. After about 15 minutes it is marked Interrupted: "The Signalith server stopped while this playbook ran, so its last step may or may not have happened." Check the finding and finish by hand.
  • If no server runs the jobs for a while, playbooks start for the findings raised meanwhile once one does, up to 24 hours back. Steps that need approval still wait for it.
  • With detections.scheduler: false on every server, no playbook runs.

docs.title: Where the playbooks live
docs.text:
Playbooks are kept in playbooks.yaml in the lookups folder (setting playbooks.file, environment SIGNALITH_PLAYBOOKS_FILE; a relative path is relative to the config file). They hold no secrets: channels and actions are named, not copied, so their secrets stay in their own files. Edit them on the page rather than by hand.

Like the notifications file, the playbooks file belongs to the server that runs the jobs. On other servers the page shows the playbooks but cannot change them, and names the server to use. If the jobs could move to a server whose playbooks file differs, the Servers page says so; copy the file to every server that may run the jobs.

If the file cannot be read, no playbook starts, and the page shows the error.

docs.title: Example: block, then open a case
docs.text:
1. On Response actions, add the Block IP on OPNsense/pfSense (alias API) template and call it "Block IP on the edge firewall". It is disruptive.
  2. On Notifications, add a Slack channel #soc.
  3. On Playbooks, choose Contain after approval (or Add playbook):
  4. When: only auth-brute-force and auth-password-spray, at high or above.
  5. Then: Notify #soc; Run Block IP on the edge firewall on the Source; Open a case titled Brute force from {src} with the reuse box on; Set the finding to In progress.
  6. Ask for approval in: #soc.

When brute force from 203.0.113.7 fires, Slack #soc gets the finding, then a message that the playbook waits for approval to send the firewall request for 203.0.113.7, with a link to the Approvals page. An analyst opens Approvals, adds "Confirmed in VPN logs" and approves. The address is blocked, case C-12 "Brute force from 203.0.113.7" is opened with the finding in it, and the finding is set to In progress. A second burst an hour later waits for its own approval and goes into C-12 too.

docs.title: Shuffle and other SOAR tools
docs.text:
A playbook can hand off to a SOAR such as Shuffle. Add the SOAR's webhook as a response action (the Shuffle workflow webhook template, see response-actions.md), then add it to a playbook as a step. Its target is any entity, so pick the one the workflow should get, or A fixed value.

The Shuffle template is marked disruptive, so the step waits for an analyst to approve it. For a workflow that only enriches or opens a ticket, turn Disruptive off on that action: the step then runs at once (unless Wait for an analyst to approve is on), the SOAR gets the finding, and its workflow takes over. What the workflow does afterwards shows in the SOAR, not in Signalith.

docs.title: API
docs.text:
Route Who What it does GET /api/playbooks admins The playbooks, each with its summary, and the page's details: revision, file, file_error, manage (whether this server can change them) and runs_on, the channels and actions a step can use, and approval_hours PUT /api/playbooks admins Replaces the playbooks with the body (revision, playbooks). A body with problems is refused with 400 and problems (where, field, message). A stale revision, or another server running the jobs, gives 409. GET /api/playbooks/runs?status=&finding_id=&playbook_id=&limit= analysts Runs, newest first, with total and waiting (how many wait for approval). status takes one status or a comma list: running, waiting_approval, approved, queued, succeeded, failed, rejected, expired, interrupted. POST /api/playbooks/runs/{id}/approve analysts Approves the step a run waits on. Body: {"note": "..."}, optional, up to 1,000 characters. Answers with the run. POST /api/playbooks/runs/{id}/reject analysts Rejects it, with the same body.

Approving or rejecting a run that no longer waits gives 409 with "code": "decided", a sentence saying why (already approved by someone, rejected, or expired) and the run as it is now.

docs.title: Signalith query language
docs.text:
A query is a search followed by zero or more commands, each after a |. The search selects events; commands reshape the results. It reads like Splunk's SPL, but it is Signalith's own language and does not claim SPL compatibility.

datamodel=Authentication action=failure earliest=-24h
| stats count, dc(user) as users by src
| where count > 20
| sort -count
| head 10

docs.title: Search
docs.text:
Syntax Meaning datamodel=Authentication Events of one data model: Authentication, Endpoint, Network_Traffic, Change, Malware (antivirus; see antivirus.md), Filesystem, Registry, Network_Resolution, Image_Load, Script, Inventory, Configuration_Check, Alerts, Other. datamodel=Risk searches risk events, which are left out otherwise index=signalith-authentication-2026.10.* One pattern of Signalith's daily indices, <prefix>-<datamodel>-YYYY.MM.DD. It must start with the configured opensearch.index_prefix and -; index=* means all events, as when index= is left out. Lists (a,b), exclusions (-x), other indices and system indices, other clusters (remote:x) and date math are refused field=value Exact match, case-insensitive field=val* Wildcard match with * and ? field=* The field has any value src=10.0.0.0/8, src=fe80::/10 An IPv4 or IPv6 address range (CIDR) field!=value Does not match field=~"pattern" Regular expression (RE2 syntax), found anywhere in the value unless ^ or $ anchor it, and case-sensitive unless it starts with (?i). Also works in where. Word boundaries (\b), (?m) and ^/$ other than at the ends are refused, since the search runs in OpenSearch field>10, >=, <, <= Numeric (or text) comparison field IN (a, b, c) Any of several values word or "a phrase" Text anywhere in the raw event (_raw) NOT term, ( ... ) Negation and grouping a OR b Either. As in SPL, OR binds tighter than the implicit AND, so x a OR b means x AND (a OR b) earliest=-7d@d latest=now Time range; overrides the UI time picker

Relative times: -30s, -15m, -4h, -7d, -2w, -1mon, -1y, optionally snapped with @d, @h, @w. Absolute times are ISO 8601 (2026-10-01T00:00:00Z).

Quote values that contain spaces or symbols: process_path="C:\Windows\System32\cmd.exe". Inside quotes, \" is a quote and \\ is one backslash; any other backslash is kept as typed, so Windows paths work without doubling. In a regular expression that means \. stays \., and a literal backslash is \\\\ (two backslashes after quoting, which the expression reads as one).

docs.title: Commands
docs.text:
Command Example Notes stats stats count, dc(user) as users, avg(bytes) by src, dest Functions: count, count(f), dc(f), sum(f), avg(f), min(f), max(f) timechart timechart span=1h count by action One aggregation when splitting by a field; span picked automatically if omitted top top limit=10 process_name by host Adds count and percent where where count > 20 AND users >= 2 AND binds tighter than OR here, as in most languages sort sort -count, src - for descending head head 20 Also limit table table _time, user, src Also fields; wildcards allowed rename rename src as source_ip enrich enrich or enrich user, dest Adds asset and identity context: <field>_priority, _category, _bunit, plus _owner, _location for assets and _name, _email, _manager, _watchlist for users. With no fields it enriches user, src_user, src, dest, host, src_host, dest_host and risk_object threatmatch threatmatch or threatmatch src, dest Keeps only events where a field equals a threat intel indicator. Runs inside OpenSearch, so it must come right after the search (before stats and other commands). Adds threat_match_field, threat_match_value, threat_indicator, threat_type, threat_source, threat_weight, threat_description and threat_target (the system on your side) to each event intel intel or intel src, url Adds <field>_intel_source, _intel_type, _intel_weight and _intel_description where a value is a known indicator. Works on any result, including after stats

With no fields, threatmatch and intel check src, dest, src_ip, dest_ip, dest_host, domain, query, url_domain, url, the hash fields (process_sha256, process_sha1, process_md5, process_hash, file_hash, file_sha256, file_sha1, file_md5, hash, md5, sha1, sha256) and the email fields (sender, recipient, src_user, user). The threat_* columns are added after OpenSearch returns events, so aggregate on event fields and add intel afterwards: * | threatmatch src | stats count by src, dest | intel src.

Columns produced by stats are referenced by name in later commands, for example sort -dc(user) or where avg(bytes) > 1000.

docs.title: Asking in plain English
docs.text:
The box above the query editor (and signalith ask "...") turns a question into a query. It understands:

You write It adds logins, processes, connections, account changes, risk datamodel=... failed, successful, blocked, allowed, created, deleted action=... from 10.0.0.5, to web1, on dc01, by alice, port 22, user bob field filters; not/except negates powershell, cmd, certutil, mimikatz.exe, spawned by winword process_name, parent_process_name containing mimikatz, "quoted text" process=*...* for processes, text search otherwise last 4 hours, past 7 days, today, yesterday, this week earliest= and latest= how many, distinct users, total bytes, average bytes stats count, dc(), sum(), avg() per user, by source ip, for each host by ... top 10 users, most common processes, rare processes top or stats ... \| sort \| head more than 5, at least 3 hosts where count>5; stats dc(dest) as distinct_dest ... \| where distinct_dest>=3 per hour, over time, daily timechart show user, src and dest table _time, user, src, dest

Names from the asset and identity lists are recognized as users or hosts. When an AI model is configured, questions with unknown words go to it; see Writing queries in the README.

docs.title: How queries run
docs.text:
• The search and any where commands that come before the first stats, timechart or top run inside OpenSearch, so they scale with the cluster.
  • stats and top use composite aggregations and page through every group (up to 50,000 groups, then results are marked truncated).
  • threatmatch becomes terms filters of indicator values (10,000 per clause) and prefix filters for networks, so matching runs inside OpenSearch too.
  • Commands after that run in the Signalith server on the aggregated rows.
  • An event search without stats returns the newest 100 events, or up to search.max_events (at most 100,000) when later commands need to sort or filter them all.
  • Wildcard values (*, ?) can be up to 1,000 characters long, and the wildcard values in where commands up to 4,096 characters together (where runs over every row in the server, so put long filters in the search before the first |). An IN list holds at most 1,000 values.
  • At most 8 searches run at once (detections are counted separately), and one user's searches take at most 4 of those turns. Others wait their turn for up to 15 seconds, then fail with "Signalith is busy running other searches" (or "You already have several searches running"); try again shortly.

Use Explain in the UI, or signalith query -explain "<query>", to see the plain-English steps and the exact OpenSearch request.

docs.title: Releasing
docs.text: How a Signalith release is made, for maintainers. Users want Install from packages.

docs.title: What a release contains
docs.text:
The Release workflow (.github/workflows/release.yml) runs when a tag such as v0.1.0 is pushed. It:

  1. Builds the programs for Linux (amd64, arm64) and Windows (amd64), the .deb and .rpm packages (deploy/packages, built with nFPM) and the .msi (deploy/windows/msi, built with the WiX Toolset v5).
  2. Tests each package: installs the latest earlier release, upgrades it to the new one, signs in, removes it and installs it again, on Ubuntu with systemd, in Rocky Linux 9 and Fedora containers, and on Windows Server. CI runs the same tests on every pull request (the Packages workflow), upgrading from the latest release.
  3. Builds the container image for amd64 and arm64, pushes it to ghcr.io/jrsamsanchez/signalith:<version> (and :latest unless the version has a - suffix such as -rc.1), signs it with Sigstore and attaches its SBOM and provenance. (Between releases, the Image (main) workflow publishes the same kind of signed image as :main on every push to main; the Docker quick start runs it.)
  4. Writes the SBOM (SPDX and CycloneDX, made by Syft from the Linux program), SHA256SUMS, its Sigstore signature, its GPG signature when the key is set up (below), and GitHub build provenance for every file.
  5. Publishes it all on the Releases page, with install and verify steps (.github/release-notes.md) above the generated list of changes. A version with a - suffix is marked as a pre-release.
  6. Once it has published, the Website workflow adds the new packages to the apt and dnf repositories on signalith.io (below), so apt upgrade and dnf upgrade find them.

Run workflow on the Release workflow's page (Actions > Release) is a dry run: it builds and tests everything for the version you enter and keeps the files as a workflow artifact named release, and publishes nothing.

docs.title: Making a release
docs.text:
1. Make sure CI is green on main.

  2. Tag and push:

    git checkout main && git pull
git tag -a v0.1.0 -m "Signalith 0.1.0"
git push origin v0.1.0

  3. Watch Actions > Release. When it is green, the release is on the Releases page and the image on GHCR.

The first time an image is pushed, check that the package is public: the repository's Packages list > signalith > Package settings > Change visibility > Public.

docs.title: Signing keys
docs.text: Every release is signed with Sigstore and has GitHub build provenance without any setup: GitHub vouches for the workflow that built it.

docs.title: GPG (Linux packages and checksums)
docs.text:
apt, dnf and rpm check packages with GPG keys. When the repository has a SIGNALITH_GPG_PRIVATE_KEY secret, the .rpm and .deb packages and SHA256SUMS are signed with it, and the public key is published with each release as signalith-release-key.asc. It also signs the apt and dnf repositories at https://signalith.io/apt and https://signalith.io/rpm, which the Website workflow rebuilds from the five newest releases after every Release run (deploy/repos/build.sh; packages from before the key existed are signed there). Until the secret is set, the website has no repositories.

To make the key (with Docker, on any computer), in an empty folder:

docker run --rm -v "${PWD}:/out" alpine:3.20 sh -c "apk add -q gnupg && gpg --batch --passphrase '' --quick-gen-key 'Signalith releases <releases@signalith.io>' rsa4096 sign 3y && gpg --armor --export-secret-keys > /out/signalith-release-private.asc && gpg --armor --export > /out/signalith-release-key.asc"

Then on GitHub: the repository's Settings > Secrets and variables > Actions > New repository secret, name SIGNALITH_GPG_PRIVATE_KEY, and paste the whole of signalith-release-private.asc (from -----BEGIN to the last -----). Keep a copy of that file somewhere safe and offline, then delete it from the computer. If the key has a passphrase, add it as SIGNALITH_GPG_PASSPHRASE. The key expires after three years; make a new one before then.

docs.title: Content updates
docs.text:
The weekly Content workflow (.github/workflows/content.yml) rebuilds the SigmaHQ and Splunk packs from the newest upstream rules, runs every pack check, and publishes them as a signed bundle on the content release, which servers check for (see Content updates). It signs with an Ed25519 key in the SIGNALITH_CONTENT_KEY secret; without the secret it builds and tests but publishes nothing. Servers only take bundles signed by a key listed in internal/content/trusted.keys, so a new key reaches them with the next release.

To make the key (with Docker, on any computer; the same line works in PowerShell):

docker run --rm alpine:3.20 sh -c 'apk add -q openssl && openssl genpkey -algorithm ed25519 -outform DER -out /k && echo private: $(tail -c 32 /k | base64) && echo public: $(openssl pkey -inform DER -in /k -pubout -outform DER | tail -c 32 | base64)'

(signalith content keygen prints the same pair.) Then on GitHub: the repository's Settings > Secrets and variables > Actions > New repository secret, name SIGNALITH_CONTENT_KEY, and paste the private key line. Add the public key line to internal/content/trusted.keys (the workflow log also prints it, and warns while it is missing). Keep a copy of the private key somewhere safe and offline. To replace a key, add the new public key next to the old one, release, switch the secret, and remove the old key in a later release.

docs.title: Windows code signing
docs.text:
The Release workflow signs the .msi and signalith-windows-amd64.exe with Authenticode through SignPath Foundation, which signs open-source projects for free; the code signing policy is the page it asks projects to publish. Until SignPath is set up, the Windows files are released unsigned and SmartScreen warns before running the installer.

To set it up:

  1. Apply at signpath.org for the Signalith repository.
  2. Once accepted, in SignPath: create the project signalith, connect it to GitHub as its trusted build system, add the artifact configuration from deploy/windows/signpath/artifact-configuration.xml, and create the signing policy release-signing with yourself as approver. Make an API token for a CI user that may submit requests.
  3. On GitHub, Settings > Secrets and variables > Actions: add the secret SIGNPATH_API_TOKEN, and on the Variables tab the variable SIGNPATH_ORGANIZATION_ID. (SIGNPATH_PROJECT_SLUG and SIGNPATH_SIGNING_POLICY_SLUG change the two names above if you chose others.)

From then on, each release run sends the two files to SignPath and waits up to four hours for you to approve the request there (SignPath emails you), checks the signatures on Windows, and publishes the signed files. Every signalith.exe carries its name and version (made by go-winres at build time), which the artifact configuration requires.

docs.title: Version numbers
docs.text: Versions are MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH, with an optional -rc.N style suffix for pre-releases. Windows Installer uses only the three numbers, so a pre-release and its final release share an MSI version; the installer allows that, and the final one replaces the pre-release.

docs.title: Licences of the build tools
docs.text: nFPM (MIT), Syft (Apache 2.0), Sigstore cosign (Apache 2.0) and MkDocs Material (MIT) are open source. The WiX Toolset is MS-RL; from v6 its prebuilt binaries come with an Open Source Maintenance Fee agreement for revenue-making users, so the build pins WiX v5, which has none. None of these tools is shipped inside Signalith.

docs.title: Response actions
docs.text:
A response action is something Signalith does outside itself when an analyst asks: block an IP on the firewall, disable a user in Active Directory, isolate a host, or start a workflow in a SOAR. Admins set the actions up on the Response actions page (under Detect & respond). Analysts run them from a finding or a case with Respond.

Every run goes the same way:

  1. The analyst picks an action, and the target is filled in from the finding's or the case's entities with the right kind (an IP for a block action, a user for a disable action). They can change it.
  2. Actions marked disruptive need a reason. Every action that changes something is disruptive unless an admin says otherwise; "enable" (undo) actions are not by default.
  3. A confirm step says exactly what will happen, for example Disable the AD account jdoe in corp.example.com. Nothing runs before the analyst confirms.
  4. The server checks the target strictly for its kind, writes the run to the audit log, runs the action, and shows the result and output.
  5. The run is noted on the case timeline (where it cannot be removed) or in the finding's activity, and kept in the audit log with who ran it, why, on what, and what came back.

Signalith does not run actions by itself. Playbooks, which will run actions automatically, are planned; they will call the same code and be recorded the same way, as playbook <name>.

docs.title: Who can do what
docs.text:
Role Can Viewer See the timeline entries of runs on a case. Analyst Run actions from a finding or a case, see past runs. Admin Add, change, test and delete actions on the Response actions page.

Each user may start at most 30 runs a minute; more are refused with 429 Too Many Requests until the minute is over.

docs.title: Targets
docs.text:
An action acts on one kind of target, or on any:

Kind Accepted Refused ip One IPv4 or IPv6 address (IPv4-mapped IPv6 is turned into IPv4) Ranges, zones (fe80::1%eth0), 0.0.0.0 and ::, loopback, multicast, broadcast domain Two or more DNS labels: letters, digits and hyphens, up to 253 characters; lower-cased, trailing dot removed Internationalized names (use their xn-- form), a last label that is a number host A host name (one or more labels as above) or an IP address The same as domain and ip user Letters and digits of any script, . _ - @ \ and single spaces, up to 256 characters; one @ and one \ at most (jdoe@corp.example.com, CORP\jdoe) A leading - or ., quotes, control characters, shell or template syntax any Any of the above. The kind is the one of the entity the analyst picked, else guessed: an address is ip, a value with @, \ or a space is user, one with a dot is domain, anything else is host.

These rules apply to every action, whatever it does with the target, so a value can never be read as an option (-rf), a second argument or a template.

docs.title: Send a webhook
docs.text:
Kind http. Sends one HTTP request: a method, a URL, headers, and a body built from a template.

  • Placeholders: {{.ip}}, {{.domain}}, {{.user}}, {{.host}} (the target, under its kind), {{.target}} and {{.target_kind}}, {{.finding_id}}, {{.case_id}}, {{.actor}} (who ran it) and {{.reason}}. A placeholder of another kind is empty: {{.ip}} is empty when the target is a user.
  • No template injection: the text is read once and each placeholder is replaced by its value escaped for where it stands. The result is never read again, so a value can never add placeholders, template code, JSON or URL syntax.
  • In the URL, values are path-escaped before the ? and query-escaped after it. Placeholders cannot stand in the scheme, host or port, so a target can't send the request elsewhere.
  • In a JSON body, values are escaped as the inside of a JSON string; put placeholders between quotes: {"ip": "{{.ip}}"}. The body must be valid JSON once filled in, which is checked when you save.
  • A form body query-escapes values; a text body takes them as they are.
  • Headers are saved encrypted and never shown again. Use Authorization: Bearer <token> for a token, or the user name and password fields for Basic sign-in (not both). Signalith sets Host, Content-Length, Content-Type, Transfer-Encoding and Connection itself.
  • The request must use the target, in the URL or the body.
  • Success is any 2xx answer. The answer's first 64 KB are kept as the run's output, with every saved secret replaced by [hidden].

Outbound safety rules, for every request (tests too):

  • A 10-second timeout, no proxy, TLS certificates always checked. An action may trust one more CA: paste its PEM under Advanced.
  • Redirects are followed (up to three) only on the same scheme, host and port, so a redirect cannot carry the headers to another server.
  • Private networks (10/8, 172.16/12, 192.168/16, fc00::/7) are allowed: firewalls and automation servers live there. The server's own addresses (loopback) are refused unless Allow this server's own addresses is ticked, and cloud metadata addresses (169.254.169.254 and the like) and OpenSearch's own address are always refused. Addresses are checked after the name is looked up, on the connection itself, so DNS cannot be used to get around it.

docs.title: Block an IP on OPNsense or pfSense
docs.text:
The Block IP on OPNsense/pfSense template adds the IP to a firewall alias:

  1. In OPNsense, Firewall › Aliases: add a Host(s) alias named signalith_block, empty.
  2. Firewall › Rules on the WAN (and LAN, for outbound): add a rule that blocks source (or destination) signalith_block, at the top.
  3. System › Access › Users: make a user with only the Firewall: Alias: Edit privilege, then add an API key for it. The key and secret download as a file.
  4. In Signalith, pick the template, set the URL to your firewall (https://fw.example.lan/api/firewall/alias_util/add/signalith_block), and paste the key as API key and the secret as API secret.
  5. Add the Unblock IP on OPNsense (undo) template the same way, so analysts can take a block back.

On pfSense, install the REST API package (pfSense-pkg-RESTAPI) and point the URL at its firewall alias endpoint, with its body format; the template is a starting point.

docs.title: Shuffle
docs.text:
Shuffle is an open-source SOAR. Signalith doesn't include it: run it as its own program, on its own server, under its own license (AGPL). To start a workflow from Signalith:

  1. In Shuffle, add a Webhook trigger to the workflow, start it, and copy its URL.
  2. On the Response actions page, add the Shuffle workflow webhook template and paste the URL. It sends the target, its kind, the finding, the case, who ran it and why as JSON; use them in the workflow as $exec.target and so on.

The webhook answers at once; what the workflow does later shows in Shuffle, not in the run's output.

docs.title: Run a script
docs.text:
Kind script. Runs a program on the Signalith server that handled the request.

  • Only programs in the scripts folder can run. It is <state>/scripts (/var/lib/signalith/scripts on Linux, C:\ProgramData\Signalith\scripts on Windows), or response.scripts_dir in signalith.yaml, or the SIGNALITH_RESPONSE_SCRIPTS_DIR environment variable. It cannot be changed on a page. That is the point: an admin who can change actions on the page still can't make Signalith run any program they like, only the ones someone with access to the server's files put in that folder.
  • The program is a path inside that folder, such as isolate-host.sh or edr/isolate.ps1. It is resolved with every link followed, and must still be inside the folder (a symlink to /bin/sh is refused), a regular file, and on Linux executable and not writable by everyone.
  • No shell. The program gets the target as its one argument. It also gets SIGNALITH_TARGET, SIGNALITH_TARGET_KIND, SIGNALITH_FINDING_ID, SIGNALITH_CASE_ID, SIGNALITH_ACTOR and SIGNALITH_RUN_ID in a small environment: PATH and the few variables programs need (HOME, USER, LANG, TZ, TMPDIR; on Windows SystemRoot, TEMP, PSModulePath and the like). None of Signalith's own environment (keys, passwords) is passed on.
  • It runs in its own folder, for 60 seconds unless the action says otherwise, and at most 10 minutes; then it is stopped, with any programs it started (on Linux, its whole process group). Exit code 0 means success.
  • Its standard output and error, the first 16 KB, are the run's output.
  • Windows: .ps1 scripts run with powershell.exe -NoProfile -NonInteractive -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File <script> <target>; .exe files run directly. .cmd and .bat files are refused: cmd.exe reads its arguments again, so a target could not be passed safely.

Put scripts in the folder with an administrator account, and keep it writable only by administrators (the Security page checks it). Scripts run as the Signalith service account, so give that account only the rights the scripts need.

docs.title: Example: isolate a Linux host
docs.text:
isolate-host.sh, for hosts you manage over SSH with a key the Signalith account holds. It cuts the host off except for SSH from the management network:

#!/bin/sh
# isolate-host.sh <host>: firewall a Linux host off the network.
set -eu
host="$1"
case "$host" in -*|*[!A-Za-z0-9.:-]*) echo "bad host: $host" >&2; exit 2;; esac
ssh -o BatchMode=yes -o ConnectTimeout=10 "isolate@$host" -- sudo /usr/local/sbin/isolate-me
echo "Isolated $host (run $SIGNALITH_RUN_ID by $SIGNALITH_ACTOR)."

On each host, /usr/local/sbin/isolate-me (allowed for the isolate user in sudoers, and nothing else) keeps SSH from the management network and drops the rest:

#!/bin/sh
set -eu
nft -f - <<'EOF'
table inet isolate {
  chain input  { type filter hook input priority -10; policy drop;
                 iif lo accept; ct state established,related accept;
                 ip saddr 10.0.10.0/24 tcp dport 22 accept; }
  chain output { type filter hook output priority -10; policy drop;
                 oif lo accept; ct state established,related accept; }
}
EOF

nft delete table inet isolate on the host undoes it.

docs.title: Example: isolate a Windows host
docs.text:
isolate-host.ps1, for domain-joined hosts with PowerShell remoting, run by a service account allowed to remote into them. It turns on Windows Firewall with everything blocked except the management network:

# isolate-host.ps1 <host>: firewall a Windows host off the network.
param([Parameter(Mandatory)][ValidatePattern('^[A-Za-z0-9.-]+$')][string]$ComputerName)
$ErrorActionPreference = 'Stop'
Invoke-Command -ComputerName $ComputerName -ScriptBlock {
    New-NetFirewallRule -DisplayName 'Signalith isolation: management' -Group 'Signalith isolation' `
        -Direction Inbound -RemoteAddress 10.0.10.0/24 -Action Allow | Out-Null
    New-NetFirewallRule -DisplayName 'Signalith isolation: management out' -Group 'Signalith isolation' `
        -Direction Outbound -RemoteAddress 10.0.10.0/24 -Action Allow | Out-Null
    Set-NetFirewallProfile -All -Enabled True -DefaultInboundAction Block -DefaultOutboundAction Block
}
"Isolated $ComputerName (run $env:SIGNALITH_RUN_ID by $env:SIGNALITH_ACTOR)."

To undo, set -DefaultOutboundAction Allow again and remove the rules of the Signalith isolation group. If you have an EDR, its own isolate API (an http action) is usually the better choice.

docs.title: Velociraptor
docs.text: Velociraptor can quarantine a host (Windows.Remediation.Quarantine, Linux.Remediation.Quarantine) and collect evidence from it. Like Shuffle it is a separate program you run yourself; Signalith only calls it. Use its API from a script: give the Signalith account an API client config (velociraptor config api_client) with the investigator role, and have the script start the artifact on the client whose host name is the target with velociraptor --api_config api.yaml query "SELECT collect_client(...) FROM ...".

docs.title: Disable a directory account
docs.text:
Kind disable_user. Disables (or enables again) an account in the directory set up under Users › Directory sign-in, by LDAP.

  • Active Directory: it sets the ACCOUNTDISABLE bit (0x2) of userAccountControl; enable clears it. Other bits are left as they are. The account is found by sAMAccountName or userPrincipalName under the user base DN, among people (objectCategory=person, objectClass=user), disabled ones included. An account already in the asked state is left alone and reported so.
  • Other LDAP directories (OpenLDAP, 389 Directory Server, FreeIPA): there is no standard "disabled" flag, so the action names the attribute and value that lock an account in yours, such as nsAccountLock: TRUE on 389 DS and FreeIPA. Disable sets it; enable removes it. The account is found with the directory's user filter.
  • Writes need encryption: the directory must use ldaps:// or StartTLS, with certificates checked. Without it the action refuses to run, and the page says why.
  • The action refuses a name that matches more than one account, and refuses to change the account it signs in as.

It signs in as the directory sign-in account, or as an account of its own (bind DN and password on the action, saved encrypted). That account must be allowed to change users. In Active Directory, delegate only that:

  1. In Active Directory Users and Computers, right-click the OU that holds the users (not the domain, and not one that holds admins) and choose Delegate Control.
  2. Add the service account, choose Create a custom task to delegate, Only the following objects in the folder, tick User objects.
  3. Under permissions, tick Property-specific and then Read userAccountControl and Write userAccountControl (shown together as "Read/Write userAccountControl").

Accounts in protected groups (Domain Admins and the like) are guarded by AdminSDHolder and stay out of reach, which is what you want. If the account lacks the right, the run fails with the directory refused the change and says which right to delegate.

Test on the page signs in and looks the user up (jdoe, or what you type), and changes nothing.

docs.title: Templates
docs.text:
Add action offers templates; each fills in the form, and you change what you need:

Template Kind Acts on Block IP on OPNsense/pfSense (alias API) http ip Unblock IP on OPNsense (undo) http ip Block IP via generic webhook http ip Shuffle workflow webhook http any Isolate host with a script script host Disable AD user disable_user user Enable AD user (undo) disable_user user

docs.title: Testing an action
docs.text: Test on the edit form checks an action without changing anything, as far as its kind allows: an http action fills in its request (shown with secrets hidden) and checks the server's address; a script action finds its program; a disable_user action signs in and finds the user. Send test request really sends an http action's request, after asking; it is recorded in the audit log like any run.

docs.title: Audit log
docs.text:
Every run is a document in the <prefix>_actions OpenSearch index, created at startup. It is written before the action runs and again when it ends; if it can't be written, the action does not run. A run holds its ID (RUN-20261013-…), the action, kind, target and its kind, who ran it (or the playbook, and who approved it), the reason, the finding and case, the status (running, succeeded, failed), a summary, the output, the error, the server that ran it, and start and end times. A run left running by a server that stopped is shown as interrupted: check the target, since it may or may not have happened.

Each run is also logged (response action started, then response action succeeded or response action failed, with audit=true), and so are changes to the actions (response actions changed) and tests.

docs.title: Settings
docs.text:
Actions added on the page are saved in lookups/response.yaml, with passwords, headers and bind passwords encrypted with the server's key. It is not meant to be edited by hand; if it can't be read, the page says so and nothing runs. To move it, set:

response:
  file: /var/lib/signalith/lookups/response.yaml   # or SIGNALITH_RESPONSE_FILE
  scripts_dir: /var/lib/signalith/scripts          # or SIGNALITH_RESPONSE_SCRIPTS_DIR

signalith rotate-master re-encrypts the file with the rest.

Several servers: each server reads its own response.yaml and its own scripts folder, and an action runs on whichever server handled the analyst's request. Copy the file (with the same master key) and the scripts to each server that serves the web UI, or put them on a shared folder.

docs.title: API
docs.text:
Method and path Role GET /api/respond/actions analyst The actions analysts can run, without their settings. POST /api/respond/run analyst Run one: {"action", "target", "target_kind"?, "finding_id"?, "case_id"?, "reason"}. Returns the run. GET /api/respond/runs analyst Past runs, newest first: ?finding_id=, ?case_id=, ?action=, ?limit= (50, at most 500). GET /api/respond/config admin The actions with their settings (secrets show only as set or not), templates, scripts. PUT /api/respond/config admin Replace the actions: {"actions": [...]}. A secret is {"value": "..."} to set it or {"keep": true} to keep the saved one. POST /api/respond/test admin Test one action: {"action", "target", "send"}.

A saved secret is kept only while the action still sends it to the same place: the same scheme, host and port for an http action (and the same user name for its password), the same bind DN for a disable_user action. Change the URL to another server and the page asks for the secrets again, so whoever can change an action can't have its key sent somewhere else.

A run refused before it starts answers 400 (with the field at fault), 404 (no such action, finding or case), 429 (too many runs) or 503 (the audit log can't be written). A run that started always answers 200 with the run, whose status says how it went.

docs.title: Data retention
docs.text:
Signalith keeps events in daily OpenSearch indices, one per data category and day (<prefix>-endpoint-2026.10.12). Retention policies decide, for each category:

  • how many days it stays searchable,
  • how large it may grow,
  • when old days are compacted to save space,
  • whether days are archived to files before they are deleted.

Findings and investigations have their own policy. A disk guard keeps OpenSearch from filling its disk.

Set everything on the Data retention tab of Settings (admins only): select a category to change its policy, or edit the default policy and the disk guard under Defaults. The dialog shows what saving would delete, archive or compact before you save, including days that are already due and go in the same run, and asks again before anything is deleted. Changes apply at once: saving starts a retention run, with no restart. If a run or restore is going, the new run starts as soon as it ends, and the run in progress already skips anything the new settings keep. The same settings can be written in signalith.yaml instead (see Settings in signalith.yaml).

docs.title: Categories
docs.text:
Category ID Stored in Policy Authentication authentication <prefix>-authentication-YYYY.MM.DD Event policy Endpoint endpoint <prefix>-endpoint-YYYY.MM.DD Event policy Network traffic network_traffic <prefix>-network_traffic-YYYY.MM.DD Event policy Change change <prefix>-change-YYYY.MM.DD Event policy Filesystem filesystem <prefix>-filesystem-YYYY.MM.DD Event policy Registry registry <prefix>-registry-YYYY.MM.DD Event policy Network resolution network_resolution <prefix>-network_resolution-YYYY.MM.DD Event policy Image load image_load <prefix>-image_load-YYYY.MM.DD Event policy Script script <prefix>-script-YYYY.MM.DD Event policy Inventory inventory <prefix>-inventory-YYYY.MM.DD Event policy Configuration check configuration_check <prefix>-configuration_check-YYYY.MM.DD Event policy Alerts alerts <prefix>-alerts-YYYY.MM.DD Event policy Other events other <prefix>-other-YYYY.MM.DD Event policy; listed once it has data or a policy Risk events risk <prefix>-risk-YYYY.MM.DD Event policy Findings findings <prefix>_findings Delete closed findings after N days Investigations cases <prefix>_cases Delete closed cases after N days Threat intel intel <prefix>_intel Managed by feeds: indicators expire through each feed's max_age

Days are UTC days, the same days the index names use.

docs.title: Event policies
docs.text:
Setting Meaning Keep (keep_days) Days a category stays searchable. 0 keeps it forever. A day is deleted once it is more than keep_days days old, so 90 keeps today and the 90 days before it Size cap (max_size_gb) Largest the category may be, in GB (1 GB = 2^30 bytes) of disk, replicas included. Over the cap, its oldest days are deleted until it fits. 0 means no cap Compact after (compact_after_days) Days after which a day is made read-only and force-merged to one segment. 0 never compacts. Must be less than keep_days Archive before deleting (archive) Write each day to a compressed file before deleting it, so it can be restored later

A category without its own policy uses the default policy. Until you save a default on the page, the default is retention.days from signalith.yaml (90 days, nothing else), which is exactly how retention worked before policies existed. A default saved on the page replaces retention.days. To make the default a fixed limit that the page cannot change, set retention.default in signalith.yaml.

Compaction makes old days smaller and cheaper to search: fewer segments, deleted documents purged, and less memory for OpenSearch. Today and yesterday are never compacted. A compacted day is read-only. If an agent sends events for that day later, OpenSearch refuses them and they are lost; the server logs "some events were rejected". So set Compact after above the longest time your agents can be offline. For laptops that may be away for a week, use 14 or more.

Size caps are checked after keep_days. They never delete today's data or a restored day, and restored days do not count toward the cap, so restoring days for an investigation never pushes live days out. If only today's or restored data is left and the category is still over its cap, the page says so.

A day that OpenSearch cannot read, because a primary shard is missing (a red index, for example while its node is down), is left alone: it is not deleted, archived or compacted until OpenSearch recovers, and the page lists it.

docs.title: Findings and investigations
docs.text:
The policy for Findings and Investigations has one setting, keep_days. It is off by default, which keeps them forever. When it is set, retention deletes only the ones that are resolved or closed and have not changed for more than keep_days days. New, in-progress and pending items are never deleted, whatever their age.

Findings that belong to an investigation are kept as long as the investigation is, open or closed: a case stores only the IDs of its findings, so deleting them would leave the case with gaps. Once the investigation itself is deleted, its findings follow the findings policy. A case keeps its own notes, search snapshots and pinned events, so it outlives the event days it came from. If the investigations cannot be listed, or there are more than 60,000 of them, no findings are deleted in that run.

docs.title: The disk guard
docs.text:
OpenSearch protects itself when a data disk fills up. At 85% (the low watermark) it stops placing new replica shards on the node. At 90% (the high watermark) it moves shards away from the node. At 95% (the flood stage) it makes every index with a shard on that node read-only, and ingest stops until space is freed. The page counts the indices OpenSearch has blocked this way.

The disk guard acts first. When the fullest OpenSearch data disk is above Max disk use (default 85%), it deletes the oldest event days, in any category, until the disk is back under the limit:

  • It counts what the policies already delete before deleting more.
  • It never deletes the last Min days days (default 7), today, restored days, or days OpenSearch cannot read.
  • It never touches findings, cases or threat intel.
  • A category set to archive is archived first, as usual. If a day cannot be archived or deleted, the guard keeps it and picks the next oldest day instead.
  • It deletes only when that helps. When even every day it may delete cannot get the disk under the limit, usually because other files fill the disk, it deletes only the oldest days needed to keep the disk below 95%, where OpenSearch stops taking events. If that is out of reach too, it deletes nothing. Either way the page says so, and the server logs an error.

Disk use is (total - available) / total, the same formula OpenSearch's watermarks use. So space used by other files on the same disk counts too. On a cluster with several data nodes, the guard follows the fullest node's disk and counts only the shards each day has on that node.

If OpenSearch has already reached the flood stage, the guard still frees space. Blocked indices can still be read and deleted, so they are archived (when the policy says so) and deleted as usual. Compaction waits until OpenSearch lifts the block, which it does by itself once disk use falls below the high watermark.

The guard is on by default, including on servers upgraded from an earlier version. A server whose OpenSearch disk is already above 85% deletes its oldest days (older than 7 days) at the first run after the upgrade, as far as that gets the disk under the limit. To prevent this, turn the guard off or raise its limit (up to 94%) before upgrading, by setting retention.guard in signalith.yaml.

The guard runs with every retention run. Between runs it also checks the disk every 5 minutes and starts a run when the disk passes the limit. If it cannot get the disk under the limit, or days it chose could not be deleted, the page says so and the guard waits for the next scheduled run instead of checking every 5 minutes. Add disk space, lower Min days or the policies' Keep, or look for other data on the same disk. While retention.yaml has errors, the guard is paused like every other part of retention, and the page says so.

docs.title: Archives
docs.text:
With Archive before deleting on, each day is archived and checked before its index is deleted:

  1. The index is made read-only and refreshed, so the copy holds every event, including those written in the last seconds before.
  2. Every event is written to <index>.ndjson.gz, one {"_id": ..., "_source": ...} per line, then flushed to disk with fsync.
  3. A manifest <index>.json is written beside it, with the event count, file size, SHA-256 and creation time.
  4. The file is read back and checked against the manifest. Its event count must also match the index's count.
  5. Only then is the index deleted.

If anything fails (a full archive disk, a count that does not match, an OpenSearch error), the index is kept, made writable again, and the error is listed in the run's history. The next run tries again. Before writing, retention checks that the archive folder's disk has room for about half the day's size in OpenSearch, and keeps the day if it does not.

Put the archive folder on a different disk from OpenSearch's data. By default it is on the same disk (next to the lookups folder), and then archiving the days the guard picks takes space on the very disk the guard is trying to free. The page warns when both look like the same disk.

On Linux, files are written with mode 0600 in a folder with mode 0700. On Windows, the server gives the archive folder an access list of its own, not inherited from the drive: full control for SYSTEM, Administrators and the server's account, nobody else. To set it up by hand for a folder you create yourself:

icacls D:\SignalithArchive /inheritance:r /grant:r "Administrators:(OI)(CI)F" "SYSTEM:(OI)(CI)F"

Each archive records the ID (UUID) of the exact index it came from. If late events recreate a day after it was archived and deleted, the new index has a new UUID, so it is archived again before it is deleted. The new copy gets its own ID, such as signalith-endpoint-2026.07.01.2. A restored day is not archived a second time: the index notes the archives it was restored from.

The archive folder is retention.archive_dir, SIGNALITH_ARCHIVE_DIR, or an archive folder next to lookups.dir. Docker images and the systemd unit use /var/lib/signalith/archive; in Docker, mount a volume there to keep archives outside the container. Archives are plain gzip and JSON, so zcat file.ndjson.gz | head works and any tool can read them. Move older files to cheaper storage as you like: retention never deletes archive files.

Example manifest:

{
  "format": "signalith-archive/1",
  "id": "signalith-endpoint-2026.07.01",
  "index": "signalith-endpoint-2026.07.01",
  "category": "endpoint",
  "day": "2026-07-01",
  "docs": 1840221,
  "file": "signalith-endpoint-2026.07.01.ndjson.gz",
  "bytes": 211630580,
  "index_bytes": 1073741824,
  "sha256": "ace69f8245...",
  "created": "2026-10-04T03:00:12Z"
}

docs.title: Restoring
docs.text:
On the page, open Archive, select days and choose Restore. Before anything is restored, the dialog shows how much space the days take in OpenSearch and how full the disk will be. Restored days are spared by size caps and the guard, so if the restore takes the disk over the guard's limit, the guard makes room by deleting the oldest live days of other categories. The dialog then names how many days that would be, and whether they are archived, and asks you to confirm. A restore that would fill the disk to 95% needs confirmation too.

You can also use the CLI on the server:

signalith archive list
signalith archive verify signalith-endpoint-2026.07.01
signalith archive restore -keep-days 30 signalith-endpoint-2026.07.01

The CLI reads retention.archive_dir from signalith.yaml, or SIGNALITH_ARCHIVE_DIR. The systemd unit sets that variable only for the service, so on those installs give the folder with -dir:

sudo -u signalith signalith archive list -c /etc/signalith/signalith.yaml -dir /var/lib/signalith/archive

The CLI installs Signalith's index template before it restores, so restored days get the same field types as live ones, even on a new OpenSearch that the server has not started against yet. It does not check the disk first; use the page for that.

A restore works like this:

  • It checks the whole file against its manifest first, so a damaged file restores nothing.
  • It writes the events back into their original index, so ordinary searches over that day find them again.
  • Each event keeps its original ID, so restoring the same day twice does not duplicate anything. An interrupted restore can be run again to finish.
  • A restored day stays searchable for the days you choose (14 by default, up to 365). Retention, the size cap and the disk guard leave it alone until then. After that, the category's policy applies again and the day is deleted without being archived a second time.

Restores from the page run in the background, one at a time, and never during a retention run.

docs.title: Compliance examples
docs.text:
Keep 90 days searchable and 1 year archived. Set the default policy to keep 90 days and turn Archive before deleting on. Each day is archived when it turns 91 days old. Signalith never deletes archive files. To keep a year in all, delete each day's files once the day is a year old. That is about 275 days after the file was written:

find /var/lib/signalith/archive -type f -mtime +275 -delete

Each manifest records the day it holds (day). Use it instead of file times if your policy must be exact to the day.

Keep authentication events for a year, everything else for 30 days. Set the default to 30 days and give Authentication its own policy of 365 days.

Keep endpoint data under 500 GB. Give Endpoint a 500 GB size cap. Add keep_days as well if you also need a time limit.

Keep closed investigations for 3 years. Give Investigations a policy of 1095 days. Open cases are never deleted.

docs.title: Runs and history
docs.text:
Retention runs every hour (retention.interval) on the server that runs the background jobs. It also runs when settings are saved, when Run now is pressed, and when the disk guard trips. The first scheduled run is 2 minutes after the server starts running the jobs. A server with detections.scheduler: false logs a warning at startup that it never runs retention.

Each run plans first and then acts. The preview in the page's dialogs uses the same planner, so what it shows is what the next run does. Deletions run oldest day first, then compactions. Before each step, the run reads the settings again and skips any step that settings saved meanwhile no longer call for, so a correction saved during a long run takes effect at once.

Retention only touches indices named <prefix>-<category>-YYYY.MM.DD with a known category and a valid date, plus the findings and cases indices. Anything else under the prefix is listed as unmanaged and left alone. Today's and future-dated days are never deleted, and today and yesterday are never compacted. Only one run or restore happens at a time.

The page keeps the last 200 actions (what was deleted, archived or compacted, why, how much space it freed, and who made the change behind it), plus the last run's totals and errors. Every action is also logged by the server.

docs.title: Settings in signalith.yaml
docs.text:
The page saves its settings in retention.yaml in the lookups.dir folder (mode 0600). Run history goes in retention_history.json beside it. You can edit retention.yaml by hand. The server notices the change at the next run. If the file has a mistake, runs pause and the page shows the error until it is fixed.

Anything set under retention in signalith.yaml wins over the page and is shown there as "From signalith.yaml", read-only, except retention.days, which a default saved on the page replaces. Use this for settings that must not be changed from the UI:

retention:
  days: 90                 # default keep_days until a default is saved on the page (0 = forever)
  interval: 1h             # how often to enforce, 5m to 24h
  archive_dir: /srv/signalith-archive
  default:                 # replaces days; the page can no longer change the default
    keep_days: 90
    archive: true
  policies:
    authentication:
      keep_days: 365
      compact_after_days: 14
    endpoint:
      keep_days: 30
      max_size_gb: 500
    findings:
      keep_days: 365       # resolved or closed findings
    cases:
      keep_days: 1095      # resolved or closed investigations
  guard:
    enabled: true
    max_disk_percent: 85   # 50 to 94
    min_days: 7
Key Default Meaning retention.days 90 Default keep_days for event categories without a policy, until a default is saved on the page retention.interval 1h How often policies are enforced (5m to 24h) retention.archive_dir archive next to lookups.dir Archive folder; relative paths are relative to signalith.yaml. SIGNALITH_ARCHIVE_DIR overrides it retention.default none Default event policy: keep_days, max_size_gb, compact_after_days, archive retention.policies.<id> none Policy for one category (IDs above). Findings and cases accept only keep_days retention.guard.enabled true Disk guard on or off retention.guard.max_disk_percent 85 Disk use the guard keeps OpenSearch under (50 to 94) retention.guard.min_days 7 Days before today the guard never deletes

signalith validate checks all of these and names each problem.

docs.title: More than one server
docs.text:
When several Signalith servers share one OpenSearch, they form a cluster and share the retention policies, the default and the disk guard (see Shared feeds and retention policies). A change on the Data retention page of any server applies to all of them at once, and every server shows the same page. One of the servers runs the background jobs, retention among them; only servers with detections.scheduler: true and the cluster key take part, and another one takes over if that server stops. The page says which server runs retention.

  • Run now on another server asks the server that runs retention to run: the page shows "Asked siem-a to run retention", then whether siem-a started the run or queued it behind one already going. The run is made there, and its result shows on siem-a's Data retention page, as each server keeps its own run history. Saving a change asks siem-a in the same way to apply it now. Restores of archived days are still made on the server that runs retention.
  • Where each value came from. Under a policy, the default and the guard, the page says where a value that was not set on the page came from, such as "Applied from signalith.yaml on siem-b, 2026-10-01" or "Imported from the files on siem-a".
  • Changes at the same moment. If someone else changed the retention settings (any policy, the default or the guard) since you opened the page, your change is refused: the page says so and shows theirs.
  • When the shared settings cannot be used on a server, for example while it cannot reach OpenSearch or misses the cluster key, changes there are refused and the page says why.

Policies that wait to be confirmed. When the cluster is made, the retention policies of the server that founds it become the shared ones. If another server that ran in the last 7 days had policies of its own that differ, the page shows an amber alert, and retention runs only the disk guard and freezes, archives and deletes nothing else until an admin looks at the policies and selects Confirm these policies. Change any of them first if they should be another server's.

signalith.yaml. retention.days, retention.default, retention.policies and retention.guard apply to the shared settings only when they change: a server that starts with a changed value applies it to every server, and the page says so. An unchanged file never undoes a change made on the page, so these settings no longer make the page read-only. The Servers page lists a value that differs from the shared one. retention.archive_dir, retention.schedule and the archive settings are still each server's own.

Archives are written on the server that runs retention, in its archive folder. While any policy archives, set retention.archive_dir to the same shared folder on every server: a server that uses a different folder does not take retention over by itself. Signalith names that folder with a small file in it, .signalith-archive-id; leave it there. Restore from the server that runs retention, or with the CLI after copying the files to where you run it.

Before every step that deletes or changes data, retention checks with OpenSearch that its server still runs the background jobs, and stops if not. When OpenSearch's disk is full, it refuses every write, so no server can confirm that in the usual way. The server that runs the jobs then keeps them, as long as it can read that nothing changed, and runs only retention, so the disk guard can delete the oldest days and free space. Detections and feed downloads wait until OpenSearch accepts writes again.

Servers that are not part of the cluster (an older version, or a server without the cluster key) keep using their own files: page settings in their own lookups.dir, and retention in signalith.yaml. They show the page read-only, say which server runs retention, and refuse changes, Run now and restores, and they never take retention over. Give them the cluster key (see signalith cluster).

docs.title: Upgrading
docs.text:
• Retention used to run on every server, then on every server with detections.scheduler: true. It now runs on one of those at a time. Upgrade every server that shares an OpenSearch together: an older version ignores which server runs the jobs. Or first set detections.scheduler: false on the servers you upgrade last.
  • The disk guard is on by default; see The disk guard.
  • With shared settings, the first server of this version to run the jobs brings its own retention policies to every server, and another server's differing policies wait to be confirmed (see More than one server). Every other server needs the cluster key to take part (see Upgrading servers you set up by hand).

docs.title: API
docs.text:
All routes need an admin. Request bodies reject unknown fields, so a typo is an error rather than a setting that does nothing.

Method and path Body Response GET /api/retention Categories with sizes, days and policies; the default; the guard and disk; the archive; the schedule; pending actions; the last run and recent actions. With shared settings also shared: true, etag (also in the ETag header), hold when the policies wait to be confirmed ({"reason"}), and from on the default, the guard and each category whose value was applied from a signalith.yaml or imported ({"source","node","at","note"}) PUT /api/retention/policies/{id} {"keep_days":30,"max_size_gb":0,"compact_after_days":14,"archive":true} {"category","policy","source":"ui","run_started","run_queued"} DELETE /api/retention/policies/{id} Back to the default: {"category","policy","source","run_started","run_queued"} PUT /api/retention/default A policy {"policy","source":"ui","run_started","run_queued"} PUT /api/retention/guard {"enabled":true,"max_disk_percent":85,"min_days":7} The guard plus source, run_started and run_queued POST /api/retention/preview {"category":"endpoint","policy":{...}}, {"category":"endpoint","policy":null}, {"default":{...}} or {"guard":{...}} What the run that saving starts would do: summary and steps for the change, due, due_steps and due_records for what is already due, records, deletes_data, guard, notes POST /api/retention/run 202 {"started":true}; 409 while a run or restore is going. On a server that does not run retention, with shared settings: 202 {"request_id","queued_on"} (see below) POST /api/retention/policies/confirm Confirms shared policies that wait to be confirmed: {"confirmed":true,"run_started","run_queued"}; 409 when none wait GET /api/retention/archive Archived days, with whether each is searchable and its latest restore POST /api/retention/archive/preview {"ids":[...],"keep_days":14} What the restore does to the disk: bytes, percent_after, over_limit, flood, the live days the guard would delete (steps, deletes, unarchived), needs_confirm and message POST /api/retention/archive/restore {"ids":["signalith-endpoint-2026.07.01"],"keep_days":14,"confirm":false} 202 {"restores":[...]} with each restore's state; 409 {"error","check"} when the restore needs "confirm":true

run_started is true when saving started a run; run_queued when a run or restore was going and a new run starts as soon as it ends. With shared settings, saving on a server that does not run retention asks the one that does to run: both are then false, and the answer adds request_id and queued_on (the server asked). GET /api/requests/{id} then has "result":{"result":"started"}, or "queued" when a run or restore was going there.

Requests. GET /api/requests/{id} follows a request: state is queued, running, done or failed, with claimed_by (the server doing it), started, finished and the result. Finished requests are kept for 7 days.

Changes at the same moment. With shared settings, send the etag of GET /api/retention as If-Match on a change: when someone changed the settings meanwhile, the change is refused with 412 and the error says who changed them and when. Without If-Match the change is made whatever happened meanwhile.

Errors:

  • An invalid setting returns 400 with error, problems and fields (the settings at fault).
  • A setting that comes from signalith.yaml returns 409.
  • On a server that keeps its own settings and does not run the background jobs (with detections.scheduler: false, or while another server runs them), every change, Run now and restore returns 409 with an error that says which server runs retention; GET /api/retention has schedule.read_only and schedule.read_only_why. With shared settings only restores are refused there.
  • With shared settings, a change made while this server cannot use them (it cannot reach OpenSearch, or misses the cluster key) returns 503.
  • An unknown category or archive ID returns 404.
  • When OpenSearch cannot be reached, previews and restore checks return 503.

docs.title: Roadmap
docs.text:
Signalith aims to be a complete, general-purpose open-source SIEM: collect events from the systems you run, find the attacks in them, and help you respond. This page says where it stands. It has no dates: Signalith is a personal project built in the open, and things ship when they are ready and tested.

Ideas and requests are welcome as feature requests on GitHub.

docs.title: Done Available
docs.text:
The first three phases are complete, and the fourth has started.

Search foundation

  • Fluent Bit agents for Windows and Linux, set up from the Add data page, plus syslog and CEF from network devices and OpenTelemetry logs over OTLP.
  • Parsing into CIM-style data models (Authentication, Endpoint, Network traffic, Change).
  • A pipe-based query language that reads like SPL, plain-English questions that become queries, a visual query builder, and an optional AI model.
  • A Docker quick start and installers for Linux (systemd) and Windows (service).

Detect and triage

  • Scheduled detections mapped to MITRE ATT&CK, with throttling, a findings queue for triage, and an ATT&CK coverage map.
  • Sigma rule import.

Security depth

  • Risk-based alerting with asset and identity context.
  • Threat intel feeds (lists, CSV, STIX, TAXII 2.1) matched against your events.
  • A security posture dashboard and dashboards of your own.
  • Sample data with attacks hidden in it, to try everything out.

Respond and scale (started)

  • Investigation cases that collect findings, notes, searches and evidence.
  • Several Signalith servers sharing one OpenSearch, taking over each other's background jobs.

Built in from the start

  • HTTPS by default, a secured OpenSearch, and encrypted passwords and keys.
  • Users and roles, with Active Directory and LDAP sign-in.
  • Data retention policies with archives and a disk guard.
  • A security check of how each server is set up.

docs.title: Being built now In progress
docs.text: Detection content pack with rule tests A large, curated set of detections built on community Sigma content, each one with test events that prove it fires, checked on every change. Tuning and suppression of noisy rules, and signed content updates so new rules arrive without upgrading Signalith. Endpoint visibility with osquery File integrity monitoring, hardware and software inventory, and configuration checks against published security baselines, from osquery on Windows and Linux, with agents managed from Signalith. Alerts and response actions Send findings to email, webhooks, Slack and Microsoft Teams. Act on them from Signalith: disable a directory account, block an IP address, isolate a host or run a script, alone or as playbooks, with an approval step where it matters. Releases, packages and documentation Numbered releases with signed .deb, .rpm and .msi packages and a software bill of materials (SBOM), this documentation site, and a contributor guide.

docs.title: Next Planned
docs.text: Compliance content and evidence export Detections and reports mapped to PCI DSS 4.0, NIST SP 800-53, CIS Controls v8, HIPAA, ISO/IEC 27001 and SOC 2, compliance dashboards, retention presets, and evidence an auditor can take away. Load testing and an OpenSearch cluster guide A load test run in CI with the numbers published, so you know what one server handles, plus a guide to running OpenSearch as a cluster, and backup and restore. Add a server Adding a Signalith server to an existing install from the UI, with settings shared between servers instead of copied by hand.

docs.title: Later Exploring
docs.text: Network sensor An optional sensor role running Zeek and Suricata with the free Emerging Threats Open rules, feeding network events and alerts into Signalith. Vulnerability scanning: more Scanning with Nmap and CVE matching is built (vulnerabilities.md). Still to come: a scanner server for each network zone, and OpenVAS as an option for deeper scans. Hardening and 1.0 Fuzzing of every parser that reads data from the network, an outside security review, a public demo, and then version 1.0.

docs.title: Sample data
docs.text:
