Sample data fills Signalith with a realistic week of security activity for a fictional company, with a handful of attacks hidden in it, so you can try the SIEM on data that makes detections fire, fills the triage queue, builds risk on users and hosts, matches threat intel and lights up the dashboards. Load it in one click, look around, and remove it in one click when you are done.

Everything is made up and safe to load next to real data:

  • the company is fictional and its domain is corp.example (a reserved documentation name, RFC 6761);
  • every address, the company's own hosts included, is from the documentation ranges (RFC 5737): its hosts use 192.0.2.0/24, and the outside world 198.51.100.0/24 and 203.0.113.0/24. None of them can be a host on your network, so the sample's asset list never describes one of your machines;
  • the generator is deterministic and offline: it reads nothing from the network or disk.

Every document the sample writes carries a hidden marker field, signalith_sample, holding the load's ID. Removal deletes exactly what has the marker and nothing else. The marker is kept out of search results and field lists, so it never clutters what you see.

Only the sample-data load can set the marker. Signalith removes it from every event that agents and syslog senders send, so nobody can hide their own events from the detections, or have them deleted with the sample data, by adding it.

docs.title: Load and remove it
docs.text:
In the browser (admins): open Add data under Data. The Try it with sample data card loads the week, shows its progress, then lists things to try (each opens a view covering the whole week) and removes it again behind a confirm. While it loads, the detections run over the week so findings and risk appear at once. On a server with no events in the last seven days, Dashboards and Search show admins a one-line pointer to it.

From the shell (or in Docker):

signalith sample-data load               # a full week (about 27,000 events)
signalith sample-data load -size small   # the same attacks with less background
signalith sample-data status             # whether it is loaded, and the counts
signalith sample-data remove             # take all of it out

# In Docker:
docker compose -f deploy/docker/docker-compose.yml exec signalith signalith sample-data load

Loading twice is refused: remove the set first, then load again. Loading and removing are logged as admin actions and run in the background. Only one runs at a time, across the web page, the command line and every server that shares your OpenSearch: a load started from the shell, or on another server, shows its progress on the card, with where it runs.

signalith sample-data status needs to reach OpenSearch, like load and remove: the record of what is loaded is kept there (see Several servers).

If a load stops part way (an error, a restart, or Ctrl-C), what it wrote so far is recorded. The card says The last load did not finish and offers Remove what was loaded; signalith sample-data remove does the same. A new load is refused until it is removed. A removal that stops part way works the same way: the card says The last removal did not finish and offers Finish removing, and signalith sample-data remove finishes it too.

When you stop or restart a server (or its container) in the middle of a load or removal, it notes that the job did not finish before it exits, so the card says so as soon as the server is back. If signalith sample-data remove finds a load or removal recorded as running somewhere else, it first checks, for up to a minute, whether that is still going: it waits for it if so, and finishes the job if not.

docs.title: What it contains
docs.text:
• A fictional organisation: about 50 users and 40 hosts: finance, IT and operations workstations, a few Linux servers (web, app, database, jump host), two domain controllers and a file server.
  • A week of background activity with a working-hours and weekday rhythm: sign-ins, process starts, network connections, firewall traffic and DNS lookups: ordinary noise for the attacks to hide in, plus a benign look-alike to practise closing as a false positive.
  • Antivirus events: Microsoft Defender on the Windows hosts and ClamAV on the Linux servers, with a daily definitions update on every host, detections inside the attack stories, a trojan outbreak, failing updates and an EICAR test, plus one Trend Micro Apex One detection sent over syslog (standard size only). They fill the Malware dashboard; see antivirus.md.
  • An OT flavour: an engineering workstation, two HMIs and three PLCs, with the HMIs polling the PLCs over Modbus (TCP 502) and writing to a historian. It is all normal; no detection targets OT, it just shows the plant floor in the data.
  • Context and intel: asset and identity entries for the company (with priorities, categories and a watchlist entry), and seven threat-intel indicators (three attacker addresses, a malware update domain, a phishing domain and two malware hashes), each of which the events match.
  • A sample investigation, Sample: phishing intrusion on ws-fin-07, holding the phishing story's findings in the order they fired, to open and practise on.

Two sizes load the same attacks; only the volume of background activity differs. Standard is a full week, about 27,000 events. Small keeps two days of light background, a few hundred events in all.

docs.title: A guided tour of the attacks
docs.text:
Seven stories are woven into the week. Five are intrusions designed so that every built-in detection that is on fires; the other two are benign activity that trips detections you can close as benign.

Some detections raise a finding on the Findings page. Others only add risk to the users and hosts involved, which shows on the Risk page and counts toward the risk findings below. The table keeps them apart.

Story What happens Raises findings Adds risk only SSH brute force from the internet An external host (203.0.113.45) password-sprays SSH on the database server db-01, breaks the account bob.okafor, logs in as root and reads /etc/shadow, then drops a miner that ClamAV quarantines. auth-brute-force, auth-password-spray, auth-brute-force-success, auth-shadow-file-access, threat-activity, malware-detected auth-ssh-root-login, auth-sudo-failures Phishing to credential theft and C2 A finance workstation (ws-fin-07, Alice Nguyen) looks up a look-alike sign-in site, opens a malicious invoice that launches encoded PowerShell, downloads a tool with certutil, dumps credentials with Mimikatz, turns off Defender’s real-time protection, runs discovery, installs persistence and beacons to a C2 that is in the sample intel. endpoint-office-child-shell, endpoint-encoded-powershell, endpoint-credential-dumping, threat-activity, malware-detected and malware-not-removed (Defender finds Mimikatz but can’t remove it), av-protection-disabled, av-rule-block (on ws-fin-02, where the same invoice is opened, attack surface reduction stops Word starting PowerShell) endpoint-lolbin-download, endpoint-discovery-burst, endpoint-scheduled-task, endpoint-service-created, network-shell-port Hidden admin account on the domain controller On dc-01 the attacker creates svc-helpdesk and adds it to Domain Admins, then deletes a stale contractor account. change-admin-group-add change-account-created Ransomware preparation on the file server Using the stolen domain-admin account, the attacker reaches file-01 over SMB, tries to turn off Defender’s real-time protection (tamper protection blocks it), adds an antivirus exclusion for C:\ProgramData\SyncSvc, and deletes the volume shadow copies and recovery configuration. Defender quarantines the first copy of the ransomware; the exclusion lets the second copy run, and controlled folder access stops it changing the finance share. endpoint-shadow-copy-delete, av-tamper-blocked, av-exclusion-added, malware-ransomware, av-rule-block Trojan spreads from a file share A fake “payroll update” (Trojan:Win32/Fakepay.A) on \\file-01\public is opened on four operations workstations within a quarter of an hour. Defender quarantines it on ws-ops-01, ws-ops-03 and ws-ops-04, but fails to on ws-ops-05. malware-detected, malware-outbreak, malware-not-removed Antivirus upkeep Definitions updates fail twice on web-01 (ClamAV) and on ws-ops-02 (Defender). ClamAV’s nightly scan on app-01 finds a web shell in an upload folder but only reports it, so the file stays. IT tests Defender on ws-it-02 with the EICAR test file. av-definitions-failing; malware-left-clamav and malware-detected for the web shell; malware-detected for the EICAR test, a finding to close as benign Nightly scan finds vulnerable servers Signalith's own vulnerability scan of the server network finds Apache httpd 2.4.49 on web-01 with two vulnerabilities attackers are known to use (CVE-2021-41773 and CVE-2021-42013) and a critical one (CVE-2023-25690), a critical OpenSSH flaw on app-01 (CVE-2023-38408), and Telnet still open on the jump host jump-01. The results are events in Search; the Vulnerabilities page lists only your own scans. vuln-known-exploited, vuln-critical, vuln-cleartext-remote-login Benign activity that looks malicious A backup job on file-01 runs encoded PowerShell, and IT fetches a tool with certutil. endpoint-encoded-powershell on file-01: one finding to close as benign endpoint-lolbin-download on ws-it-02

The risk that builds up then raises two more findings on its own:

  • risk-threshold-exceeded: a user or host passed the risk threshold;
  • risk-multiple-tactics: risk from several ATT&CK tactics on one entity.

So 33 of the 35 built-in detections fire from the sample, all of them on. Each detection adds its risk once per thing it found, so the totals on the Risk page and the dashboards are the same every time you load.

docs.title: Detections that do not fire
docs.text:
Two built-in detections are off by default, so the load does not run them. The sample has data for both. To see them fire, turn them on on the Detections page, then remove the sample data and load it again (the load runs the detections over the whole week; once it is loaded, a detection you turn on only looks at the last few minutes):

  • change-account-deleted: the contractor account the domain-persistence story deletes.
  • network-remote-admin-port: the SMB connection the ransomware story makes from the workstation to the file server (port 445). It is off by default because it needs tuning for your own admin tools.

docs.title: How it stays apart from your data
docs.text:
• Detections. The load runs the detections over the sample's own events only, so nothing real is ever marked as sample. The live detections leave the sample's events and risk out, so they raise nothing from them while it is loaded, however long it stays.
  • Assets and identities. The sample's entries live in their own files next to your lists (sample-data-assets.csv and sample-data-identities.csv in the lookups folder). Your assets.csv and identities.csv are never rewritten. Where one of your entries and a sample entry share a name, yours always wins. The Assets page shows the sample's entries after yours, with the business unit Sample data; your CSV download and uploads hold only your own.
  • Threat intel. The indicators have the source Sample data, which no feed can have, so your feeds and the sample never mix.
  • Source health. The sample stays out of source health on the dashboards, because it is loaded and removed all at once and would otherwise show as a source that goes stale the moment you remove it.

docs.title: How removal works
docs.text:
Removal deletes exactly what has the load's marker, and nothing else:

  • the sample events, across every data model, and its risk events;
  • the findings the load raised;
  • the sample investigation. A case of your own that holds a sample finding is kept: the sample finding is unlinked from it, and your notes and timeline stay;
  • the sample threat intel (source Sample data);
  • the sample asset and identity entries (its own two files).

Your own events, findings, cases, detections, intel feeds and lists are never changed, even where they mention a host or user with the same name as a sample one. If retention has already made a day that holds sample events read-only, removal lifts that for the delete and puts it back.

The load's ID is kept in a record in OpenSearch (see Several servers). If that record does not say which load it was (it was damaged, or changed by hand), Signalith cannot tell the sample's events, findings and investigation from yours, so it deletes none of them. It removes only the sample threat intel and the sample asset and identity entries, then clears the record, and the card (or signalith sample-data remove) says so. What an earlier load made stays:

  • Its findings and its investigation, Sample: phishing intrusion on ws-fin-07, stay on the Findings and Cases pages. Close them there by hand.
  • Its events stay until retention deletes them on its usual schedule. Detections ignore them, as they ignore all sample events.

You can then load the sample data again. Remove later deletes what that new load adds, but not what the earlier load left.

docs.title: Several servers
docs.text:
When several Signalith servers share one OpenSearch (see servers.md), they share one set of sample data:

  • Upgrade every server first. The server that runs the background jobs must run a version that knows about sample data: an older one's scheduled detections would raise findings from the sample that removal cannot tell from yours, and its threat intel downloads would delete the sample's indicators. While it runs an older version, a load is refused with a message that names it.
  • Load or remove it on any of them. It is not one of the background jobs, so it does not wait for the server that runs those. The detections the load runs over the sample's week run on the server you loaded from, and only over the sample's own events. The scheduled detections, on the server that runs the jobs, leave the sample out as always.
  • Every server shows the same thing. The record of what is loaded, and of a load or removal that is running, is kept in OpenSearch, in the <prefix>_runtime index where the servers find each other. So the card shows the same set on every server, a second load is refused wherever you try it, and a load running on one server shows its progress on the others.
  • Threat intel, asset and identity entries follow. Each server keeps the threat intel in memory, and the sample's two lookup files in its own lookups folder. The server you load from has them at once. The others read the threat intel again, and add the lookup files, as soon as their card shows the load (within a minute when nobody has the card open), and take them out the same way after a removal, wherever it was made.

If a server stops in the middle of a load or removal without saying so (it crashed, or lost touch with OpenSearch), the others wait until its record has not changed for a minute, then treat the job as stopped: the card offers Remove what was loaded or Finish removing, on any server. That minute is timed by each server's own clock from the last change it saw, so a computer whose clock is wrong cannot make a running job look stopped.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• All events fall within the last six days, ending a few minutes before you load. The load keeps their own times even if your server's maximum event age is shorter. If retention keeps a kind of data for fewer days, it deletes the older sample days on its usual schedule; nothing else changes.
  • After an upgrade, the findings and investigations indices learn the sample's marker field from the server that runs the background jobs. Loading sample data adds that one field itself if it is not there yet, so you need not wait for that server to get to it. Every server must still run the new version (see Several servers).

docs.title: Security checks
docs.text:
The Security page (Settings > Security) and the signalith security command check how this server is set up: what is encrypted on the network and on disk, who can sign in, how passwords and keys are kept, and how Signalith runs on this computer. They say what to fix first and how, and they are honest about what Signalith can't see.

  • How the checks run
  • What the states mean
  • In transit
  • At rest
  • In use
  • Accounts and sign-in
  • This server
  • Standard or strict certificate authority
  • Always on
  • Not checked here
  • The signalith security command
  • API

docs.title: How the checks run
docs.text:
• The server checks itself 30 seconds after it starts, then every hour, and after each step of a change of certificate authority. Re-check on the page runs the checks again, at most once every 10 seconds.
  • A whole run takes 15 seconds at most. Each part has its own time limit, so a slow disk or a slow OpenSearch never holds up the server or a page. A part that runs out of time shows Can't tell with "Signalith couldn't finish this check in time."
  • The server logs a line when what is at risk changes: security check: at risk (a warning, with the ids of the checks) or security check: nothing at risk.
  • Only admins can see the page and the report. It names files, folders and this server's addresses, but never shows a password, token or key.
  • Every server that shares the same OpenSearch checks itself, whether or not it runs the jobs (see docs/servers.md). The page shows the counts of the others too, with a link to each one's own page.
  • Many checks look at the computer itself: its disks, its files and the process. signalith security run on the server as root or Administrator can see more than the service can; see The signalith security command.

docs.title: What the states mean
docs.text:
State Meaning At risk Right now, someone on the network or another account on this computer could read or change Signalith's data, or sign in, without anything special. Needs attention Weaker than it should be, or a step was left half-done. Nobody gets in because of it today. Can't tell Signalith can't see this from where it runs. This is never counted as a problem. The check says how to look by hand. Good Set up safely. Some good checks have a Make it stronger tip.

A check that doesn't apply is left out, rather than shown as "not applicable". For example, Directory sign-in appears only while directory sign-in is on.

A check with several problems shows the worst one, and lists the others under it.

Fix first lists everything at risk, then everything that needs attention, in the order that matters most: OpenSearch open to the network and HTTPS first, then passwords and tokens anyone can look up, then how keys are kept, then the rest. The page shows the top three; signalith security lists them all.

docs.title: In transit
docs.text: Whether data is encrypted as it crosses the network.

docs.title: HTTPS
docs.text:
Looks at: the HTTPS setting (server.tls.mode), the listen address (server.listen) and Trusted reverse proxies (server.trusted_proxies). While HTTPS is off behind a proxy, the server also notes computers that signed in, and agents that sent events, directly over plain HTTP in the last day, not through the proxy. It keeps up to 50 addresses of each, in memory only. Computers and agents on the server itself aren't counted: what they send doesn't cross the network.

  • Good: HTTPS is on; or HTTPS is off but Signalith answers only on this computer (such as 127.0.0.1:8080); or a trusted reverse proxy serves HTTPS.
  • Needs attention: a proxy serves HTTPS, but people signed in, or agents sent events, to Signalith directly over plain HTTP; or HTTPS is left to a reverse proxy that Signalith believes only because signalith.yaml was written before HTTPS was the default (an https:// public address and no server.tls section). List that proxy under Trusted reverse proxies.
  • At risk: HTTPS is off, and Signalith answers other computers directly.

To fix: turn on HTTPS, as in Upgrading from plain HTTP. Behind a proxy, set the listen address so only the proxy reaches Signalith (Behind a reverse proxy).

How to check by hand: from another computer, curl -sI http://siem.example.com:8080/ prints Location: https://... when Signalith serves HTTPS itself.

docs.title: HTTPS certificate
docs.text:
Looks at: the certificate Signalith serves, for HTTPS or syslog over TLS: when it expires, its key and signature, and the names it covers. With your own files, it also looks at whether they cover the host in server.public_url and include the certificate of the authority that issued them. With Signalith's own certificate, it looks at when the certificate authority expires.

  • At risk: the certificate has expired.
  • Needs attention: it expires soon (30 days for your own files; 21 days for Signalith's own, which means renewal failed), it leaves out names people or agents use, it uses a key or signature that is too weak (RSA under 2048 bits, or SHA-1), your own certificate covers only IP addresses (so agents have no host name to check it against, see Agents and syslog), or Signalith's certificate authority expires within 180 days.

To fix: see Use your own certificate, or Names the certificate can cover. Signalith renews its own certificate by itself 30 days before it expires; if it can't, it says why in its log when it starts.

How to check by hand:

openssl s_client -connect siem.example.com:8080 -servername siem.example.com </dev/null 2>/dev/null \
  | openssl x509 -noout -subject -enddate -ext subjectAltName

docs.title: Certificate authority
docs.text:
Shown with Signalith's own certificate (HTTPS set to Automatic).

Looks at: how far the certificate authority in use may vouch, what Certificate authority reaches (server.tls.ca_scope) is set to, and whether a change of certificate authority is in progress. After a switch, it counts the computers that refused the new certificate (from failed TLS handshakes, over HTTPS and syslog).

  • Good: a standard or a strict certificate authority, whichever you chose. Neither is better for everyone; see Standard or strict certificate authority. One made by an earlier version also vouches for the names under this server's names, such as x.siem-1; the line says so, and a new one covers each name exactly.
  • Needs attention: a new certificate authority is ready but not switched to yet; the previous one is still kept after a switch; the one in use was made by an older version and can vouch for any website; the one in use was made by an older version and isn't limited to websites, so a stolen key could sign programs or email that computers trusting it accept; or the one in use isn't the kind you chose.

To fix: follow Switching to a new certificate authority.

How to check by hand:

sudo openssl x509 -in /var/lib/signalith/tls/ca.pem -noout -subject -enddate -ext nameConstraints,extendedKeyUsage

A standard one lists private names such as .local and .corp and private ranges. A strict one lists only this server's names and addresses. Under Excluded, the server's names with a dot in front keep the names under them out. No name constraints at all means it was made by an older version. X509v3 Extended Key Usage should read TLS Web Server Authentication alone; without it, it was made before the website-only limit.

docs.title: Agents on plain HTTP
docs.text:
Shown while HTTPS is on.

Looks at: Agents on plain HTTP (server.tls.plaintext_ingest), and which agents sent events over plain HTTP in the last day. An agent on the server itself is counted apart: its events don't cross the network.

  • Good: agents can only send over HTTPS.
  • At risk: agents on other computers still send over plain HTTP.
  • Needs attention: plain HTTP is still accepted, though only agents on this computer, or none, use it.

To fix: give each agent a new configuration from Add data, then choose Refuse them. An agent that was missed keeps its events, and the Health page names it. See Upgrading from plain HTTP.

How to check by hand: the Health page lists agents that send over plain HTTP.

docs.title: Syslog
docs.text:
Shown when a syslog listener is on (syslog.udp, syslog.tcp or syslog.tls).

Looks at: which listeners are on and the addresses they listen on, syslog.allow, and how many devices sent over each protocol in the last day. A listener on a loopback address, such as 127.0.0.1:5514, takes syslog only from this computer, so only the others count.

  • Good: syslog arrives only over TLS; or plain syslog is accepted only from this computer, or only from the addresses in syslog.allow. Plain syslog isn't encrypted, which is normal for devices that can't use TLS.
  • Needs attention: plain syslog is accepted from any computer that can reach the port. Anyone could send fake events.
  • Can't tell: in Docker Desktop, every device seems to come from the same address, so Signalith can't limit who sends. Limit who reaches the port with this computer's firewall instead.

To fix: list the addresses or ranges of the devices that send syslog under syslog.allow, such as 10.0.0.0/8. Devices that can use TLS, such as rsyslog, syslog-ng and many firewalls, can send over TLS instead (Agents and syslog).

How to check by hand: sudo ss -lntup | grep signalith shows the ports Signalith listens on, and on which addresses. Check the computer's firewall for those ports.

docs.title: Connection to OpenSearch
docs.text:
Looks at: the OpenSearch address (opensearch.url), whether Signalith checks OpenSearch's certificate (opensearch.tls_skip_verify, opensearch.ca_file), whether it sends a password, and the certificate OpenSearch presents. The demo certificate that OpenSearch ships with is issued by Example Com Inc. Root CA; its key is public.

  • Good: HTTPS with the certificate checked; or plain HTTP to OpenSearch on this computer.
  • Needs attention: plain HTTP to OpenSearch on the same Docker network; or, for OpenSearch on this computer, the demo certificate or certificate checks turned off.
  • At risk: certificate checks are off for OpenSearch on another computer; events or the password cross the network over plain HTTP; or OpenSearch on another computer uses the demo certificate.

To fix: see Point Signalith at it and Make the certificates.

How to check by hand:

openssl s_client -connect opensearch.example.com:9200 </dev/null 2>/dev/null | openssl x509 -noout -issuer -enddate

docs.title: AI assistant and threat intel
docs.text:
Shown when the AI assistant is set up or a threat intel feed is on.

Looks at: whether the AI assistant (assistant.url) and each feed are reached over https://, and whether a key, password or header is sent with them.

  • Good: everything is reached over HTTPS, or the assistant runs on this computer.
  • Needs attention: a feed is downloaded over plain HTTP, so someone on the network could change what it says.
  • At risk: an API key or a feed's password crosses the network over plain HTTP.

To fix: use the https:// address of the assistant (Settings) or the feed (Threat intel), if it has one.

docs.title: Trusted reverse proxies
docs.text:
Shown when Trusted reverse proxies is set, or when Signalith believes a proxy only because signalith.yaml was written before HTTPS was the default.

Looks at: each entry in server.trusted_proxies, and the proxies believed for the older reason in the last day.

  • Good: only the listed proxies are believed. With Client address header empty, a tip says that everyone behind them counts as one shared address for the sign-in limits, and how to count each person instead.
  • Needs attention: an entry is wider than a /16 (IPv4) or /48 (IPv6), so any computer in it can claim a browser used HTTPS (and, with Client address header set, choose the address its failed sign-ins are counted under); or a proxy is believed only because of the older config.

To fix: list only the proxies' own addresses. See Behind a reverse proxy.

docs.title: At rest
docs.text: Whether stored passwords, keys and events are protected on disk.

docs.title: Master key
docs.text:
Looks at: where the master key comes from (a file, a systemd credential, Windows protection, a Docker volume or secret, or the SIGNALITH_MASTER_KEY environment variable), who can read the key file, and whether an older key or an unused copy is still kept. On Windows it reads the file's access list; it never trusts file modes there.

  • Good: only Signalith's account can read the key, or Windows protects it.
  • Needs attention: a group can read it, it belongs to another account, it is in an environment variable, or an older key or unused copy is still kept.
  • At risk: every account on this computer can read the key.

To fix: see The master key, Keeping the key elsewhere and Changing the key.

How to check by hand: sudo signalith secrets status says where the key is. On Linux, sudo ls -l /var/lib/signalith/keys should show -rw------- and Signalith's account. On Windows, icacls C:\ProgramData\Signalith\keys\master.key.dpapi.

docs.title: Stored passwords and keys
docs.text:
Looks at: the passwords and keys in signalith.yaml, settings.yaml, directory.json and intel_feeds.yaml: whether each is encrypted with the master key, and who can read a file that holds one as plain text. Values that come from environment variables aren't stored, so they aren't counted.

  • Good: every stored password and key is encrypted.
  • Needs attention: some are plain text; a password is written into an address, where it can't be encrypted; some are still encrypted with the previous master key; or some can't be decrypted.
  • At risk: plain text values are in a file other accounts can read.

Signalith's HTTPS keys and the Docker setup's generated secrets are protected by file permissions, not by the master key (see File permissions).

To fix: sudo signalith secrets encrypt (see What Signalith encrypts and Commands).

How to check by hand: sudo signalith secrets status lists each value and how it is stored, without showing it.

docs.title: Disk encryption
docs.text:
Looks at: the disks that hold Signalith's state folder, its lookups folder and its config file. Each disk is reported once.

  • On Linux, it reads /proc/self/mountinfo and /sys to find the disk under each folder, and looks for an encryption layer such as LUKS (dm-crypt), eCryptfs or gocryptfs. It needs no access to /dev. Self-encrypting drives don't show this way.
  • On Windows, only administrators may ask whether BitLocker is on. Run signalith security in a PowerShell opened as Administrator: it asks Windows and saves the answer for the page. The page uses a saved answer for 30 days.

  • It also notes a virtual machine (QEMU, KVM, VMware, Hyper-V, Xen, VirtualBox, Parallels and the big clouds), a network share, memory, ZFS and containers.

  • Good: the disk is encrypted, or Signalith's files are kept in memory only.

  • Needs attention: a physical disk with no encryption, as far as the system can tell; or BitLocker is off or suspended.
  • Can't tell: a virtual disk (its host may encrypt it), a container, a network share, ZFS, or Windows without a saved answer.

To fix: encrypt the disk, or move Signalith's folders to an encrypted one; see Disk encryption.

How to check by hand:

  • Linux: lsblk -o NAME,TYPE,FSTYPE,MOUNTPOINTS. A crypt line above the disk means it is encrypted.
  • Windows, as Administrator: manage-bde -status C:, or & "$env:ProgramFiles\Signalith\signalith.exe" security, which also saves the answer for the page.
  • Docker Desktop: check the drive of the computer it runs on, with manage-bde -status C: on Windows or fdesetup status on macOS.
  • ZFS: zfs get encryption <dataset>.
  • A virtual machine or cloud server: check the disk's settings in the provider's console, or ask whoever runs the host.

docs.title: Archived days
docs.text:
Shown when the archive folder holds archives, or a retention policy archives days.

Looks at: the archive folder (retention.archive_dir): how many days it holds and their size, who can read it, and the disk under it, as for Disk encryption. Signalith doesn't encrypt archives itself.

  • Good: on an encrypted disk, readable only by Signalith.
  • Needs attention: other accounts can read the archives, or the disk isn't encrypted.
  • Can't tell: Signalith can't see the disk or share under them.

To fix: keep the archive folder on an encrypted disk, readable only by Signalith; see Archives. Copies of archives you move elsewhere are only as safe as where you put them.

docs.title: Where OpenSearch keeps events
docs.text:
Looks at: when OpenSearch runs on this computer and Signalith isn't in a container, it asks OpenSearch for its data folder (path.data), with Signalith's own account, and checks the disk under it, as for Disk encryption. A folder that doesn't exist here (OpenSearch in a container of its own reports the container's folder) isn't checked.

  • Good: an encrypted disk, or a folder kept in memory only.
  • Needs attention: a disk that isn't encrypted, as far as the system can tell.
  • Can't tell: OpenSearch runs on another computer or in its own container; its folder isn't on this computer's disks as Signalith sees them; Signalith's account may not look inside a folder on the way (such as /home under the systemd unit); or OpenSearch didn't answer.

How to check by hand: on the computer OpenSearch runs on, find path.data in opensearch.yml and check the disk that holds it, with the commands under Disk encryption. In the Docker quick start, events are in the opensearch-data volume, on the disk of the computer Docker runs on.

docs.title: Who can read OpenSearch
docs.text:
Looks at: whether OpenSearch answers a search with no sign-in at all. Signalith sends one request with no user name, password or client certificate, to count the events in its own indices, and gives it 5 seconds. When OpenSearch is on this computer, it also tries the same port on this computer's other addresses, to see whether OpenSearch listens on the network. If OpenSearch keeps an audit log, it records this as a refused request.

  • Good: OpenSearch turns away anyone who doesn't sign in.
  • Needs attention: anyone on this computer can read events, but OpenSearch doesn't listen on the network.
  • At risk: anyone who can reach OpenSearch can read events without signing in.
  • Can't tell: OpenSearch couldn't be reached just now. The Health page shows why.

To fix: turn on OpenSearch's security plugin with your own certificates, as in OpenSearch on Linux or Windows (or Docker quick start).

How to check by hand: this should print 401, not 200:

curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' --cacert root-ca.pem 'https://localhost:9200/signalith-*/_count'

docs.title: In use
docs.text: Whether secrets stay private while Signalith runs.

docs.title: Memory
docs.text:
Looks at: on Linux, whether the process may write a crash dump (its core limit and whether it is dumpable), and whether swap could hold its memory. On Windows, whether Windows is set to keep full memory dumps of crashing programs.

  • Good: Signalith's memory can't be saved in a crash dump. A tip says when swap is on and not encrypted, and when a confidential VM would protect memory from the host too.
  • Needs attention: a crash dump could hold passwords.

To fix: restart Signalith with this version, which turns crash dumps off; under systemd, keep LimitCORE=0 in the unit. On Windows, leave signalith.exe out of the LocalDumps setting. See In use.

How to check by hand:

  • Linux: grep 'core file' /proc/$(systemctl show -p MainPID --value signalith)/limits shows 0, and swapon --show lists swap.
  • Windows: reg query "HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\Windows Error Reporting\LocalDumps" /s.

docs.title: Confidential virtual machine
docs.text:
Shown only when found, on Linux: AMD SEV-SNP (/sys/class/misc/sev-guest) or Intel TDX (/sys/class/misc/tdx_guest, or tdx_guest in /proc/cpuinfo). Such a machine is built to keep even its host from reading its memory. Some platforms hide these markers, so not finding one proves nothing, and Signalith doesn't report it as a problem.

How to check by hand: your cloud provider's console says whether the VM is confidential.

docs.title: Accounts and sign-in
docs.text: Who can sign in, and how well passwords and tokens are kept.

docs.title: Built-in admin's password
docs.text:
Looks at: whether the built-in admin still has the public example password, the first password the Docker setup made, a password set in the SIGNALITH_ADMIN_PASSWORD environment variable, or one read from the file in SIGNALITH_ADMIN_PASSWORD_FILE; and how strongly it is hashed.

  • Good: it has a password of its own.
  • Needs attention: the Docker setup's first password, which is kept as plain text in a Docker volume; a password in an environment variable, or in a file named by one; or an older, weaker hash.
  • At risk: the example password change-me-please, which anyone can look up.

To fix: sudo signalith passwd, then restart Signalith; see The built-in admin.

docs.title: Everyday sign-in
docs.text:
Looks at: when the built-in admin last signed in, and how many other people have admin accounts.

  • Good: people sign in with their own accounts, or only the built-in admin exists so far (with a tip to give yourself an account, so the audit log shows who did what).
  • Needs attention: the built-in admin signed in during the last 7 days, though others have admin accounts. Keep it for emergencies.

To fix: see The built-in admin.

docs.title: Temporary passwords
docs.text:
Shown when there are local users.

Looks at: enabled local users who still have the temporary password they were given more than 7 days ago.

To fix: remind them to sign in and choose a password, or disable their account until they need it (Managing local users).

docs.title: Directory sign-in
docs.text:
Shown while directory sign-in is on.

Looks at: the directory addresses (main and failover): ldaps://, or ldap:// with StartTLS, and whether Signalith checks the directory server's certificate.

  • Good: passwords go to the directory encrypted, and its certificate is checked.
  • At risk: ldap:// without StartTLS, so passwords cross the network unencrypted; or certificate checks are off, so someone could pose as the directory and collect passwords.

To fix: use an ldaps:// address or turn on StartTLS, give the directory's CA certificate, and turn off Skip certificate check (Set it up).

How to check by hand: openssl s_client -connect dc1.corp.example.com:636 </dev/null 2>/dev/null | openssl x509 -noout -subject -issuer.

docs.title: Sign-in sessions
docs.text:
Looks at: Sign out after (auth.session_timeout, 12 hours by default): how long a sign-in lasts without use. An open tab's own refreshes (the Health card, dashboards and other timers) don't count as use, so a tab left unattended still signs out. Someone who ticks Keep me signed in isn't signed out for being idle; every sign-in ends after 7 days at most.

  • Good: 24 hours or less.
  • Needs attention: longer than 24 hours.

To fix: set Sign out after to 12h or less on the Settings page.

docs.title: Agent tokens
docs.text:
Shown when there are agent tokens: tokens made on Add data or with signalith tokens, or shared tokens from signalith.yaml (ingest.tokens), SIGNALITH_INGEST_TOKEN or SIGNALITH_INGEST_TOKEN_FILE. See agent-tokens.md.

Looks at: whether a shared token (one every agent uses) is still accepted, when an agent last sent with it, how long it is, and whether it is the public example token. A shared token copied from any one agent works for all of them, and can't be turned off for one agent alone.

  • Good: no shared token is accepted; each agent group sends with its own token ("Each agent group sends with its own token (N active)."). A shared token you chose Stop accepting on counts as retired, even while it is still in the configuration.
  • Good, with a tip: a shared token is accepted but no agent has ever sent with it, and either agent tokens exist or this is the Docker quick start, whose setup step makes one ("No agent sends with a shared token, though one is still accepted."). The tip says to choose Stop accepting on it.
  • Needs attention:
  • a shared token is accepted and an agent sent with it in the last 7 days ("Some agents still send with a shared token, so a copy taken from any one of them works for all of them.");
  • a shared token is accepted though no agent has used it in the last 7 days;
  • a shared token is shorter than 24 characters;
  • a shared token is accepted and the tokens couldn't be read from OpenSearch, so how it was used isn't known.
  • At risk: the example token change-this-ingest-token, which anyone can look up, is accepted. On a Docker quick start upgraded from an older version, whose agents all have it, Signalith accepts it from them over plain HTTP while Agents on plain HTTP accepts them, even when it isn't in ingest.tokens. Choose Refuse them once every agent has its configuration from Add data; that ends it for good.
  • Can't tell: the agent tokens couldn't be read from OpenSearch (for example when signalith security runs while OpenSearch is down).

On the Docker quick start the check also says why the old example token is refused: the install started new, it was upgraded and agents on plain HTTP were refused since a date, or Signalith couldn't yet ask OpenSearch which it is. See The Docker quick start's old example token.

To fix:

  1. Open Add data and give each agent a configuration with its own token.
  2. Under Agent tokens, choose Stop accepting on the shared token once its Last used is older than the last agent you updated.
  3. That's all. You may also delete it from signalith.yaml (ingest.tokens) or SIGNALITH_INGEST_TOKEN; on the Docker quick start, leave docker-compose.yml as it is.

See Replace a shared token.

docs.title: Signalith's OpenSearch account
docs.text:
Shown when OpenSearch requires sign-in and has its security plugin.

Looks at: what OpenSearch says Signalith's account may do (/_plugins/_security/authinfo), and whether Signalith signs in as admin with the demo password admin. The password is compared in memory and never shown.

  • Good: an account without admin rights.
  • Needs attention: an account that can do anything in OpenSearch (all_access, security_manager or the admin backend role).
  • At risk: admin with the password admin.
  • Can't tell: OpenSearch couldn't be reached, or didn't say.

To fix: give Signalith its own account with the signalith_server role, ideally signing in with a certificate (Load the security settings).

How to check by hand:

curl -s --cacert root-ca.pem --cert signalith.pem --key signalith-key.pem 'https://localhost:9200/_plugins/_security/authinfo?pretty'

docs.title: This server
docs.text: How Signalith runs on this computer.

docs.title: Account Signalith runs as
docs.text:
Looks at: the account of the Signalith process: root or not on Linux and in containers, and on Windows whether it is Local System, an administrator, or its own service account.

  • Good: its own account (signalith under systemd, NT SERVICE\Signalith on Windows), or an unprivileged account in a container.
  • Needs attention: root, Local System or an administrator, so a flaw in Signalith could reach the whole computer.
  • Can't tell: on Windows, the service runs as an account Windows couldn't say is an administrator or not, such as a domain account while the domain can't be reached.

To fix: on Linux, install the systemd unit from Linux; on Windows, run install.ps1 from this version again (Windows). In Docker, remove a user: line that overrides the image's account.

How to check by hand:

  • Linux: ps -o user= -p $(systemctl show -p MainPID --value signalith).
  • Windows: sc.exe qc Signalith shows SERVICE_START_NAME.
  • Docker: docker compose -f deploy/docker/docker-compose.yml exec signalith id.

docs.title: Service protections
docs.text:
Shown on Linux. On Windows, Account Signalith runs as covers the service.

Looks at: the protections the systemd unit in deploy/systemd sets up, as the process sees them: no new privileges, a system-call filter, no extra capabilities, a read-only system, hidden processes, a private /dev and private new files. In a container: no new privileges, no capabilities, a read-only system and no core dumps.

  • Good: all of them are in place. Linux before 5.8 can't hide processes, so there it isn't counted as missing.
  • Needs attention: some are missing, or Signalith doesn't run as a systemd service.

To fix: install the current unit and restart, as in Linux. If you changed the unit on purpose, compare it with systemctl cat signalith. In Docker, keep read_only: true, cap_drop: [ALL], security_opt: [no-new-privileges:true] and ulimits: core: 0 in docker-compose.yml.

How to check by hand: systemd-analyze security signalith.

docs.title: File permissions
docs.text:
Looks at: who may read or change Signalith's keys (the HTTPS keys in tls/, the sign-in key signin.key, a key file for OpenSearch, and the files named by SIGNALITH_*_FILE variables), its private files (users.json, directory.json, settings.yaml, intel_feeds.yaml, the admin password hash), its folders, and signalith.yaml with its folder. The master key is left to Master key. On Windows it reads each file's access list; on Linux and macOS, the owner and mode.

  • Good: only Signalith's account (and administrators) can change them, and only they can read the keys and private files. For signalith.yaml and the folders, it looks only at who can change them. Whether others can read plain passwords in signalith.yaml is part of Stored passwords and keys.
  • Needs attention: a group or other accounts can read private files, or a group can change a folder; or the state folder is on a network share, so keys cross the network each time they are read.
  • At risk: every account can read a key, or change the config or a folder.

To fix: the check gives the exact commands for each file. On Linux, sudo chmod -R go-rwx /var/lib/signalith covers the state folder. On Windows, running install.ps1 from this version again resets access in C:\ProgramData\Signalith. Keep the state folder on a local disk (Identity).

How to check by hand:

  • Linux: sudo ls -la /var/lib/signalith /var/lib/signalith/tls /etc/signalith.
  • Windows: icacls C:\ProgramData\Signalith /t.

docs.title: Standard or strict certificate authority
docs.text:
With Signalith's own certificate, computers that trust its certificate authority accept any certificate it makes. Certificate authority reaches (server.tls.ca_scope) chooses how far that goes. Neither choice lets it vouch for other public websites: of public names, only this server's own, each exactly.

  • Standard, the default, can also vouch for private network names and addresses, such as intranet.corp or 192.168.1.5. A new address for this server works right away.
  • Strict can vouch only for this server's own names and addresses. A stolen key then lets someone pose only as this server's website, but a new name or address later means a new certificate authority, which every browser and agent must trust again.

Strict suits a server whose name and address won't change, especially when many computers trust it. Both are Good on the page. The setting only applies to a certificate authority made from now on; see How far the certificate authority reaches and Switching to a new certificate authority.

docs.title: Always on
docs.text:
The report also lists protections that can't be turned off, as they apply to this server:

  • With HTTPS on, passwords, API sign-ins and sessions are refused over plain HTTP, and the sign-in cookie is sent over HTTPS only.
  • With HTTPS on, browsers that reach Signalith by name are told to use HTTPS only (HSTS).
  • Every page has a strict Content Security Policy and can't be shown inside another site.
  • Guessing passwords is slowed: after 10 wrong tries for one account from one address in 15 minutes, sign-in pauses for 15 minutes. The API is limited the same way.
  • Sign-ins end after 7 days at most, even with Keep me signed in.
  • Passwords are stored only as bcrypt hashes.
  • Logs, pages and the API never show stored passwords or keys.
  • With HTTPS on, agents set up from Add data check the server's certificate before sending.
  • Sign-ins, sign-outs and every change to users and settings go to the audit log.

docs.title: Not checked here
docs.text:
Signalith can't see these, so it says so once rather than showing Can't tell for them every time:

  • Firewalls: which computers can reach Signalith's ports (8080 by default, and the syslog ports) and OpenSearch's (9200 by default). Check the firewall of this computer and of the network.
  • Backups, and whether the master key is kept apart from them (see Backing up the key).
  • Updates for Signalith, OpenSearch and the operating system. Signalith doesn't contact the internet to check.
  • Two-step sign-in. Signalith has none of its own.
  • The computers agents run on.
  • Copies of events outside Signalith, such as exports, moved archives and OpenSearch snapshots.

docs.title: The signalith security command
docs.text:
sudo signalith security            # Linux
sudo signalith security -json      # the same report as JSON

& "$env:ProgramFiles\Signalith\signalith.exe" security    # Windows, as Administrator

docker compose -f deploy/docker/docker-compose.yml exec signalith signalith security

It runs the same checks as the page, from the files and processes on this computer, and prints the report as plain text: a summary, Fix first with the commands for this kind of install, then every check by group. Docs links are printed in full.

  • On Linux it uses the folders, files and master key the service is given in its systemd unit, like validate, settings and secrets do, and looks at the running service's process. In Docker it looks at the container's first process. When it finds no running service for the config file (it is stopped, or was started another way), the checks of the process say so. The Security page checks them either way.
  • On Windows, run as Administrator, it also asks whether BitLocker is on and saves the answer for the page. It says so on standard error, so the report itself stays the same.
  • It can't see what only the running server sees: agents and devices that sent in the last day, sign-ins over plain HTTP, and computers that refused a new certificate. The checks that need those say so, rather than claiming "none". The page has them.
  • Without root or Administrator, it may not be able to read the config file. It then stops and says to run it with sudo or as Administrator. A folder or file it can't read makes that check Can't tell.
  • -json prints the same JSON as GET /api/security, without what only the running server sees (others, seen_names and refusals). Notes go to standard error, so the output stays JSON.

Exit codes, for scripts and monitoring:

Code Meaning 0 Nothing is at risk. 2 Something is at risk. 1 The command couldn't run, for example the config file couldn't be read.

Needs attention and Can't tell never change the exit code.

docs.title: API
docs.text:
Both routes are for admins only.

  • GET /api/security returns the last report as JSON. It never waits for a new run, unless there is no report yet. ?recheck=1 runs the checks again first (at most once every 10 seconds). ?format=text returns the plain text report, and &download=1 saves it as a file.
  • POST /api/security/ca takes the steps of a change of certificate authority: {"action": "prepare"} (with "scope": "standard" or "strict" to change server.tls.ca_scope too), switch, rollback, discard or prune. It returns the new report. See Switching to a new certificate authority.

The report has checked_at, server, summary (counts by state), fix_first (check ids), groups, checks, always_on, not_checked, and, with Signalith's own certificate, ca. Each check has its id, group, title, state (risk, attention, unknown or good), line, details, and a fix or tip with steps, a setting, a page, commands and a docs link.

docs.title: Agents and syslog
docs.text:
Signalith takes events from three kinds of senders:

  • Fluent Bit agents on Windows and Linux, set up from the Add data page;
  • syslog (RFC 5424, RFC 3164 and CEF) from firewalls, switches, appliances and servers without an agent;
  • OpenTelemetry Collectors and SDKs over OTLP/HTTP (see OpenTelemetry).

docs.title: Agents
docs.text:
Open Add data, pick Linux or Windows, and follow the steps: install Fluent Bit, save Signalith's CA certificate and the generated configuration, and restart it. The configuration already contains the server address and ingest token, and sends over HTTPS, checking the server's certificate with that CA.

The configuration also sends two short headers with every batch: the computer's name (X-Signalith-Agent, which Fluent Bit fills in itself) and which Signalith version made the configuration and which certificate authority it trusts (X-Signalith-Config). With them, the Endpoints page lists each agent once, even when it sends to several servers, and says when one needs a new configuration. They are labels only: the agent token is what lets an agent in. OpenTelemetry Collector configurations send the second header only; Signalith takes a Collector's computer name from its events.

Agents on other machines must send to an address they can reach, such as https://192.168.1.20:8080, not localhost. Enter it under Agents send to on that page (or set server.public_url or SIGNALITH_PUBLIC_URL), and allow the port, 8080 by default, through this computer's firewall.

docs.title: What each source becomes
docs.text:
Events are sorted into data models with common (CIM-style) field names, so one search or detection covers every source of the same kind.

Source Data model Windows Security log: 4624, 4625 logons; 4648 explicit credentials; 4768, 4769, 4771 Kerberos; 4776 NTLM credential checks Authentication Windows Security log: 4688 process creation Endpoint Windows Security log: 4720, 4726, 4738, 4781 accounts; 4741, 4742 computer accounts; 4727, 4728, 4729, 4730, 4732, 4737, 4756 group changes; 4798, 4799 group listings; 4698, 4699, 4701, 4702 scheduled tasks; 4886, 4887 certificates; 1102 log cleared Change Windows Security log: 5140, 5145 network share access Filesystem Sysmon: 1 process create, 5 process terminated, 8 remote thread, 9 raw disk read, 10 process access; 3 network connection; 6 driver and 7 DLL load; 11 file create, 23 and 26 file delete; 12, 13, 14 registry; 22 DNS query Endpoint, Network_Traffic, Image_Load, Filesystem, Registry, Network_Resolution PowerShell script block logging: 4104 (Microsoft-Windows-PowerShell/Operational; see Detections) Script Linux sshd, sudo, su (auth.log, secure, or journald) Authentication Linux audit log (auditd: audit.log, or its syslog plugin) Other, sourcetype linux:audit Linux useradd, userdel, usermod, gpasswd Change Syslog from any device (see below), including CEF Authentication, Change, Network_Traffic or Other OpenTelemetry Collector or SDK logs over OTLP/HTTP (OpenTelemetry) the same models for Windows, Linux and syslog records; Other for app logs Anything else Other (searchable by text and fields)

sshd prints the user name a client sends, and on a failed key sign-in the key ID of the certificate it offers, as they were sent. When either copies sshd's own "from port " so that the real address cannot be told, the event is stored without src and with src_ambiguous=true. Search src_ambiguous=true to find these sign-in attempts; host says which server they were made against.

docs.title: Ingest limits
docs.text:
Agents send batches to /api/ingest, and OpenTelemetry Collectors to /api/otlp/v1/logs. One request can be up to 16 MB, with up to 200,000 records of at most 1 MB each, nested at most 32 levels deep; Fluent Bit's requests are far smaller. A request over a limit is refused with 413 (400 for broken JSON) and a message saying what to change, and nothing from it is stored. When many agents send at once, the extra requests wait their turn and then get 503, so Fluent Bit sends them again.

A batch is read in full before it waits for its turn, so a slow sender never holds up other agents. Batches still arriving may hold 256 MB of memory in all, and one sender (an IPv4 address or an IPv6 /64) a quarter of that; past it, the sender gets 503 and sends again shortly. Senders behind one proxy or NAT can be listed in server.shared_addresses. A batch has 2 minutes to arrive; one still arriving at least 16 KB every 30 seconds gets more time, up to 10 minutes, so slow links work. A batch that stalls or takes longer is refused with 408 and a message saying to send smaller batches (a lower Flush in Fluent Bit's [SERVICE] section), and the server log notes it.

Each event keeps its own time unless that is older than ingest.max_event_age (a week by default, or the shortest retention period if shorter) or more than an hour ahead. Then it is filed under the time it arrived and its own time is kept in device_time, so a wrong clock or a forged date cannot create indices for other days. Search device_time=* to find these events.

Field names that senders choose (JSON keys, syslog structured data, CEF extensions) are limited so they cannot fill OpenSearch's mapping: at most 200 fields per event, names of up to 128 letters, digits and _ - @ : / in at most 5 dot-separated parts, and at most 1,000 new names per daily index each time Signalith starts. With several servers, those 1,000 are shared among the servers that stored events in the last 10 minutes (at least 100 each), and no server adds new names to a day whose index already has 1,600 fields (see Servers). Fields Signalith itself produces are always kept, so an event is never lost to extra fields. Fields left out are counted in the event's dropped_fields (search dropped_fields>0), their values stay in _raw, and the Health page and /api/health show the totals under ingest (retimed, fields_dropped).

A few field names belong to Signalith, which sets them itself: @timestamp, datamodel, device_time, dropped_fields and the sample-data marker signalith_sample. When a sender's event has one of them, it is left out and counted in dropped_fields the same way; the event is stored without it. The one exception is the time of a JSON record: its date (Fluent Bit sends one) is the event's time, or its @timestamp when it has no date. These two are read as the time, not stored as fields and not counted. When a record has both, its @timestamp is not used.

docs.title: Syslog
docs.text:
Firewalls, switches, routers, appliances and servers without an agent can send syslog. Point them at this server's address on UDP or TCP port 514, or over TLS on port 6514. signalith init turns all three on; the Docker quick start publishes port 514. Syslog over TLS uses the web UI's certificate (see HTTPS).

Open Add data and pick Syslog for copy-ready setup for rsyslog, syslog-ng, Cisco IOS and ASA, Palo Alto, FortiGate, pfSense and OPNsense, UniFi and Windows, with this server's address filled in; rsyslog and syslog-ng send over TLS when it is on, with the CA certificate to save. Send the test message it shows and watch it arrive on the same page. When syslog is off, the page gives the steps to turn it on for this system: the UDP and TCP address on the Settings page, then Restart now, plus the port permission for a Linux service or the Windows Firewall rules. By hand, forwarding a Linux server's logs with rsyslog is one line in /etc/rsyslog.d/90-signalith.conf, then a restart of rsyslog:

*.* @@siem.example.com:514

@@ sends over TCP; a single @ sends over UDP. Signalith reads RFC 5424 and RFC 3164 syslog (including the usual variations, such as Cisco IOS, IOS XR, NX-OS and ASA), and CEF (Common Event Format) from security products, mapped to CIM fields like src, dest, dest_port, user and action. Forwarded sshd, sudo, su and user-management messages land in Authentication and Change like agent data, so the built-in detections apply. Events have sourcetype=syslog (or cef), host from the message, dvc set to the sender's address, and facility and severity. The event time is the one in the message, unless it is older than ingest.max_event_age (a week by default, or the shortest time any event category is kept when that is shorter) or more than an hour ahead; then it is the time Signalith received the message, and the device's own time is kept in device_time, as for agent data (see Ingest limits).

To accept syslog only from known senders, list them in Allowed senders on the Settings page, or under syslog.allow:

syslog:
  udp: 0.0.0.0:514
  tcp: 0.0.0.0:514
  allow: [10.0.0.0/8, 192.0.2.10]

Over UDP the sender address can be forged, so for trusted senders use TCP or TLS, and restrict the port with a firewall as well. The Windows installer limits its firewall rules to the syslog.allow senders.

Ports below 1024 need extra permission on Linux. The systemd unit grants it; when running Signalith another way, use a port such as 0.0.0.0:1514. When devices send to a different port than Signalith listens on, because Docker or a firewall forwards it, set syslog.public_port so Add data shows the right one (the Docker quick start listens on 5514 and sets it to 514). The Health page (and /api/health, under syslog) shows the listeners, how many messages were received, dropped, not written and rejected, and the most recent senders.

docs.title: Servers
docs.text:
Several Signalith servers can share one OpenSearch, for example two servers behind a load balancer. Each one is a whole Signalith: it serves the web pages, receives agent and syslog data, and searches. They find each other through OpenSearch, so there is nothing to connect between them.

One thing they do not all do: the background jobs. Exactly one server at a time runs them. The Servers page shows which one.

docs.title: The Servers page
docs.text:
Open Servers in the navigation, under Health, or press Ctrl+K and type "servers". The page is for admins. When something stops for everyone, such as no server running detections or OpenSearch's disk being full, every signed-in person sees a red banner at the top of every page, and the Health card in the sidebar turns red.

The line above the list says how many servers there are, which one runs the jobs, which version they run and how OpenSearch is doing. The page updates itself every few seconds.

Column What it shows Server The server's name (cluster.node_name), This server on the one you are signed in to, and its address (server.node_url) Status Running, Starting, Stopping, Stopped (shut down on purpose), Not answering (no sign of life for 30 seconds), Couldn't start (a restart after a settings change failed with the new settings and the old ones: it receives nothing, runs no jobs and tries again every 30 seconds; its log says why), Identity in use (see Identity), or, on this server only, what keeps it from using OpenSearch, such as Can't reach OpenSearch (see When this server can't use OpenSearch). Below it: how long it has been up, or when it was last seen, counted by the server that answered the page, so neither the other server's clock nor yours matters. A clock more than 2 seconds off is shown here too Background jobs Runs jobs on the server that runs them. Standby on a server that would take them over, or why it would not. Doesn't run them on a server that may not, with the reason Settings How it uses the shared settings: Shared when it uses the settings every server shares; Its own files when it is not part of the cluster (amber when it misses the cluster key, or could not reach OpenSearch when it started); Saved copy when it cannot read the shared settings now and works from its copy; Missed a key change or Settings gone when it needs signalith cluster (see signalith cluster). Hover over it for what to do. Below it, a shared setting that was changed outside Signalith or by a newer version (the server keeps its last good copy), the settings in its signalith.yaml or environment that differ from the shared ones, how many settings wait for its restart, and how many shared values it could not use Version The Signalith version it runs

A server's name opens a panel with its settings: those that wait for its restart, the shared values it could not use (it keeps its own value of each, see Settings on several servers), how its last restart went, what differs in its own files, and, for 7 days after the settings became shared, the values its own Settings page had that differ from the shared ones. Open its settings opens the Settings page at that server.

With one server, the page shows that server and nothing to set up. To add one, see Adding a server by hand. Servers that run a version of Signalith from before this one are not listed: they do not write a sign of life (see Upgrading servers you set up by hand).

A server stopped on purpose stays in the list, after the running ones, as Stopped with when it stopped, and is not counted. It leaves the list 7 days after it stopped. A server that got a new identity shows up once under its new identity and once, stopped, under its old one until then.

Alerts above the list appear only when something needs attention: amber when it should be looked at, red when something is not running. Each one names the server and says what to do. Problems another server finds with itself, such as a state folder that was moved from another computer, are shown here too.

While this server cannot use OpenSearch, its status says why, a red alert says what to do, and the other servers stay as it last saw them.

docs.title: When this server can't use OpenSearch
docs.text:
A server that can't use OpenSearch runs no background jobs. On its own Servers page, its status says why and a red alert says what to do. It tries again by itself every few seconds, so it never needs a restart once the cause is fixed. The Health page shows the same for OpenSearch itself.

Some of the steps below send you to OpenSearch's log. With the Docker quick start, show it from the Signalith folder with docker compose -f deploy/docker/docker-compose.yml logs opensearch. Otherwise it is in /var/log/opensearch, or in the logs folder where you unpacked OpenSearch.

Status What it means What to do Can't reach OpenSearch Nothing answers at OpenSearch's address: OpenSearch is stopped, the address is wrong, or a firewall is in the way Check that OpenSearch is running. Test connection on the Settings page says what is wrong with the address OpenSearch didn't answer in time OpenSearch took the request but answered too late, usually because its computer is short of memory or CPU Nothing at first: Signalith keeps trying. If it lasts more than a few minutes, check that OpenSearch's computer has enough memory and CPU, and what OpenSearch's log says OpenSearch security not loaded OpenSearch runs its security plugin, but its security settings (who may sign in, and what each may do) aren't loaded, so it refuses every request. OpenSearch loads them by itself only as it starts with none stored yet, and tries just once, which can fail on a slow computer; they then stay unloaded, also after OpenSearch restarts If OpenSearch started only a few minutes ago, wait. Otherwise, with the Docker quick start, run docker compose -f deploy/docker/docker-compose.yml up -d again from the Signalith folder: it re-runs the step that loads OpenSearch's security settings. If that doesn't load them, follow If OpenSearch's security settings aren't loaded. Without Docker, load them with securityadmin.sh, as Load the security settings shows OpenSearch too busy OpenSearch answered that it could not do the request in time Nothing at first: Signalith keeps trying. If it lasts more than a few minutes, check that OpenSearch's computer has enough memory and CPU, and what OpenSearch's log says OpenSearch refuses the sign-in OpenSearch does not accept the user name and password, or the client certificate, Signalith signs in with Check them on the Settings page OpenSearch refuses Signalith Signalith's OpenSearch user may not use <prefix>_runtime Give it the right to create, read and write <prefix>_runtime (or <prefix>_*) OpenSearch refuses writes A block stops OpenSearch from taking writes. OpenSearch sets one by itself when its disk is full, and an admin can set one, such as cluster.blocks.read_only Give OpenSearch more disk, or remove the block OpenSearch not ready OpenSearch is starting, or its nodes can't find each other Wait a few minutes. If it lasts, OpenSearch's log says why OpenSearch answers with an error Any other error, such as a closed <prefix>_runtime index. The alert quotes it OpenSearch's log may say more

docs.title: The background jobs
docs.text:
These run on one server only:

  • detections on their schedule,
  • threat intel feed downloads,
  • notifications about new findings,
  • playbooks for new findings, and the approved steps,
  • data retention, including the disk guard and archiving,
  • index upgrades after a new version.

Searching, dashboards, investigations and receiving data work on every server, and so does loading or removing the sample data.

Working on the same finding or case from two servers. Analysts on different servers (or in two browser tabs) can comment on, triage and add to the same finding or investigation at the same moment: each change is saved on top of the others, so none is lost. In the rare case that many people change one item in the same instant, one of them sees "Someone else changed this investigation at the same moment. Try again." Nothing was saved for that person; doing it again works.

How they move. The server that runs the jobs confirms every 10 seconds, in OpenSearch, that it still does. If it stops confirming (it crashed, its computer stopped, or it lost OpenSearch), another server takes the jobs over within about 40 seconds. When a server is stopped on purpose, it hands them over first, so another server has them within seconds. Two servers do not run them at once: a server that cannot confirm for 20 seconds stops its jobs by itself, on a timer of its own, before anyone else may start them after 30 seconds. Detections, feed downloads, notifications and playbooks also check, before each run, send or step, that their server still runs the jobs.

Detections after a takeover. The server that takes the jobs over makes up the detection runs that were missed while no server ran them, oldest first and up to detections.catch_up back (6 hours unless changed). A run the previous server had already done, or started, does not raise its findings or risk a second time. See Schedules and missed runs. The run state is kept in OpenSearch, so every server shows the same Detections page, detection health and warnings, and Run now works on any of them.

Which servers may run them. Every server, unless Run detections on schedule (detections.scheduler) is turned off on its Settings page; once the servers share their settings it is called May run background jobs (cluster.leader_eligible, or SIGNALITH_LEADER_ELIGIBLE), one of each server's own settings. Leave it on: the servers take turns by themselves. Turn it off only on a server that should never run the jobs, for example one that only receives data. A change applies at the server's next restart.

Changing retention and feeds. Once the servers are a cluster (see Shared feeds and retention policies), the Data retention and Threat intel feed settings can be changed on any server. Notifications and Playbooks settings, and both on a server that is not part of the cluster yet, can be changed only on the server that runs the jobs.

docs.title: When a server will not take over
docs.text:
Notifications, playbooks and custom detections are still kept in files on each server, and so are retention policies and threat intel feeds on a server that is not part of the cluster yet (on the servers of the cluster they are shared, so they never differ). A server whose files differ from those of the server that runs the jobs does not take the jobs over by itself: it would delete, download or alert differently. The list shows it as Standby with "Won't take over" and the reason, and an alert says what to copy:

What differs What to make the same Retention policies retention.yaml in the lookups folder, and retention in signalith.yaml Threat intel feeds intel_feeds.yaml in the lookups folder, and intel in signalith.yaml Notification channels notifications.yaml in the lookups folder (only once a channel or rule is set up) Playbooks playbooks.yaml in the lookups folder (only once a playbook is set up) Detections folder The custom detection files in detections.dir Archive folder Only while a retention policy archives: every server must use one shared archive folder. Set retention.archive_dir to the same shared folder on each server. Signalith names the folder with a small file in it, .signalith-archive-id; leave it there

Copy the files from the server that runs the jobs, then restart the server you copied them to. The alert goes away within a minute.

If the server that runs the jobs stops while no other server may take over, a red alert says that nothing runs detections, threat intel downloads or retention. Start the server that ran them again, or fix the other server's files and restart it.

docs.title: When OpenSearch's disk is full
docs.text:
When OpenSearch runs out of disk, it refuses new events. The page shows a red alert, and the server that runs the jobs keeps only the disk guard running: unless it was turned off on the Data retention page, it deletes the oldest days until there is room. Detections and feed downloads wait. New events are stored again by themselves once there is room; agents keep theirs until then. To make room sooner, give OpenSearch more disk.

While the disk is full, servers cannot write their sign of life, so the list keeps showing them as they were last seen instead of marking them all as not answering.

docs.title: Clocks
docs.text: Detections are scheduled by the clock. The list warns when a server's clock is more than 2 seconds off OpenSearch's. A server more than 30 seconds off leaves the jobs to a server whose clock is right while one is up; a server on its own runs them anyway, with the warning. Keep every server's clock in sync with NTP (Windows Time on Windows).

docs.title: Identity
docs.text:
Each server keeps its identity in its state folder (node.id). Never copy a state folder to another server, for example by cloning a virtual machine. Two servers with one identity are found out within seconds. The one that started last stops (it refuses to start), and the one that was running goes on and shows an alert. A server that finds another one using its identity later shows Identity in use, runs no jobs, and tells load balancers to send it nothing.

To give a server a new identity, stop it, delete node.id from its state folder and start it again. In Docker the state folder is the data volume, and the image has no shell, so, from the folder you cloned Signalith into:

docker compose -f deploy/docker/docker-compose.yml stop signalith
docker run --rm -v docker_signalith-data:/d busybox rm /d/node.id
docker compose -f deploy/docker/docker-compose.yml up -d

docker volume ls shows the volume's name (here docker_signalith-data).

The state folder. Signalith keeps the files it makes for itself in one folder: its master key (keys), its HTTPS certificate and certificate authority (tls), admin-password-hash when the admin password was changed with signalith passwd (not used while the server shares the users of its cluster), admin-password-local with the break-glass password signalith passwd -local sets on a member of a cluster, the key for the cookie that recognizes browsers that signed in before (signin.key, see failed sign-in limits), and this server's identity (node.id, and cluster/lock while it runs). The server and every command (signalith secrets, signalith initial-password, signalith settings and the others) pick the same folder:

  1. SIGNALITH_STATE_DIR when it is set. The systemd unit and the Docker image set it to /var/lib/signalith.
  2. Otherwise a local folder Signalith used before instead of the folder that holds lookups.dir (it notes this in a used_instead_of file there). If files turn up in the usual folder later, for example from a command run without the service's settings, the server stays where it is, and signalith validate and the log name the files it does not use.
  3. Otherwise the folder that holds lookups.dir, when it already holds any of those files. An upgrade therefore keeps using the folder it used before, wherever that is, and leaves nothing behind.
  4. Otherwise the folder that holds lookups.dir, when it is on a local disk and the service's user can write in it.
  5. Otherwise a local folder: the systemd StateDirectory, then /var/lib/signalith on Linux, C:\ProgramData\Signalith on Windows. A folder that already holds another install's identity, certificate or admin password, or that another install noted as its own, is skipped, so two installs never share one. The log says why, and Signalith keeps using that folder from then on. Signalith makes the folder private when it creates it (on Windows only SYSTEM, Administrators, the Signalith service and the account that made it can open it).
  6. Otherwise the folder that holds lookups.dir anyway. The server then does not start, and says what is wrong: set SIGNALITH_STATE_DIR to a local folder.

Only the server, and signalith passwd when it keeps the password there, write the used_instead_of note. Commands that only look (signalith validate, signalith secrets status and the others) change nothing. Commands run by hand read the service's settings (systemctl show signalith, including its StateDirectory) so they find the same folder.

The folder should be on a local disk, never on a network share, since the identity's lock cannot be trusted there. A folder on a network share that already holds a master key or a certificate is still used, so nothing is lost, and the log warns: move its files to a local folder and set SIGNALITH_STATE_DIR to it. Servers that share lookups.dir on a network share must each set their own SIGNALITH_STATE_DIR. On Docker Desktop and WSL bind mounts, which may not lock files, Signalith starts with a warning. signalith validate says when the folder is not the usual one, and what is wrong with it, if anything.

docs.title: Adding a server by hand
docs.text:
Until servers can be added from the Servers page:

  1. Install Signalith on the new computer as usual.
  2. Give it the same OpenSearch settings as the first server: opensearch.url, its user and password, and opensearch.index_prefix.
  3. Agent tokens made on Add data are kept in OpenSearch, so the new server accepts them as soon as it starts, and a token revoked on one server is refused by all of them within seconds (see agent-tokens.md). Shared tokens from older setups (ingest.tokens) are in each server's own configuration: give the new server the same ones, so agents that still use them can send to either server. Each server has its own master key, so passwords and tokens stored encrypted (enc: values) cannot be copied as they are: set them on the new server with signalith secrets set, or put them there in plain text and run signalith secrets encrypt (see docs/encryption.md).
  4. Give it the cluster key (see Shared settings and the cluster key): signalith cluster export-key on a server that has it, signalith cluster import-key on the new one. If the cluster was made with a key file (SIGNALITH_CLUSTER_KEY_FILE), the same file on the new one does it too. It then uses the shared feeds and retention policies, and can take the jobs over.
