IPv4 addresses written as IPv6 (::ffff:127.0.0.1, 64:ff9b::7f00:1) are checked as IPv4. Private ranges (10.0.0.0/8, 192.168.0.0/16 and so on) are allowed, since MISP and OpenCTI servers often live there.
  • intel.allow_loopback_feeds: true allows loopback, for a feed server on the same machine. It never allows link-local or metadata addresses. A proxy from the environment may be on this machine either way.
  • Signalith's own OpenSearch (the host and port of opensearch.url) is never allowed, by name or by any address the name resolves to, even with allow_loopback_feeds. An OpenSearch without its security plugin answers anyone who reaches it, so this keeps a feed URL from reading it.
  • Through a proxy, the proxy looks up host names and connects, so only addresses written in the URL are checked; limit what the proxy may reach if that matters. Only the connection to the proxy itself skips the check: a feed URL that names the proxy's own address (such as http://localhost:3128/, which Go never sends through a proxy) is checked like any other.
  • At most 5 redirects, each checked by the same rules. No Referer is sent, since the feed URL's query may hold a key. API key headers and the password are only sent on a redirect that stays on the same host and port (or only moves from http to https).
  • Downloads stop at 256 MB and 2 million indicators and time out after 5 minutes (TAXII: 30 minutes, 2 minutes a page); a test stops at 4 MB and 1 minute, and at most two run at once; listing TAXII collections times out after 30 seconds.
  • Logs and error messages never show API keys, passwords or the query part of a URL (which often holds a key); URLs are logged as https://host/path?…, and a server's error text is shown with any secret replaced by [hidden].

docs.title: Feeds in signalith.yaml
docs.text:
Feeds can also be listed in signalith.yaml, for example when the file is managed by configuration tools. They use the settings above, and header and password values may use ${ENV_VAR} so keys stay out of the file:

intel:
  feeds:
    # Botnet command-and-control servers
    - name: feodo-tracker
      url: https://feodotracker.abuse.ch/downloads/ipblocklist.txt
      weight: 1.5
    # Malware download URLs from the last 30 days
    - name: urlhaus
      url: https://urlhaus.abuse.ch/downloads/text_recent/
      type: url
    # Recent malware file hashes
    - name: malwarebazaar
      url: https://bazaar.abuse.ch/export/txt/sha256/recent/
      type: sha256
    # Your own platform exporting STIX 2.1 over HTTPS
    - name: our-export
      url: https://cti.example.com/export/signalith.json
      format: stix
      headers: {Authorization: "Bearer ${CTI_API_KEY}"}
  # feeds_file: lookups/intel_feeds.yaml
  # allow_loopback_feeds: false

docs.title: Manual indicators and uploads
docs.text:
Add one indicator on the Threat intel page, or upload a file:

value,type,description,weight,expires,tags
203.0.113.9,,Scanner seen in incident 42,2,30d,scanner|ssh
login-bank.example,domain,Phishing site,,2026-12-31,phishing

Only value is required; type is detected when empty. expires is a date, an RFC 3339 time or a duration such as 30d. A plain list with one value per line also works. Every bad line is reported and nothing is saved unless the whole file is valid. Uploads add to the manual indicators (a value already present is updated). One file can be up to 16 MB and 2,000,000 indicators; split a larger one. Delete manual indicators on the page; feed indicators come back with the next download, so turn the feed off instead. Indicators kept from a deleted feed can be deleted one by one.

docs.title: The threat intel match detection
docs.text:
threat-activity is built in and enabled. Every 5 minutes it runs

* | threatmatch
| head 1000

over the last 10 minutes and raises one finding per indicator and target system per 24 hours, titled for example Threat intel match on src 203.0.113.9 (feodo-tracker). The finding's result has the matched field and value, the indicator, its sources, weight and description. Risk is 60 times the indicator's weight, added to threat_target (system) and user. It does nothing until there are indicators. Matching is forward-looking; to check older events, search with a longer time range.

docs.title: threatmatch
docs.text:
| threatmatch [fields] keeps only events where a field equals an active indicator. It runs inside OpenSearch: the server sends the indicator values as terms filters (10,000 values per clause, upper- and lower-case for hashes) and IPv4 networks as prefix filters, so events are never streamed through Signalith. It must come right after the search. Up to about 800 network clauses are used (a /24 or /16 is one; a /20 is 16); networks beyond that are matched only by | intel. IPv6 networks match only with | intel.

Each event gets:

Column Meaning threat_match_field, threat_match_value The event field and value that matched (the highest-weight match if several did) threat_indicator, threat_type The indicator, such as the network the address is in threat_source Every source listing it threat_weight, threat_description From the strongest indicator threat_target The system on your side: the destination when the source matched, otherwise the source or reporting host

docs.title: intel
docs.text:
| intel [fields] checks any result in the Signalith server and adds <field>_intel_source, <field>_intel_type, <field>_intel_weight and <field>_intel_description where a value is an indicator. It also matches URLs by host against domain indicators and Sysmon process_hash lists. Use it after stats:

datamodel=Network_Traffic | stats count, sum(bytes) as bytes by dest | intel dest | where dest_intel_source=*

docs.title: Storage and scale
docs.text: Indicators are stored in the <prefix>_intel OpenSearch index, which event searches never read, and every server keeps the active ones in memory (about 200 bytes each), reloading within a minute when another server changes them. A few hundred thousand indicators are fine; the threatmatch filter for 200,000 IP indicators is a few megabytes per search.

docs.title: API
docs.text:
Every change needs a signed-in session (or basic sign-in) and is refused from other sites, like the rest of the API. Secret values are never returned: headers come back as {"name": "X-Api-Key", "set": true} and the password as {"set": true}.

Method and path Purpose GET /api/intel Counts by type and source, and every feed with its status GET /api/intel/feeds Every feed with its settings and status, plus downloads (whether this server downloads feeds), manage (whether feeds can be changed here), shared (whether the feeds are shared), feeds_file (empty when shared), formats, types, file_error when the feeds file cannot be read, and for admins etags, each feed's version by name. A shared feed that was not added on the page has from, such as "applied from signalith.yaml on siem-b" POST /api/intel/feeds Add a feed (body below); it downloads at once PUT /api/intel/feeds/{name} Change a feed added on the page. Settings left out stay as they are; an empty secret keeps the saved one. 409 for a feed from signalith.yaml, unless the feeds are shared. With If-Match and the feed's etag, 412 when it changed meanwhile; the answer's ETag is its new version DELETE /api/intel/feeds/{name}?indicators=remove\|keep Delete a feed added on the page; remove (default) deletes its indicators, keep lets them age out. Takes If-Match like PUT POST /api/intel/feeds/{name}/refresh Download a feed now. With shared feeds, on a server that does not download them: 202 {"feed","request_id","queued_on"}, followed with GET /api/requests/{id} (see the retention API), whose result is the feed's status, or {"already_running":true} when it was downloading already POST /api/intel/feeds/test Download without saving; the body is a feed, or {"feed": "<name>"} plus any settings to try on a saved feed with its saved secrets GET /api/intel/catalog The catalog, each entry with added and the feed made from it POST /api/intel/catalog Add catalog feeds: {"ids": ["feodo-tracker", "spamhaus-drop"]} returns {"added": [feeds], "skipped": [{"id", "reason"}]} POST /api/intel/taxii/collections A TAXII server's collections: {"url", "username", "password", "headers"} or {"feed": "<name>"} GET /api/intel/indicators?q=&type=&source=&limit=&offset= List indicators, newest first POST /api/intel/indicators Add one: {"value": "...", "type": "auto", "description": "...", "weight": "1", "expires": "30d", "tags": []} DELETE /api/intel/indicators/{id} Delete a manual indicator, or one kept from a deleted feed POST /api/intel/upload Add manual indicators from CSV or a list; returns {"lines": [{"line", "msg"}]} on errors GET /api/intel/lookup?value= Check one value against every indicator

Adding a feed:

POST /api/intel/feeds
{
  "name": "partner",
  "url": "https://feeds.partner.example/ips.txt",
  "format": "auto",
  "type": "auto",
  "interval": "30m",
  "max_age": "7d",
  "weight": 1.5,
  "description": "Partner list",
  "tags": ["partner"],
  "enabled": true,
  "headers": [{"name": "X-Api-Key", "value": "the key"}]
}

Only name and url are required (kind, collection, column, username, password and catalog are optional; catalog fills empty settings from that catalog entry). On a change, a header {"name": "X-Api-Key"} without a value keeps the saved value, {"name": "X-Api-Key", "clear": true} removes it, and "clear_password": true removes the password. The answer is the feed:

{
  "name": "partner", "source": "ui", "kind": "url",
  "url": "https://feeds.partner.example/ips.txt",
  "format": "auto", "type": "auto", "interval": "30m", "max_age": "7d", "weight": 1.5,
  "description": "Partner list", "tags": ["partner"], "enabled": true,
  "headers": [{"name": "X-Api-Key", "set": true}], "password": {"set": false},
  "has_headers": true, "indicators": 0, "status": {"count": 0, "added": 0, "removed": 0}
}

source is ui for feeds added on the page and config for feeds from signalith.yaml; problem explains why a feed is not downloaded. Invalid settings answer 400 with every problem and the setting it belongs to:

{
  "error": "Please fix these settings: interval must be at least 5m; feeds update far less often",
  "problems": ["interval must be at least 5m; feeds update far less often"],
  "fields": {"interval": "interval must be at least 5m; feeds update far less often"}
}

A test answers 200 whether or not the download worked:

{
  "ok": true, "format": "csv", "column": "dst_ip", "type": "ip",
  "total": 2, "by_type": {"ip": 2}, "skipped": 0,
  "samples": [{"type": "ip", "value": "203.0.113.9"}, {"type": "ip", "value": "198.51.100.4"}],
  "bytes": 187, "duration_ms": 412
}

{
  "ok": false, "http_status": 403,
  "error": "The server answered 403 Forbidden. This feed may need an API key. It said: \"missing or wrong API key\"",
  "total": 0, "by_type": {}, "skipped": 0, "samples": [], "bytes": 0, "duration_ms": 95
}

Other fields: skipped_example (the first value that was not an indicator), reserved (private and reserved addresses skipped), truncated and note (only part of the feed was read). Listing TAXII collections answers {"ok": true, "title": "...", "collections": [{"api_root", "id", "title", "description", "can_read", "media_types"}]}, or {"ok": false, "error": "...", "collections": []}.

docs.title: Users and sign-in
docs.text:
Everyone who signs in to Signalith has one of three roles. People can sign in in three ways:

Account Where it lives Managed on The built-in admin auth.admin_user and auth.admin_password_hash in signalith.yaml The server, with signalith passwd Local users users.json in the lookups folder The Users page Directory users Your Active Directory or LDAP server; Signalith keeps a record after their first sign-in The directory; on the Users page you can only disable or delete them

Servers that share one OpenSearch keep all of this in OpenSearch instead, once every one of them runs this version: see Users on several servers.

docs.title: Roles
docs.text:
Each role can do everything the roles above it can.

Role For Can Viewer Managers, auditors, other teams Run searches and see dashboards, findings, investigations, detections, risk and intel. Cannot change anything. Analyst SOC analysts Also triage findings, work investigations, build dashboards, use Ask and add or remove intel indicators by hand. Admin Whoever runs Signalith Also create and change detections, add and change threat intel feeds and upload intel, edit asset and identity lists, set up agents and create and revoke agent tokens, manage users and set up directory sign-in, and change server settings.

By area:

Area Viewer Analyst Admin Search, query builder, explain, field lists Yes Yes Yes Ask (plain English; can call a paid AI model) No Yes Yes Dashboards: view and run Yes Yes Yes Dashboards: create, edit, delete, add panels No Yes Yes Findings: view Yes Yes Yes Findings: status, owner, comments, bulk changes, create No Yes Yes Investigations: view Yes Yes Yes Investigations: create, edit, add findings, notes, entities No Yes Yes Investigations: remove someone else's note, pinned event or search No No Yes Detections and ATT&CK coverage: view Yes Yes Yes Detections: create, edit, delete, test, run, Sigma import No No Yes Risk, asset and identity context: view Yes Yes Yes Asset and identity lists: edit No No Yes Threat intel: view and look up Yes Yes Yes Threat intel: add or remove indicators by hand No Yes Yes Threat intel: add, change, test and refresh feeds, upload files No No Yes Playbooks: see runs, approve or reject steps that wait No Yes Yes Playbooks: create, edit, delete, turn on and off No No Yes Add data (agent setup, agent tokens) No No Yes Agent tokens: list names and use (API only) No Yes Yes Users and directory sign-in No No Yes Server settings (Settings page, restart) No No Yes Change your own password (local users) Yes Yes Yes

Dashboards have no owner: any analyst can change or delete any custom dashboard. Investigation notes, pinned events and saved searches are evidence: an analyst can remove only the ones they added, and an admin any of them.

When someone tries something their role does not allow, Signalith answers 403 and says what is needed, for example "This needs the Analyst role, and your role is Viewer. Ask an admin if you need access." The API section lists the role of every route.

A role change, disabling or deleting a user takes effect on that user's next request: Signalith looks up the role every time instead of remembering it in the session. If they have Signalith open and try something their new role does not allow, the page reloads to match the new role and says why.

docs.title: The built-in admin
docs.text:
The account in auth.admin_user (admin unless you changed it) always works, even when the directory server is down or every other admin has been removed, so you can always get back in. It shows on the Users page as Built-in and cannot be edited, disabled or deleted there. Change its password on the server (on servers that share their users, see The built-in admin on several servers):

signalith passwd -c /etc/signalith/signalith.yaml

With the Docker quick start, run docker compose -f deploy/docker/docker-compose.yml exec signalith signalith passwd and then docker compose -f deploy/docker/docker-compose.yml restart signalith. There the first password comes from a file the setup step made (signalith initial-password shows it), and the new one is kept in admin-password-hash in the signalith-data volume, where it replaces the first one.

Keep its password somewhere safe and use your own account day to day. No local user or directory user can have the built-in admin's name.

docs.title: Managing local users
docs.text:
Admins manage users on the Users page (Settings > Users).

Add a user. Enter a username, optionally a name and email address, and pick a role (Viewer if you don't). Usernames are 1 to 64 lower-case letters, digits, dots, dashes, underscores or @, starting with a letter or digit; they are not case sensitive. Signalith makes up a temporary password and shows it once (or you can type one, at least 8 characters). Give it to the person: at their first sign-in they must choose their own password before they can do anything else.

Change a user. Edit their name and email, change their role, disable or enable them, reset their password (they get a new temporary password and must change it at the next sign-in), or delete them. Disabling, deleting or resetting a password signs that user out everywhere at once.

To stop anyone locking everyone out:

  • You cannot disable, delete or change the role of your own account. Ask another admin.
  • Signalith always keeps at least one enabled admin, and the built-in admin counts as one.

Passwords are stored as bcrypt hashes and never shown again.

docs.title: Changing your password
docs.text:
Local users change their password from the user menu (Change password): enter the current password and the new one (at least 8 characters, at most 72 bytes). Every other browser signed in as you is signed out, on every server that shares the users file too. Scripts using your old password with HTTP Basic auth stop working at once.

Directory users change their password in the directory (for example with Ctrl+Alt+Del on Windows). The built-in admin's password is changed with signalith passwd; on servers that share their users, the built-in admin can also change it here, from the user menu or Change password on its own row of the Users page.

docs.title: Signing in
docs.text:
Sign-in checks the name in this order:

  1. The built-in admin. If the name is auth.admin_user, only its password works.
  2. Local users. If a local user has the name, only the local password works. The directory is never asked about a local username, even with a domain in front (CORP\jane).
  3. The directory, if directory sign-in is on.

Failed sign-ins all get the same answer, "Username and password don't match.", so they do not reveal which usernames exist. Other answers are:

code When wrong_credentials (401) Wrong username or password, or an empty one disabled (403) The account is disabled in Signalith not_in_group (403) A directory user in no group mapped to a role: "Your directory account is not in a group that can use Signalith." password_expired (403) Active Directory says the password expired or must be changed directory_unavailable (503) The directory server could not be reached, or too many directory sign-ins are being checked at once locked_out (429) Too many wrong passwords; see below

Failed sign-in limits. Wrong passwords are counted so that guessing stays slow, but someone guessing your password cannot keep you out:

Counted Limit Then One address, one account 10 in 15 minutes That account is refused from that address for 15 minutes, even with the right password One address, any accounts 30 in 15 minutes That address is refused for 15 minutes One account, from browsers and addresses that never signed in to it 30 in an hour Their next tries at that account wait: 1 second, then twice as long after each wrong password, up to 15 minutes. The account itself is never locked

A successful sign-in clears only the count for its own address and account, so signing in to one account never helps someone guess another's password. Sign-ins still being checked count too, so a burst of parallel guesses cannot get past the limit. Wrong directory passwords count; an unreachable directory does not. Basic auth, Test a user with a password, and Change password share these limits. An IPv6 address is counted with the rest of its /64 network, since one computer can usually use any address in it. Servers that share their users share these limits too (see Failed sign-in limits on several servers).

Browsers you signed in with keep working. When you sign in, Signalith gives your browser a cookie that says it has signed in to that account before. The cookie is sent only over HTTPS, cannot be read by scripts on the page, and lasts a year from your last sign-in. While someone elsewhere guesses your password, that browser is not slowed down, and it keeps working even when its address is paused for wrong passwords to other accounts. An address you signed in from in the last 30 days is not slowed down either, which keeps scripts using HTTP Basic auth working (they keep no cookies). Your own wrong passwords count against that browser or address only: 10 in 15 minutes pause it for 15 minutes. Browsers that signed in before share 30 wrong passwords an hour per account, and addresses that did share another 30; past that they wait like everyone else, so the guesses an account can take stay limited. Someone else at an address you once used, such as an office or hotel network, can use up the addresses' share, but not your browser's. Changing or resetting the password of a local user or the built-in admin makes every browser and address sign in once more before it is recognized again (the browser you change your own password in stays recognized). A built-in admin password from SIGNALITH_ADMIN_PASSWORD or SIGNALITH_ADMIN_PASSWORD_FILE keeps its browsers recognized across restarts while it stays the same. Change password counts against your signed-in browser, so it works while someone else is guessing your password. The cookie needs HTTPS: over plain HTTP no browser is remembered. Each server keeps its own key for these cookies, signin.key in its state folder; deleting it only means every browser signs in once more before it is recognized. Servers that share their users use one key instead, made from the cluster key, so a browser recognized by one server is recognized by every one.

Many people behind one address. When people reach Signalith through one address, such as a reverse proxy, a load balancer, a NAT gateway or Docker Desktop's port forwarding, Signalith sees that address for all of them, and 30 wrong passwords from anyone behind it would pause sign-ins for everyone. To avoid that, list the address on the Settings page:

  • A reverse proxy (nginx, Caddy, IIS, most load balancers): add it under Trusted reverse proxies (server.trusted_proxies). If the proxy sets X-Forwarded-For itself, also choose X-Forwarded-For under Client address header (server.client_header); for nginx that takes proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-For $proxy_add_x_forwarded_for; (see Behind a reverse proxy). Signalith then counts and logs each person by the address the proxy got the request from: the right-most address in the header that is not a trusted proxy, since the addresses further left come from the sender. It reads the header only from the addresses listed there, since anyone else could send a made-up one. Without Client address header, or for a request that comes from the proxy without the header, the proxy counts like an address under Proxies and gateways.
  • Anything else (a NAT gateway, a proxy that cannot send the header): add it under Proxies and gateways (server.shared_addresses). Wrong passwords from that address are counted for each account only, so it is never refused as a whole, and one person's wrong passwords never affect another account.

When an address is refused as a whole, the server log says so and names these settings.

The web UI keeps you signed in with a session cookie. Sessions end after auth.session_timeout without activity (12 hours by default), after 7 days with Keep me signed in, when you sign out, when your password is changed, or when an admin disables, deletes or resets your account. Servers that share the users file end them too, within a second or so. Servers that share their users in OpenSearch keep the sessions there, so a session works on every server at once (see Sessions on every server).

Scripts and API clients can use HTTP Basic auth with the same username and password. Signalith remembers a correct username and password briefly so it does not check the hash or ask the directory on every request: for 10 minutes for local users and the built-in admin, and 2 minutes for directory users. Changing or resetting a local password, or changing the directory settings, ends that at once. A password changed in the directory keeps working for Basic auth for up to 2 minutes. Group changes and accounts disabled in the directory are picked up as described in Directory users who change or leave.

Temporary passwords. Signing in with a temporary password works, but the reply says "must_change_password": true and the sign-in page asks for a new password. Until it is changed, every request other than GET /api/me and POST /api/me/password answers 403 with code password_change_required.

docs.title: Sign in with Active Directory or LDAP
docs.text: Directory sign-in lets people use their Active Directory or LDAP account, with their role decided by the groups they are in.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
When someone signs in with a name that is not the built-in admin or a local user:

  1. Signalith connects to the directory server (the failover server if the first cannot be reached), over TLS when set up to.
  2. It signs in as the service account (or searches anonymously if there is none).
  3. It searches under the user base DN with the user filter, the typed name in place of {username}. Exactly one entry must match; none or several refuse the sign-in. CORP\jane is looked up as jane, and with the Active Directory filter jane@corp.example.com works too.
  4. It checks the password by signing in to the directory as that entry's DN. Empty passwords are refused before anything is sent: many LDAP servers treat a sign-in with an empty password as anonymous and let it through.
  5. It finds the user's groups and maps them to a role. A user in several mapped groups gets the highest role. A user in none is refused, unless you choose to let such users in as viewers.
  6. The user appears on the Users page as a directory user, with their name, email and DN from the directory. Their role is updated at every sign-in, and checked again every few minutes while they use Signalith (see below).

Directory users who have never signed in are not listed. You can disable a directory user in Signalith (they stay out whatever the directory says), or delete their record (it comes back at their next sign-in). Turning directory sign-in off signs out every directory user at their next request.

docs.title: Directory users who change or leave
docs.text:
While a directory user is signed in, Signalith looks them up again with the service account (without their password) every 5 minutes, and right away when the directory settings are saved:

  • Groups changed. Their role follows their groups from their next request.
  • No longer in a mapped group, disabled or deleted in the directory. Their sessions end, and the Users page shows them with no role and the reason. With the Active Directory preset, disabled accounts are not found, so they count as deleted. A refused sign-in does the same at once.
  • The directory cannot be reached. They keep the access they had and are checked again 5 minutes later. If the settings were changed since their role was last checked, their sessions end instead.

So someone who leaves keeps access for at most about 5 minutes. To stop someone at once, disable them on the Users page.

docs.title: Set it up
docs.text:
On the Users page, open Directory sign-in and click Set up directory sign-in:

  1. Pick Active Directory or OpenLDAP. This fills in the filter and attribute defaults below; change any of them if your directory differs.
  2. Enter the server address and, if you have one, a failover server.
  3. Enter the service account's DN and password. The saved password is only used with the saved servers, bind DN and TLS settings: change any of those and you type the password again, so it can never be sent to a server someone else chose.
  4. Enter the user base DN. A group base DN is optional: when it is empty, Signalith searches for groups in the whole domain (the DC= part of the user's DN).
  5. Map groups to roles by their full DN.
  6. Click Test connection, then Test a user with your own account, then turn directory sign-in on and save.

Settings can be saved switched off while you work on them; they are only required to be complete when directory sign-in is on.

Use an encrypted connection. Passwords are sent to the directory to check them. Use ldaps://host (port 636), or ldap://host (port 389) with StartTLS. Signalith accepts TLS 1.2 or newer and checks the server's certificate against the system's trusted CAs plus any CA certificate you paste. Plain ldap:// without StartTLS works but shows a warning, and so does turning certificate checks off.

The service account needs only read access to users and groups. In Active Directory any domain user account can do this; a dedicated account whose password does not expire is best, so sign-in does not stop when it expires.

docs.title: Active Directory
docs.text:
Setting Example Server ldaps://dc1.corp.example.com Failover server ldaps://dc2.corp.example.com Service account DN CN=svc-signalith,OU=Service Accounts,DC=corp,DC=example,DC=com User base DN DC=corp,DC=example,DC=com Admin groups CN=Signalith Admins,OU=Groups,DC=corp,DC=example,DC=com Analyst groups CN=SOC Analysts,OU=Groups,DC=corp,DC=example,DC=com Viewer groups CN=SOC Viewers,OU=Groups,DC=corp,DC=example,DC=com

The Active Directory preset:

  • finds users by logon name or user@domain, and skips disabled accounts: (&(objectCategory=person)(objectClass=user)(|(sAMAccountName={username})(userPrincipalName={username}))(!(userAccountControl:1.2.840.113556.1.4.803:=2)))
  • reads sAMAccountName (username), displayName (name) and mail (email)
  • reads groups from memberOf, and with Nested groups on (the default) also counts groups inside groups: if IT Leads is a member of Signalith Admins, members of IT Leads are admins. The domain controller works this out with the LDAP_MATCHING_RULE_IN_CHAIN rule (1.2.840.113556.1.4.1941).

Your domain controllers need an LDAPS certificate for ldaps:// (most domains with Active Directory Certificate Services have one). Paste your enterprise root CA's certificate in CA certificate if the Signalith server does not trust it already.

docs.title: OpenLDAP
docs.text:
Setting Example Server ldap://ldap.example.org with StartTLS on, or ldaps://ldap.example.org Service account DN cn=signalith,ou=services,dc=example,dc=org User base DN ou=people,dc=example,dc=org Group base DN ou=groups,dc=example,dc=org Admin groups cn=signalith-admins,ou=groups,dc=example,dc=org Analyst groups cn=soc,ou=groups,dc=example,dc=org

The OpenLDAP preset finds users with (&(objectClass=inetOrgPerson)(uid={username})), reads uid, cn and mail, and finds groups by searching the group base DN with a filter that covers the three usual kinds of group:

(|(&(objectClass=groupOfNames)(member={dn}))(&(objectClass=groupOfUniqueNames)(uniqueMember={dn}))(&(objectClass=posixGroup)(memberUid={username})))

{dn} is the user's DN and {username} their username as stored in the directory. If your server has the memberof overlay, you can set Groups to memberOf attribute instead. Nested groups are only followed on Active Directory.

The same preset works for 389 Directory Server and FreeIPA (users under cn=users,cn=accounts,dc=..., groups under cn=groups,cn=accounts,dc=...).

docs.title: Testing
docs.text:
Test connection connects to each server, signs in as the service account and checks that the base DNs exist. It tests what is in the form, saved or not. Each step says what worked or, in plain words, what went wrong and what to do: a name that does not resolve, a port nothing listens on, a firewall, an untrusted certificate, a certificate for another name, a refused service account password, a base DN that does not exist.

Test a user looks a user up exactly as sign-in would and shows their DN, every group found, the groups that matched a role, and the role they would get, or why they would be refused. Enter their password too to check it; a wrong password there counts toward the failed sign-in limit like a real sign-in.

docs.title: Setting it in signalith.yaml
docs.text:
Instead of the Users page you can put the settings in signalith.yaml under auth.ldap, for example to deploy the same settings to several servers. The Users page then shows them read-only, marked From signalith.yaml, and changes made in the file apply when Signalith restarts.

auth:
  ldap:
    type: ad
    url: ldaps://dc1.corp.example.com
    failover_url: ldaps://dc2.corp.example.com
    ca_cert_file: /etc/signalith/corp-root-ca.pem
    bind_dn: CN=svc-signalith,OU=Service Accounts,DC=corp,DC=example,DC=com
    # bind_password: set SIGNALITH_LDAP_BIND_PASSWORD instead
    user_base_dn: DC=corp,DC=example,DC=com
    admin_groups:
      - CN=Signalith Admins,OU=Groups,DC=corp,DC=example,DC=com
    analyst_groups:
      - CN=SOC Analysts,OU=Groups,DC=corp,DC=example,DC=com
    viewer_groups:
      - CN=SOC Viewers,OU=Groups,DC=corp,DC=example,DC=com

Directory sign-in is on whenever auth.ldap is present, unless it says enabled: false. type defaults to ad. Keep the service account's password out of the file with the SIGNALITH_LDAP_BIND_PASSWORD environment variable (for example in the systemd unit's EnvironmentFile, or the container's environment). That variable only applies to auth.ldap in signalith.yaml: settings made on the Users page keep their own password in directory.json, and Signalith logs a warning at start-up when the variable is set without auth.ldap.

On servers that share their users, auth.ldap no longer makes the page read-only: the settings in signalith.yaml are applied to the shared ones only when they change (see Directory settings on several servers).

signalith validate checks the settings, so run it with the same environment as the service. signalith passwd works without the variable, so the built-in admin's password can always be reset from a shell.

docs.title: Settings reference
docs.text:
The keys are the same in signalith.yaml and the API.

Key Default Meaning enabled off on the Users page; on in signalith.yaml Directory sign-in on or off type ad ad or openldap; fills in the defaults marked preset url required ldaps://host[:port] or ldap://host[:port] failover_url none Tried when url cannot be reached (not when it refuses a password) start_tls false Encrypt an ldap:// connection before anything else is sent ca_cert none PEM certificate(s) of the CA that issued the server's certificate, added to the system's trusted CAs ca_cert_file none signalith.yaml only: read ca_cert from this file tls_skip_verify false Accept any certificate. Only for testing: anyone who can intercept the connection can read passwords connect_timeout_seconds 5 How long to wait for a server to answer a connection (1-120) timeout_seconds 10 How long to wait for each request (1-300) bind_dn none (anonymous) The service account that searches for users bind_password none Its password. The API never returns it, only bind_password_set. Leave it empty to keep the saved one, which only works while url, failover_url, bind_dn, start_tls, tls_skip_verify and ca_cert are unchanged. In signalith.yaml, SIGNALITH_LDAP_BIND_PASSWORD can provide it instead user_base_dn required Where to search for users user_filter preset LDAP filter with {username} for the typed name (escaped, so * and ( match only themselves) username_attribute preset Attribute holding the username: sAMAccountName, uid name_attribute, email_attribute preset displayName or cn; mail group_search preset memberof (read the user's memberOf) or search (search with group_filter) nested_groups true for ad Count groups inside groups (Active Directory only) group_base_dn the whole domain Where to search for groups (nested groups and search). Empty uses the DC= part of the user's DN, such as DC=corp,DC=example,DC=com group_filter preset Filter for search, with {dn} and/or {username} admin_groups, analyst_groups, viewer_groups none Group DNs whose members get each role; the highest wins. Compared the way the directory compares DNs (case and spacing do not matter) default_role none Role for users in no mapped group: none refuses them, viewer lets them in as viewers

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
Start with Test connection and Test a user; their messages name the problem. Every sign-in failure is also in the server log with the reason (see Audit log).

"The server's TLS certificate is not trusted." Paste the certificate of the CA that issued the directory server's certificate (for Active Directory, usually the enterprise root CA, exported as Base-64) under CA certificate.

"The server's TLS certificate is for dc1.corp.example.com, not 10.0.0.5." Use a name that is on the certificate in the server address, not an IP address.

"The server did not answer with TLS." The port does not speak LDAPS. Use ldaps:// with port 636, or ldap:// with port 389 and StartTLS.

"refused the connection" or "did not answer within 5 seconds". Check the address and port, and that firewalls let the Signalith server reach the directory.

"The directory refused the service account's bind DN or password." Check the full DN (not CORP\svc-signalith) and the password. Active Directory adds a reason, such as password expired or account disabled.

"The server does not allow anonymous searches." Enter a service account. Active Directory always needs one.

"The server only accepts sign-ins over an encrypted connection." Use ldaps:// or StartTLS. Active Directory with LDAP signing required refuses plain binds.

"No user matches." Check the user base DN (the user must be under it) and the user filter. With the Active Directory preset, disabled accounts are never found.

"More than one entry matches." The filter is too loose, for example two accounts with the same uid in different branches. Narrow the base DN or the filter.

A user is refused with "Your account can’t use Signalith yet". Test a user lists every group found. Map one of them to a role, or set default_role: viewer. Check that the DN in the mapping is the group's full DN. Group changes in the directory apply within about 5 minutes, or at the user's next sign-in.

Nested groups are not counted. Nested groups only work on Active Directory with Nested groups on. The groups must be under the group base DN; leave it empty to search the whole domain. For OpenLDAP, map each group directly.

"Enter the service account's password again." You changed the server address, the failover server, the bind DN or a TLS setting. The saved password is only sent to the saved servers, so type it again.

"Too many failed sign-ins." See failed sign-in limits. Wait the time shown, or sign in as another admin, from another address, or as the built-in admin if it is not the account being guessed. The log shows which address and account failed. If everyone behind one proxy or NAT gets this message, list that address as described under Many people behind one address in Signing in.

"Many wrong passwords were tried for this account, so sign-ins to it from new browsers are slowed down." Someone is guessing that account's password. Sign in from a browser you have signed in to the account with before, which is not slowed down, or wait the time shown. The log's sign-in failed lines show where the guesses come from.

"Your directory password has expired or must be changed." Active Directory accepted the password but requires a new one first. The user changes it (for example by signing in to Windows) and signs in again.

"Signalith could not reach the directory server." Sign-in with the built-in admin and local users still works. Fix the connection, or add a failover server.

A directory user who left still has access. Signed-in directory users are looked up again every 5 minutes (see Directory users who change or leave), and Basic auth credentials are checked with the directory again after at most 2 minutes. If the directory cannot be reached, they keep their access until it can. Disable them on the Users page to stop them at once.

signalith validate says to set SIGNALITH_LDAP_BIND_PASSWORD. Your shell does not have the service's environment. Load the service's environment file first, for example sudo sh -c 'set -a; . /etc/signalith/signalith.env; signalith validate -c /etc/signalith/signalith.yaml'.

docs.title: Users on several servers
docs.text: Servers that share one OpenSearch as a cluster (see servers.md) share their users too, once every one of them runs this version: the local users, the directory users seen so far, their roles and password hashes, the built-in admin's password, the directory sign-in settings and the sign-in sessions. A user added, changed, disabled or deleted on any server's Users page is the same on every server within a couple of seconds, and a session made on one server works on all of them. Give the OpenSearch user the right to create, read and write <prefix>_sessions too (or <prefix>_*).

docs.title: When the users become shared
docs.text:
• A new cluster shares them from the start.
  • Servers upgraded from an earlier version share them once every server that ran in the last 24 hours runs this version: a server of an earlier version would not see them. Until then each server keeps its own users.json, directory.json and sessions, as before, and the Users page and the Servers page say which servers still need the upgrade. A server removed for good stops counting 24 hours after it was last seen. Once the users are shared, a server of an earlier version refuses to start on this OpenSearch and says it needs a newer version.
  • Where they come from. The server that founded the cluster brings in its users, its directory settings and the built-in admin's password in use there (an admin-password-hash file from signalith passwd included), as soon as every server runs this version, whether or not it runs the background jobs. While it is down, the Servers page says the users wait for it. If it has not been seen for 7 days, the server that runs the jobs does it instead, and the Servers page names the servers whose users differed from its own. Users that only another server had are not brought in: add them again on the Users page. users.json and directory.json stay as they were, unused.
  • Sessions carry over when the users become shared: a browser signed in to a server stays signed in to it, as long as the shared users have its user as they were there (same source, role and password, enabled). The others, such as a server's own users that were not brought in, or a built-in admin whose password differed, sign in once more. A carried session works on the server that made it, until it ends as any session does (a new password, disabled, signed out, idle, 7 days) or that server stops; signing in again gives a session that works on every server.

What stays per server: auth.session_timeout (each server ends idle sessions after its own value) and the Basic auth cache. auth.admin_user is taken from the server that brought the users in; a server whose auth.admin_user differs logs a warning and uses the shared name.

Password hashes in OpenSearch. Users are kept in the <prefix>_config index, signed with the cluster key, so a user changed or added in OpenSearch outside Signalith is refused. Their bcrypt password hashes are stored as they are, not encrypted: encrypting them with the cluster key would lock everyone out after signalith cluster reset-key. Anyone who can read <prefix>_config can read the hashes, as anyone who can read Signalith's indices can read your events: give that right only to Signalith's own OpenSearch user. The directory's service account password is encrypted with the cluster key.

docs.title: Sessions on every server
docs.text:
A session cookie made by one server works on every server at once, so a load balancer needs no sticky sessions, and when a server stops, the people it served keep working on the others. Signing out, a password change or reset, disabling or deleting a user ends their sessions on every server within about 2 seconds (at most 15 seconds if a server cannot read OpenSearch meanwhile). A user has at most 50 sessions; a 51st ends the oldest.

The session cookie is a __Host- cookie, which browsers keep for exactly the address they used. Through one load balancer address, people sign in once; reaching siem-a.example.com and siem-b.example.com directly takes a sign-in on each.

docs.title: The built-in admin on several servers
docs.text:
The built-in admin has one password for every server.

  • signalith passwd on any server of the cluster changes it for every server within a few seconds, with no restart. When OpenSearch cannot be reached, or the users are not shared yet, it changes this server's files as before and says what that does on a member: a password it keeps in admin-password-hash in the state folder (the Docker quick start, or a service given the password) is used only while this server keeps its users in its own files, not as the cluster's password and not while OpenSearch is down; one it writes to auth.admin_password_hash in signalith.yaml becomes the password of every server the next time this server starts with OpenSearch available, since the file changed. Run it again once OpenSearch answers to change the cluster's password at once.
  • On the page. Signed in as the built-in admin, use Change password in the user menu, or on the built-in admin's row on the Users page. Other admins cannot change it there.
  • signalith passwd -local keeps a password on this server only. On a server that was ever a member of a cluster it is kept in admin-password-local in its state folder and works only while the shared settings cannot be used (OpenSearch down or refusing writes), within a few seconds and with no restart, so you can always sign in to fix that. It is the only break-glass password: an admin-password-hash an earlier signalith passwd wrote (as on Docker and service installs) is not used once the users are shared, so a password that leaked before does not come back while OpenSearch is down. Change or delete admin-password-local when the person who knew it should no longer have it. On a server that was never a member, -local writes admin-password-hash, which replaces the configured password at the next restart, as signalith passwd does there.
  • auth.admin_password_hash, SIGNALITH_ADMIN_PASSWORD and SIGNALITH_ADMIN_PASSWORD_FILE apply only when they change: a server that starts with a changed value sets it as the shared password and logs auth.admin_password_hash applied from the environment on siem-b. An unchanged value, such as the Docker quick start's password file, never undoes a later signalith passwd.

docs.title: Directory settings on several servers
docs.text:
The servers share one set of directory sign-in settings, which an admin can change on the Users page of any server, also when they came from auth.ldap in signalith.yaml. The page says where the settings in use came from: applied from signalith.yaml, saved on the page, brought in, or the service account password set from SIGNALITH_LDAP_BIND_PASSWORD, with the server and the time.

auth.ldap and SIGNALITH_LDAP_BIND_PASSWORD apply only when they change, like the admin password above: an unchanged signalith.yaml never undoes a change made on the page, and a server whose file differs without having changed only notes it in its heartbeat (settings_drift). SIGNALITH_LDAP_BIND_PASSWORD is used only on a server whose signalith.yaml has auth.ldap, and only while the shared settings connect to the same servers, as the same bind DN and with the same TLS settings as that file: when someone changed them on the page, a new password from the environment is not used with them, and the server logs a warning instead.

The service account's password is encrypted with the cluster key for the saved servers, bind DN and TLS settings: change any of them and it must be typed again, so it can never be sent to a server someone else chose, even by editing OpenSearch.

Signed-in directory users are looked up again every 5 minutes, and right after the settings change, by the server that runs the background jobs, for every server. The other servers ask the directory only to sign people in.

docs.title: Failed sign-in limits on several servers
docs.text: Each server counts wrong passwords, with the limits divided by the number of servers that are up, but never below 3: with two servers, 5 wrong passwords for one account from one address pause it, and 15 from one address pause the address. A pause on one server applies on every server within seconds. As on one server, an account is never locked, only slowed down for strangers, and an address under Proxies and gateways is never paused as a whole. While OpenSearch cannot be used, each server applies its own limits only.

docs.title: Changes at the same moment
docs.text: GET /api/users gives each user's version (etag), and GET /api/auth/directory the settings'. A change sent with If-Match and that version is refused with 412 when someone changed the user or the settings meanwhile; the answer says who, on which server and when, and the page says so and shows their change. Without If-Match, a change applies to the user as they are now, so a change made on another server at the same moment is kept. While a server cannot write the shared settings, changes there answer 503.

docs.title: When OpenSearch cannot be used
docs.text:
When a server cannot reach OpenSearch, or OpenSearch refuses writes because its disk is full:

  • Sessions it has already checked keep working for 5 minutes after it last confirmed them with OpenSearch.
  • Only admins can sign in, with a session or with HTTP Basic credentials: the built-in admin (with the password this server last read, or the one signalith passwd -local set), and local admins when this server's copy of the users is at most 24 hours old. Everyone else gets 503 with the code degraded, which does not count as a failed sign-in. Their session works on this server only, for at most an hour, and the log says so. Once OpenSearch takes writes again, it is stored for every server if the user is still an enabled admin whose password did not change meanwhile; otherwise it ends. Directory users and everyone else sign in again once OpenSearch is back.
  • Changes on the Users page answer 503. Last sign-ins and pauses of addresses are not shared meanwhile.

docs.title: Where user data is stored
docs.text:
File Holds Default place users.json Local users (with bcrypt password hashes), directory users seen so far, last sign-in times The lookups folder (lookups.dir), or auth.users_file / SIGNALITH_USERS_FILE directory.json Directory sign-in settings from the Users page, including the service account's password Next to users.json

The lookups folder is:

Install Folder Docker /var/lib/signalith/lookups in the signalith-data volume Linux (systemd) /var/lib/signalith/lookups Windows C:\ProgramData\Signalith\lookups Anywhere else lookups next to signalith.yaml

Both files are written with permissions 0600 (readable only by the account Signalith runs as), by writing a new file and renaming it so a crash never leaves half a file. Back them up with the rest of the lookups folder. Edit them only while Signalith is stopped.

Signalith reads directory.json at start-up. It also looks at users.json while it runs, because servers that share a lookups folder share that file (see servers.md): before every change it reads the file as it is now, and otherwise it checks for changes about once a second. While a server changes users.json it keeps a small users.json.lock file next to it; leave that file alone, it goes away by itself.

On servers that share their users, these files are only what the users were brought in from: see Users on several servers.

If users.json is damaged, Signalith refuses to start and says so. If it becomes damaged while Signalith runs, everyone signed in keeps working, but every change on the Users page fails with a message that says so. Either way, fix the file, or stop Signalith, move the file away and start Signalith again with only the built-in admin.

docs.title: Audit log
docs.text:
Signalith logs every sign-in, sign-out and change to users or directory settings to its log (journald, the Windows event log, or the container's output), with audit=true, who did it and from which address. Passwords never appear. Changes on the Settings page and restarts are logged the same way; see settings.md.

Message Fields signed in user, role, source, client, method (session or basic) sign-in failed user, client, method, reason (for example wrong password, account disabled, directory: in no group mapped to a role), locked_out (further tries are refused or slowed down for a while) sign-ins from this address are paused … client, minutes signed out user, client user created by, user, role, must_change_password user changed by, user, fields user role changed by, user, from, to user disabled, user enabled by, user, sessions_ended user deleted by, user, source, role, sessions_ended password reset by, user, sessions_ended password changed by, user, other_sessions_ended password change refused user, client, reason, locked_out directory settings changed by, enabled, servers, fields (names only) directory connection tested by, servers, bind_dn, ok directory user looked up by, user, servers, ok, code, password_checked directory user lost access by=directory, user, reason, sessions_ended directory user's role changed by=directory, user, from, to

Servers that share their users also log these:

Message Fields kept the sign-in sessions made before the users were shared kept, ended: when this server starts using the shared users (see When the users become shared) signed in while OpenSearch cannot be written; … user, method, client: a session kept on this server only (see When OpenSearch cannot be used) wrote through a session made while OpenSearch could not be written user a session made while OpenSearch could not be written ended: … user session.tamper: … session, user, node: a session in OpenSearch was changed or made outside Signalith, and is refused changed the built-in admin's password for every server of the cluster by, user (from signalith passwd) auth.admin_password_hash applied from the environment on siem-b, auth.ldap applied from signalith.yaml on siem-b setting, server

client is the address the request came from. Behind a reverse proxy listed under Trusted reverse proxies, with Client address header chosen, it is the address the proxy forwarded the request for, and peer names the proxy. When that header held no usable address, such as unknown, forwarded shows what it held, and the request counts under the proxy's own address.

For example:

level=INFO msg="user role changed" audit=true by=ann client=10.0.0.12 user=sam from=analyst to=admin
level=WARN msg="sign-in failed" audit=true user=dave client=10.0.0.40 method=session reason="directory: in no group mapped to a role" locked_out=false
level=WARN msg="sign-in failed" audit=true user=admin client=203.0.113.9 peer=10.0.0.5 method=session reason="wrong password" locked_out=false

docs.title: API
docs.text:
All routes need a signed-in user (session cookie or HTTP Basic auth) except POST /api/login, POST /api/logout, GET /api/tls/ca.pem, POST /api/ingest and POST /api/otlp/v1/logs (which take an agent token, never a session or password), and osquery's routes under /api/osquery/ (POST /api/osquery/enroll takes an agent token; the others take the node key a host got when it enrolled; see endpoints.md). Requests from a browser that change something must come from the Signalith page itself.

Every answer carries the server's version in X-Signalith-Version. Answers to signed-in requests (and to a successful sign-in) also carry X-Signalith-Config, once the server has read the shared settings. Behind a load balancer, send the X-Signalith-Config of a change's answer as X-Signalith-Config-Min on the next request, so a server that has not yet read that change reads it first (see Several servers behind one address).

docs.title: Roles of every route
docs.text:
Every role (also allowed while a password change is pending): GET /api/me, POST /api/me/password.

Viewer: GET /api/health, POST /api/search, POST /api/explain, POST /api/build, POST /api/parse, GET /api/datamodels, GET /api/fields, GET /api/fields/values, GET /api/language, GET /api/ask, GET /api/detections, GET /api/detections/{id}, GET /api/detections/{id}/yaml, GET /api/coverage, GET /api/detections/packs, GET /api/detections/content, GET /api/findings, GET /api/findings/summary, GET /api/findings/{id}, GET /api/cases, GET /api/cases/summary, GET /api/cases/{id}, GET /api/lookups/context, GET /api/lookups/{kind}, GET /api/risk, GET /api/risk/object, GET /api/intel, GET /api/intel/feeds, GET /api/intel/catalog, GET /api/intel/indicators, GET /api/intel/lookup, GET /api/posture, GET /api/dashboards, GET /api/dashboards/{id}, GET /api/dashboards/{id}/yaml, POST /api/dashboards/{id}/run, POST /api/panels/run, and the web UI.

Analyst: POST /api/ask, POST /api/findings, POST /api/findings/bulk, PATCH /api/findings/{id}, POST /api/cases, PATCH /api/cases/{id}, POST /api/cases/{id}/findings, DELETE /api/cases/{id}/findings/{fid}, POST /api/cases/{id}/entries, DELETE /api/cases/{id}/entries/{entry}, POST /api/cases/{id}/entities, POST /api/dashboards, PUT /api/dashboards/{id}, DELETE /api/dashboards/{id}, POST /api/dashboards/{id}/panels, POST /api/intel/indicators, DELETE /api/intel/indicators/{id}, GET /api/endpoints, GET /api/endpoints/{id}, GET /api/endpoints/settings, GET /api/endpoints/checks, GET /api/vulns, GET /api/vulns/hosts/{id} (what vulnerability scans found), GET /api/respond/actions, GET /api/respond/runs, POST /api/respond/run (running response actions), GET /api/playbooks/runs, POST /api/playbooks/runs/{id}/approve, POST /api/playbooks/runs/{id}/reject (the Approvals page; see playbooks.md), GET /api/agent-tokens (the names, status and use of the agent tokens, never a secret), GET /api/agents (the agents that send events, shown on the Endpoints page), GET /api/investigate, POST /api/findings/{id}/investigate/preview, POST /api/findings/{id}/investigate (Investigate with AI, once an admin turns it on).

Admin: GET /api/agents/config, POST /api/agent-tokens, PATCH /api/agent-tokens/{id}, POST /api/agent-tokens/{id}/revoke, POST /api/agent-tokens/legacy/{id}/refuse, POST /api/agent-tokens/legacy/{id}/accept (see agent-tokens.md), POST /api/tls/names, GET /api/security, POST /api/security/ca, POST /api/detections, POST /api/detections/test, POST /api/detections/sigma, POST /api/detections/enable, POST /api/detections/{id}/exceptions, DELETE /api/detections/{id}/exceptions/{exception}, POST /api/findings/{id}/suppress, PUT /api/detections/{id}, DELETE /api/detections/{id}, POST /api/detections/{id}/run, POST /api/detections/content/check, POST /api/detections/content/upload, DELETE /api/detections/content, PUT /api/lookups/{kind}, POST /api/intel/feeds, PUT /api/intel/feeds/{name}, DELETE /api/intel/feeds/{name}, POST /api/intel/feeds/test, POST /api/intel/feeds/{name}/refresh, POST /api/intel/catalog, POST /api/intel/taxii/collections, POST /api/intel/upload, GET /api/respond/config, PUT /api/respond/config, POST /api/respond/test (setting up response actions), GET /api/playbooks, PUT /api/playbooks (the Playbooks page; see playbooks.md), GET /api/sample, POST /api/sample/load, POST /api/sample/remove (the one-click sample data), PUT /api/endpoints/settings, DELETE /api/endpoints/{id}, GET /api/endpoints/blocked, DELETE /api/endpoints/blocked/{host}, POST /api/endpoints/queries, GET /api/endpoints/queries/{id} (the Endpoints page), GET /api/vulns/setup, PUT /api/vulns/settings, POST /api/vulns/networks/{id}/scan, POST /api/vulns/scans/{id}/stop (setting up and running vulnerability scans), GET /api/cluster (the Servers page; see servers.md), POST /api/cluster/restart (restart servers one at a time to apply the shared settings), GET /api/requests/{id} (work asked of the server that runs the background jobs, such as a feed download or a retention run; see servers.md), every /api/notify route (the Notifications page; see notifications.md), every /api/retention route (see retention.md), every /api/users and /api/auth/directory route below, and every /api/settings route (GET and PUT /api/settings, POST /api/settings/test/opensearch, POST /api/settings/test/assistant, POST /api/settings/restart, GET /api/settings/export; see settings.md).

A route added without a role is admin-only, and a test fails until it gets one. That includes routes registered outside the role table, straight on the server's outer router: any /api/ route there other than the public ones (sign-in, sign-out, agent ingest and the CA certificate, GET /api/tls/ca.pem) is admin-only.

A refused request:

{"error": "This needs the Analyst role, and your role is Viewer. Ask an admin if you need access.",
 "code": "forbidden", "role": "viewer", "required": "analyst"}

docs.title: The signed-in user
docs.text:
GET /api/me, and the reply to POST /api/login:

{"username": "jlee", "user": "jlee", "name": "Jordan Lee", "email": "",
 "role": "analyst", "role_label": "Analyst", "source": "local",
 "must_change_password": true, "can_change_password": true, "auth": "session"}

source is builtin, local or directory; auth is session or basic.

POST /api/me/password with {"current_password": "...", "new_password": "..."} returns the same object. Errors are 400 with a code: wrong_password (field current_password), same_password, invalid_password (field new_password), builtin or directory (those passwords are changed elsewhere). On servers that share their users, the built-in admin may change its own password here too (can_change_password says so), and the answer sets a new session cookie: the password change ended every session of the user, this one's too.

docs.title: Users (admin)
docs.text:
GET /api/users:

{
  "users": [
    {"username": "admin", "name": "", "email": "", "role": "admin", "source": "builtin",
     "disabled": false, "must_change_password": false, "created": null, "updated": null,
     "last_sign_in": "2026-10-12T15:35:22Z", "you": true, "actions": []},
    {"username": "alice", "name": "Alice Admin", "email": "alice@corp.example.com",
     "role": "admin", "source": "directory", "disabled": false, "must_change_password": false,
     "dn": "CN=Alice Admin,OU=Staff,DC=corp,DC=example,DC=com",
     "created": "2026-10-12T15:35:11Z", "updated": "2026-10-12T15:35:11Z",
     "last_sign_in": "2026-10-12T15:35:11Z", "you": false, "actions": ["disable", "delete"]}
  ],
  "roles": [{"id": "viewer", "label": "Viewer", "description": "..."}, ...],
  "directory": {"enabled": true, "from_config": false},
  "shared": false,
  "shared_pending": null
}

Each user also has etag, its version for If-Match. On servers that share their users, shared is true and last_sign_in_server names the server of the last sign-in. On a server of a cluster whose users are not shared yet, shared_pending says why: {"version": "1.6.0", "servers": [{"name": "siem-b", "version": "1.5.0"}]} lists the servers whose version must be upgraded first, and an empty servers means the users wait to be brought in (see When the users become shared).

actions lists what the signed-in admin may do to that user: edit (name and email), role, reset_password, disable or enable, and delete; and, on the built-in admin's own row when the users are shared, change_password (with POST /api/me/password). A directory user the directory no longer lets in has "role": "" and "refused" saying why, for example "in no group mapped to a role".

Route Body Reply POST /api/users {"username", "name", "email", "role", "password", "must_change_password"}; only username is required. role defaults to viewer, an empty password makes one up, must_change_password defaults to true 201 {"user": {...}, "temporary_password": "kqpp-bsqy-b6hq-mwfm"} (temporary_password only when made up) PUT /api/users/{username} Any of {"name", "email", "role", "disabled"} {"user": {...}} POST /api/users/{username}/password Optional {"password"} {"user": {...}, "temporary_password": "..."} DELETE /api/users/{username} {"deleted": "priya"}

Errors are {"error": "..."}, with "field" naming the form field when one value is the problem (username, name, email, role, password): 400 for a bad value, 404 for an unknown user, 409 for a taken name, the built-in admin, a change to your own account, the last admin, or a directory user's name, email, role or password.

PUT and DELETE /api/users/{username} and POST /api/users/{username}/password take an optional If-Match header with the user's etag. When the user changed since, they answer 412; on servers that share their users the answer says who changed it, where and when:

{"error": "it was changed on siem-b by ann at 2026-10-14T09:12:03Z; reload it", "code": "stale",
 "changed_by": "ann", "changed_on": "siem-b", "changed_at": "2026-10-14T09:12:03Z"}

While a server cannot write the shared settings, changes answer 503.

docs.title: Directory sign-in (admin)
docs.text:
GET /api/auth/directory (and the reply to a successful PUT):

{
  "settings": {"enabled": true, "type": "ad", "url": "ldaps://dc1.corp.example.com",
               "failover_url": "", "start_tls": false, "ca_cert": "", "tls_skip_verify": false,
               "connect_timeout_seconds": 5, "timeout_seconds": 10,
               "bind_dn": "CN=svc-signalith,OU=Service Accounts,DC=corp,DC=example,DC=com",
               "bind_password_set": true,
               "user_base_dn": "DC=corp,DC=example,DC=com", "user_filter": "(&(objectCategory=person)...)",
               "username_attribute": "sAMAccountName", "name_attribute": "displayName",
               "email_attribute": "mail", "group_search": "memberof", "nested_groups": true,
               "group_base_dn": "", "group_filter": "",
               "admin_groups": ["CN=Signalith Admins,OU=Groups,DC=corp,DC=example,DC=com"],
               "analyst_groups": [], "viewer_groups": [], "default_role": "none"},
  "from_config": false,
  "warnings": [],
  "presets": {"ad": {...}, "openldap": {...}},
  "directory_users": 3
}

from_config is true when the settings come from signalith.yaml on a server that keeps them in its own files; config_file then names the file, and PUT answers 409. etag is the settings' version for If-Match on PUT (412 when they changed since). from says where the settings in use came from: {"source": "yaml", "node": "siem-a", "at": "..."}, with source yaml, page, import (the first server's files, when the servers began sharing users) or env (the service account password from SIGNALITH_LDAP_BIND_PASSWORD changed); node and at are given on servers that share their users, where shared is true.

PUT /api/auth/directory takes the settings object (with bind_password instead of bind_password_set; leave it empty to keep the saved one). Settings that need fixing answer 400:

{"error": "Some settings need fixing: ...",
 "problems": ["\"http://x\" must be ldaps://host or ldap://host, with an optional :port and nothing after it"],
 "fields": {"url": "\"http://x\" must be ldaps://host or ldap://host, with an optional :port and nothing after it"}}

POST /api/auth/directory/test with an optional {"settings": {...}} (the unsaved form; the saved settings when left out):

{"ok": true, "message": "Connected and signed in as the service account.",
 "servers": [{"url": "ldaps://dc1.corp.example.com", "ok": true,
              "message": "Connected to dc1.corp.example.com over TLS 1.3.",
              "steps": [{"step": "connect", "ok": true, "message": "Connected to dc1.corp.example.com over TLS 1.3."},
                        {"step": "bind", "ok": true, "message": "Signed in as CN=svc-signalith,..."},
                        {"step": "user_base", "ok": true, "message": "Found DC=corp,DC=example,DC=com."}]}]}

A failed server has "ok": false, a code (connect, tls_untrusted, tls_hostname, tls_expired, tls_handshake, starttls_refused, ca_cert, encryption_required, bind_refused, bind_failed, bind_required, base_not_found, search_refused, search_failed), a plain message and the technical detail.

POST /api/auth/directory/test-user with {"username": "alice", "password": "...", "settings": {...}} (password and settings optional):

{"ok": true, "message": "alice would sign in as Admin. The password was not checked.",
 "user": {"username": "alice", "dn": "CN=Alice Admin,OU=Staff,DC=corp,DC=example,DC=com",
          "name": "Alice Admin", "email": "alice@corp.example.com",
          "groups": ["CN=All Staff,OU=Groups,DC=corp,DC=example,DC=com",
                     "CN=IT Leads,OU=Groups,DC=corp,DC=example,DC=com",
                     "CN=Signalith Admins,OU=Groups,DC=corp,DC=example,DC=com"],
          "matched_groups": ["CN=Signalith Admins,OU=Groups,DC=corp,DC=example,DC=com"],
          "role": "admin"},
 "password_checked": false}

When the user would be refused, ok is false and code is user_not_found, multiple_matches, wrong_password, password_expired, no_role, refused, or one of the connection codes above. warning is added when the name belongs to the built-in admin or a local user, since sign-in would then never ask the directory.

docs.title: Vulnerability scanning
docs.text:
Signalith scans the networks you list with Nmap, the free and open-source network scanner, on a schedule or when you click Scan now. Each scan finds the hosts that are up, their open ports and the software that answers on each port, then matches the software versions to known vulnerabilities (CVEs) from the U.S. National Vulnerability Database (NVD).

Everything is on the Vulnerabilities page (under Monitor):

  • Hosts: every host the latest scans found up, worst first. Hosts with a CVE that attackers are known to use come first, then by the highest CVSS score. Open a host to see its open ports, the software on each, and the CVEs that apply, with a link to each CVE in the NVD.
  • Networks: what is scanned and when, the scan running now and how far it is, and Scan now and Stop.
  • Scans: the last 200 scans, how long each took, what it found, and why one failed.
  • Scanner setup (admins): what scanning needs, whether this server has it, why, and how to fix anything missing.

Analysts can see the results. Only admins can add networks, start or stop scans, and see the scanner setup.

docs.title: Getting started
docs.text:
1. Open Vulnerabilities. The first time, the page checks the server and lists what scanning needs, with the reason for each and how to fix anything marked red.
  2. Install Nmap if the check says it is missing (see What scanning needs). Click Check again; no restart is needed.
  3. Click Add a network. Give it a name, list its addresses, pick the ports and when to scan, and confirm that you may scan it.
  4. Click Scan now, or wait for its schedule. A /24 network with the 1,000 most common ports usually takes a few minutes.

Only scan networks you own or have permission to scan. Scanning other people's networks can be against the law, and the page asks you to confirm before it adds a network.

docs.title: What scanning needs
docs.text:
What Why Needed Nmap 7.80 or later on the scanning server Finds hosts, open ports and software versions Yes Nmap can run a test scan Makes sure Nmap works under the account Signalith runs as Yes Outbound HTTPS to services.nvd.nist.gov Looks software versions up in the NVD to name the CVEs No: without it, scans still list hosts, ports and software An NVD API key Makes the first lookups about ten times faster No

Install Nmap:

  • Docker quick start: Signalith's container image includes Nmap. Pull the latest image (docker compose -f deploy/docker/docker-compose.yml pull, then up -d).
  • Debian and Ubuntu: sudo apt install nmap. The .deb package recommends it, so apt installs it with Signalith unless recommended packages are turned off.
  • Red Hat, Rocky, Alma and Fedora: sudo dnf install nmap.
  • Windows: download the latest stable installer (nmap-…-setup.exe) from https://nmap.org/download.html#windows, run it as an administrator and keep the default choices, including Npcap.

Signalith looks for Nmap on the PATH and where its installers put it (C:\Program Files (x86)\Nmap\nmap.exe on Windows, /usr/bin/nmap and /usr/local/bin/nmap on Linux). If it is somewhere else, set SIGNALITH_NMAP to its full path for the Signalith service.

Nmap's licence (the Nmap Public Source License) does not allow Signalith to ship it inside its own Windows installer or Linux packages, so it is installed on its own. Signalith only runs it as a separate program.

docs.title: CVE lookups and privacy
docs.text:
For each product a scan finds with a version, such as OpenSSH 8.2p1, Signalith asks the NVD's CVE API for the CVEs of that product (openbsd openssh) and compares the version with each CVE's affected versions itself. Only product names are sent: never addresses, host names or anything else about your network. Answers are kept in OpenSearch for a day, so later scans of the same software ask nothing.

Without an API key the NVD allows 5 requests every 30 seconds, so a first scan that finds a lot of different software takes a few extra minutes. A free key from https://nvd.nist.gov/developers/request-an-api-key makes it about ten times faster. Enter it as NVD API key in Settings, on the Server tab under Vulnerability scans: it is kept encrypted, never shown again, and used from the next lookup with no restart. It can also come from the SIGNALITH_NVD_API_KEY environment variable of the Signalith service (or a file named by SIGNALITH_NVD_API_KEY_FILE), or from vulns.nvd_api_key in signalith.yaml (signalith secrets set vulns.nvd_api_key stores it encrypted). If the server reaches the internet through a proxy, set HTTPS_PROXY for the service.

To look CVEs up in a copy of the NVD's CVE API 2.0 on your own network instead, set CVE database address in the same place (or SIGNALITH_NVD_URL).

When the NVD cannot be reached, a scan still lists hosts, ports and software, uses CVE answers kept from the last 30 days, and says on the Scans tab that lookups failed. Turn lookups off altogether in Scanner setup.

The NVD also says which CVEs are in CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog. Those are marked Exploited on the page, counted on their own, and raise their own finding: attackers are using them now, so patch them first.

docs.title: Networks
docs.text:
Setting What it does Addresses to scan One per line: an address (192.168.1.20), a network up to a /16 (192.168.1.0/24), a range in the last part of an address (10.0.5.10-50) or a host name. IPv6 networks can be up to a /112. Addresses to skip Addresses, networks or names never to scan, such as fragile devices. Ports The 100 or the 1,000 most common TCP ports (the default), all 65,535, or a list such as 22,80,443,8000-8100. When Every day or every week at an hour you pick, or only when you click Scan now. Times are in the scanning server's time zone. The default is every day at 01:00. Gentle mode Scans slowly, one probe at a time and at most 20 packets a second, with only the likeliest version probes. For networks with fragile devices such as old printers or building controllers. It takes several times longer. Scan on schedule Off pauses the scheduled scans; Scan now still works.

Each scan replaces its network's hosts with what it found: a host that is no longer up leaves the list (its earlier results stay in Search). A scan stops after 12 hours; split a network that takes longer, or scan fewer ports.

docs.title: How Nmap is run
docs.text:
Scans use TCP connect scans (nmap -sT --unprivileged -sV --open), which work the same on Windows and Linux, under any account, with no packet capture driver, raw sockets or administrator rights. -sV asks each open port which software and version answers. Hosts count as up when they answer on any of a few common ports (SSH, SMB, RDP, the web ports), which also finds Windows hosts that do not answer ping. Only TCP is scanned.

The addresses, ports and options come only from the checked settings above: nothing you type reaches Nmap's command line as an option.

docs.title: Results in Search, detections and assets
docs.text:
Each finished scan writes events to the Vulnerabilities data model: one per open port (category=open_port) and one per CVE (category=vulnerability), with dest, dest_ip, dest_port, app, product, product_version, cve, cvss, severity, known_exploited and a url to the CVE in the NVD. They carry signalith_intake=scanner. For example:

datamodel=Vulnerabilities category=vulnerability known_exploited=true | stats dc(cve) as cves by dest | sort -cves
datamodel=Vulnerabilities category=open_port app=rdp | table dest, dest_ip, product_version

The built-in Vulnerabilities dashboard (dashboards.md) sums them up over the last 7 days.

The Ask box understands questions such as "hosts with known exploited vulnerabilities" or "top CVEs".

Three built-in detections use them (see detections.md): a CVE in the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog (high), a critical CVE (CVSS 9.0 or more, medium), and Telnet open (low). Each fires once a week at most for the same host and CVE.

Hosts the scans find are added to the asset list as category=scanned, so searches and findings show them with asset context, unless your own list or the Endpoints page already has them.

docs.title: Several servers
docs.text: When several Signalith servers share one OpenSearch (servers.md), scans run on the server that runs the background jobs, and Scanner setup shows that server's own check of itself. Networks, scans and results are kept in OpenSearch (<prefix>_vulns), so every server shows the same ones. A scanner for each network zone is planned for later.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
• "Nmap was not found": install it as above. On Windows, a service only sees a PATH change after a restart, which is why Signalith also looks in Nmap's install folder.
  • The test scan fails: run nmap -sT -p 1 127.0.0.1 as the account Signalith runs as to see the whole error. On Windows, reinstall Nmap as an administrator with Npcap.
  • No hosts were up: check the addresses, and that the scanning server can reach that network (a firewall between them, or Docker's network on a Docker install).
  • Software but no CVEs: either the version has no known CVEs, Nmap could not tell the version, or lookups failed (the Scans tab says so).

docs.title: Wazuh alerts
docs.text: If you already run Wazuh, Signalith can take in the alerts your Wazuh manager raises. They are mapped onto Signalith's data models, so logons from Wazuh show up next to logons from Fluent Bit, file integrity alerts land in Filesystem, configuration assessment results in Configuration_Check, antivirus alerts in Malware, and everything else in Alerts. Detections, dashboards and searches work on them like on any other event.

docs.title: What to know first
docs.text:
• Wazuh agents keep reporting to a Wazuh manager. Wazuh agents only talk to a Wazuh manager, over Wazuh's own encrypted protocol, and Signalith does not speak it. Signalith takes the alerts from the manager, so you keep the manager (and its rules, decoders and agent enrollment) running.
  • Alerts, not every event. The manager writes an alert when an event matches one of its rules at or above its alert level (log_alert_level, 3 by default). Events that match no rule stay on the manager and are not sent.
  • New alerts only. Alerts raised before you set this up are not sent.

There are two ways to send alerts. Use Fluent Bit unless you cannot install anything on the manager.
